definition: to leave behind completely, or to give up entirely
examples: Settlers abandoned the village after the river changed course and flooded their fields every spring.
The team abandoned the experiment when the equipment repeatedly failed during testing.
cloze: After years of drought, farmers began to {{abandon}} their land and move to the cities.
mnemonic: A BAND of travelers leaves the camp behind: a-BAND-on.

definition: to become less intense or widespread
examples: The storm abated after midnight, and the ferries resumed service.
Her anxiety abated once the exam results were posted online.
cloze: Public anger did not {{abate}} even after the minister apologized.
mnemonic: A BAT flew away and the noise ABATED: it died down.

definition: to formally give up a throne or responsibility
examples: The king chose to abdicate rather than risk a civil war that would divide the country.
Parents who abdicate their responsibilities often leave their children without guidance or stable support.
cloze: The monarch was pressured to {{abdicate}} in favor of his young nephew.
mnemonic: AB-DICATE: 'dictate away' your power.

definition: departing from what is normal or expected
examples: The aberrant results in the third trial led the team to recheck their equipment.
His aberrant behavior at the party worried friends who knew him as calm.
cloze: Scientists discarded the {{aberrant}} data point because it differed wildly from every other measurement.
mnemonic: ABerrant: wandering AWAY from the path (Latin errare, to stray).

definition: a departure from what is normal, expected, or typical
examples: The warm week in January was an aberration in an otherwise freezing winter.
Her rude outburst was an aberration; she is usually unfailingly polite.
cloze: The student's failing grade was an {{aberration}}, since he had earned top marks all year.
mnemonic: ABERRATION: a mind that ERRs from the normal path.

definition: a state of temporary inactivity or suspension
examples: The plan has been held in abeyance until funds become available.
Construction remained in abeyance while the court reviewed the permit.
cloze: The old law fell into {{abeyance}} and was rarely enforced after the reforms.
mnemonic: ABEYANCE: 'a-bay-ance', a ship waiting in the bay.

definition: to regard with disgust and hatred
examples: She abhors cruelty to animals and campaigns against it at every opportunity she gets.
Many people abhor the idea of lying under any circumstances, even to protect feelings.
cloze: He would {{abhor}} any plan that required cheating his customers.
mnemonic: AB-HOR: 'a horror' of something.

definition: extremely bad, humble, or hopeless
examples: Thousands lived in abject poverty without clean water or shelter.
He offered an abject apology, begging forgiveness for his mistake.
cloze: The refugees' {{abject}} misery moved the whole town to donate food and clothing.
mnemonic: ABJECT: thrown (ject) down (ab) to the lowest point.

definition: to solemnly renounce or give up a belief or practice
examples: He abjured his former extremist views and urged others to do the same.
The king was forced to abjure his claim to the throne.
cloze: Before joining the order, the monks must {{abjure}} wealth and personal possessions.
mnemonic: AB-JURE: swear (jur = oath) AWAY from something.

definition: honest and open, with nothing hidden
examples: The negotiations were aboveboard, and every party saw the complete financial records.
She insisted the hiring process be aboveboard so no candidate felt cheated.
cloze: The auditor praised the firm's {{aboveboard}} handling of the contract bids.
mnemonic: Above the board (table), not under it: nothing hidden.

definition: to shorten a text while keeping its main content
examples: The publisher decided to abridge the lengthy novel for younger readers.
An abridged edition of the dictionary fits on a single shelf.
cloze: Editors will {{abridge}} the long speech to fit within the allotted broadcast time.
mnemonic: A-BRIDGE: a bridge makes the trip shorter.

definition: to repeal or abolish formally
examples: The new government moved to abrogate the unpopular treaty signed by its predecessors years ago.
Lawmakers voted to abrogate the old regulation that had restricted trade between the two regions.
cloze: No ruler has the power to {{abrogate}} the constitution without the consent of the people.
mnemonic: AB-ROGATE: 'rogate' = ask; undo what was asked, so repeal.

definition: to declare someone free from blame or guilt
examples: The investigation absolved the pilot of any responsibility for the crash that had killed many.
The priest absolved him of his sins after hearing a long and tearful confession.
cloze: Evidence from the security camera helped {{absolve}} the accused of the crime.
mnemonic: AB-SOLVE: solve the guilt away.

definition: to deliberately refrain from doing something
examples: She chose to abstain from voting because she felt unqualified to decide.
Patients were told to abstain from alcohol while taking the medication.
cloze: Several members will {{abstain}} from the vote rather than take either side.
mnemonic: ABSTAIN: hold (tain) yourself away (abs).

definition: moderate in eating and drinking
examples: The abstemious monk ate only one small meal a day.
Though wealthy, he led an abstemious life and rarely drank wine.
cloze: Her {{abstemious}} habits meant that she skipped dessert at every dinner party.
mnemonic: ABSTEMIOUS: abstains from 'temi' (wine); moderate.

definition: existing as an idea rather than as a physical thing
examples: Justice is an abstract concept that cannot be touched or measured directly.
The painter moved from realistic portraits to abstract shapes and bold colors in her later work.
cloze: Students often find it hard to grasp {{abstract}} ideas until they see concrete examples.
mnemonic: Think 'ab-STRACT' = pulled away (tract) from real things.

definition: difficult to understand; obscure
examples: The professor's abstruse lecture on topology left most first-year students completely lost.
Few readers could follow the abstruse philosophical argument in the final chapter.
cloze: Because the treatise was so {{abstruse}}, even specialists needed a commentary to follow it.
mnemonic: ABSTRUSE sounds like 'abstract + obtuse': too hard to grasp.

definition: existing in large quantities; more than enough
examples: Abundant rainfall in the valley allowed farmers to grow rice twice a year.
Fossils are abundant in these limestone cliffs, attracting paleontologists from around the world.
cloze: Coastal waters rich in nutrients support an {{abundant}} supply of fish.
mnemonic: A BUNDle of food: a-BUNDant means loads.

definition: extremely bad; appallingly poor
examples: The team's abysmal performance left the coach speechless and the fans furious.
Conditions in the abandoned hostel were abysmal, with no heat and broken windows.
cloze: The restaurant's {{abysmal}} service drove away even its most loyal customers.
mnemonic: ABYSS-mal: a performance so bad it sank into an abyss.

definition: to agree to a demand or request
examples: After weeks of pressure, the company acceded to the union's demands.
He acceded to his wife's wish to move closer to her family.
cloze: The prince will {{accede}} to the throne when his father steps down.
mnemonic: ACCEDE: go (cede) toward what's asked.

definition: an award or expression of praise
examples: The film won many accolades, including awards for best director and best actor.
Receiving the highest accolade in her profession brought her to tears.
cloze: The young architect earned an {{accolade}} from critics for her daring museum design.
mnemonic: ACCOLADE: 'a-collar-lade', a knight tapped on the neck with praise.

definition: gradual accumulation or growth by addition
examples: The island formed through the slow accretion of sand and sediment.
The accretion of small habits shaped his character over time.
cloze: Centuries of {{accretion}} had turned the small village into a sprawling city.
mnemonic: ACCRETION: to 'accrue' or crescent grow, bit by bit.

definition: to gradually gather or build up over time
examples: Sediment accumulates at the river mouth, slowly forming a fertile delta.
Over decades, the museum accumulated a vast collection of rare manuscripts.
cloze: Dust and ash can {{accumulate}} on the ground for months after a volcanic eruption.
mnemonic: ACCUMulate sounds like ACCUMULATor: it stores up.

definition: correct and exact in every detail
examples: Early maps were rarely accurate because explorers had no reliable way to measure longitude.
The new instrument gives more accurate readings of ocean temperature than older devices.
cloze: Historians rely on {{accurate}} records to reconstruct events from centuries ago.
mnemonic: ACCURATE = A CURE for errors.

definition: sharp and biting in tone or taste
examples: The critic's acerbic review mocked every performance in the production.
Her acerbic wit made colleagues careful about what they said in meetings.
cloze: The columnist is known for {{acerbic}} commentary that leaves politicians stinging.
mnemonic: ACERbic sounds like 'acid': sour and cutting.

definition: the highest point or peak of achievement or development
examples: The violinist's career reached its acme with a sold-out concert at the national hall.
For many climbers, summiting Everest is the acme of mountaineering ambition.
cloze: The empire's {{acme}} came under its third emperor, after which decline slowly set in.
mnemonic: ACMEs look like ACNE coming to a HEAD at the very top.

definition: to accept or comply without protest
examples: After a long argument, he finally acquiesced to his sister's demands.
The board acquiesced to the union's request for shorter working hours.
cloze: Rather than start a quarrel, she chose to {{acquiesce}} and let them have their way.
mnemonic: ACQUIESCE: 'a quiet yes' without a fight.

definition: to obtain or gain something through effort or purchase
examples: Children acquire their first language simply by listening to the people around them.
The gallery acquired several rare paintings at an auction last autumn.
cloze: Students must {{acquire}} basic research skills before beginning their thesis projects.
mnemonic: A-QUIRE: you ask (inquire) and then get it.

definition: to declare formally that someone is not guilty
examples: The jury acquitted the defendant after only two hours of careful deliberation.
Lack of reliable evidence led the court to acquit the businessman of fraud.
cloze: After reviewing the video, the panel voted to {{acquit}} the accused of all charges.
mnemonic: A-QUIT: the charges quit; he walks free.

definition: bitterness or harshness in manner or speech
examples: The divorce proceedings were marked by acrimony and constant legal battles.
Their debate descended into acrimony, with each side hurling insults.
cloze: The negotiations ended in {{acrimony}}, and neither side would speak to the other afterward.
mnemonic: ACRImony: ACRID, sour feelings.

definition: keen insight and quick judgment
examples: Her business acumen turned a small shop into a national chain.
The detective's acumen allowed him to notice details others overlooked.
cloze: With remarkable political {{acumen}}, she anticipated her rivals' moves before they made them.
mnemonic: ACUMEN: 'a cue-men' who spots every cue; ACUte mind.

definition: refusing to change one's mind; unyielding
examples: She was adamant that the report be submitted before the deadline.
Despite pleas from his family, he remained adamant about leaving the company.
cloze: The senator was {{adamant}} in her refusal to compromise on the budget bill.
mnemonic: ADAMANT: like a diamond (adamas), unbreakable.

definition: to change in order to suit new conditions
examples: Many desert plants have adapted to survive with very little water.
When the lecture moved online, students quickly adapted to the new format.
cloze: Species that cannot {{adapt}} to a warming climate may face extinction.
mnemonic: ADAPT = ADjust and APT (suited) to new surroundings.

definition: very skilled at something
examples: She became adept at repairing engines after years in her father's garage.
He is adept at turning difficult negotiations into friendly conversations.
cloze: Even as a child, she was {{adept}} at solving puzzles that stumped adults.
mnemonic: ADEPT: 'a deft' person with expert hands.

definition: enough in quantity or good enough in quality for a purpose
examples: The village lacked adequate clean water, which led to frequent illness.
Her grade was adequate to pass the course, but she hoped for higher.
cloze: Without {{adequate}} sleep, students often struggle to concentrate during morning lectures.
mnemonic: ADEQUATE: A DEcent QUAntity is enough.

definition: next to or very near something else
examples: The laboratory is adjacent to the library, so researchers can easily consult books.
Ancient farmers cleared forest in adjacent valleys to expand their cropland.
cloze: The earthquake damaged buildings in the epicenter and in several {{adjacent}} towns.
mnemonic: ADJACENT: Add-Jacent, 'jacent' lies next to it.

definition: to hear and formally settle a dispute or claim
examples: A retired judge was hired to adjudicate the dispute between the two landlords.
The committee will adjudicate all complaints about the contest before announcing a winner.
cloze: An independent panel will {{adjudicate}} the claim and issue a binding ruling next month.
mnemonic: AD + JUDGE: to act as the judge.

definition: to warn or reprimand gently but firmly
examples: The teacher admonished the students to stop talking during the test.
Her doctor admonished her to cut back on salt and sugar.
cloze: The judge will {{admonish}} the jury not to discuss the case with anyone.
mnemonic: AD-MONISH: you are given a MONITOR's warning.

definition: giving a warning or gentle reproof
examples: Her admonitory glance told the children to stop whispering during the concert.
The coach delivered an admonitory speech about the dangers of overconfidence before the final.
cloze: The teacher's {{admonitory}} tone warned the class that further pranks would be punished.
mnemonic: Admonish: an admonitory note admonishes you.

definition: clever or skillful, especially under pressure
examples: The adroit negotiator turned a tense dispute into a profitable deal within a single afternoon.
She was adroit at dodging awkward questions from reporters without ever seeming evasive.
cloze: With {{adroit}} footwork, the dancer avoided every obstacle on the crowded stage.
mnemonic: ADROIT: sounds like 'a droit' (right) hand, skillful.

definition: excessive praise or flattery
examples: The pop star basked in the adulation of thousands of screaming fans.
He grew arrogant after years of unquestioning adulation from his staff.
cloze: Politicians who crave {{adulation}} often surround themselves with people who only say yes.
mnemonic: ADULation: 'adult-ation', fans treating you like a god.

definition: to make impure by adding inferior substances
examples: Dishonest merchants sometimes adulterate milk by adding water to stretch their supply and profit.
The report claimed that the spices had been adulterated with cheap filler before reaching stores.
cloze: It is illegal to {{adulterate}} food products with unlisted ingredients.
mnemonic: ADULTERATE: related to 'adultery', corrupting what was pure.

definition: a state of hardship or misfortune
examples: She overcame adversity, growing up poor but still finishing college with high honors.
Strong friendships often form during times of adversity, when people must rely on each other.
cloze: The team showed resilience in the face of {{adversity}}, winning despite injuries to key players.
mnemonic: ADVERSity: an ADVERSE situation.

definition: to publicly support or recommend a cause
examples: The mayor advocates building more bike lanes across the city.
Doctors advocate regular exercise as part of a healthy lifestyle.
cloze: Environmental groups continue to {{advocate}} stronger limits on carbon emissions.
mnemonic: ADVOCATE: a VOICE (voc) called TO a cause.

definition: a person who has refined appreciation of beauty and art
examples: The aesthete spent hours in the gallery admiring a single watercolor.
As a devoted aesthete, he refused to live in any room lacking elegant proportions.
cloze: Only an {{aesthete}} would rearrange the furniture because the colors clashed slightly.
mnemonic: AESTHETE sounds like 'S-THEE-t': someone who sees beauty everywhere.

definition: relating to beauty and how we appreciate it
examples: The architect cared more about aesthetic appeal than about whether the building was practical to use.
Visitors admired the aesthetic harmony of the garden's carefully balanced colors and shapes.
cloze: The painter's {{aesthetic}} sense led her to arrange every object in the room with care.
mnemonic: AESTHETIC: sounds like 'ass-thet-ick', sense of beauty.

definition: friendly, good-natured, and easy to talk to
examples: The affable host greeted every guest with a warm smile.
Her affable manner made even strangers feel immediately at ease.
cloze: The shopkeeper was so {{affable}} that customers lingered just to chat with him.
mnemonic: AFFABLE: you can AFFord to talk, he's so able to be friendly.

definition: having plenty of money; wealthy and prosperous
examples: The affluent suburb boasted gated mansions, private tennis courts, and a yacht club.
Growing up in an affluent family, she never worried about tuition or rent.
cloze: Only the most {{affluent}} residents could afford the penthouses overlooking the harbor.
mnemonic: Money FLOWS in: af-FLU-ent, like a flowing river of cash.

definition: to provide or give; to make available
examples: The balcony affords a sweeping view of the harbor at sunrise.
A long walk through the woods affords an opportunity to think without distraction.
cloze: The new treaty will {{afford}} smaller nations greater protection against trade abuses.
mnemonic: Afford a view: the window OFFERS it, like handing over a gift.

definition: to increase the power, status, or wealth of; to make appear greater
examples: The dictator built giant monuments to aggrandize his own image.
He lied about his past to aggrandize his role in the project.
cloze: Rulers often {{aggrandize}} themselves by building lavish palaces.
mnemonic: AGGRANDIZE: make GRAND.

definition: a whole formed by combining several separate elements
examples: The aggregate of small donations amounted to more than a million dollars.
In the aggregate, the data show a steady rise in temperature.
cloze: The {{aggregate}} score from all three judges determined the winner.
mnemonic: AGGREGATE: a GREGarious flock gathered into one group.

definition: cheerful readiness; eager speed
examples: She accepted the invitation with alacrity and packed within the hour.
The volunteers responded to the call for help with surprising alacrity.
cloze: When offered the promotion, he accepted with {{alacrity}} and began work the next morning.
mnemonic: ALACRITY sounds like 'a lock-ready' person: ready to go at once.

definition: a seemingly magical process of transformation
examples: Medieval alchemy sought to turn lead into gold, though no one ever succeeded in doing so.
The chef's culinary alchemy transformed a few simple ingredients into an unforgettable meal.
cloze: The poet's {{alchemy}} turned ordinary words into something almost magical.
mnemonic: ALCHEMY: ancestor of chemistry.

definition: to reduce the strength of fear or doubt
examples: The doctor's reassurance allayed the family's fears about the surgery scheduled for the next morning.
Officials tried to allay public concerns about water safety by releasing the test results.
cloze: The CEO released a statement to {{allay}} investors' worries about the merger.
mnemonic: ALLAY: 'lay' your fears down to rest.

definition: to make pain or a problem less severe
examples: Painkillers can alleviate the discomfort of a headache within a few minutes of taking them.
The charity worked to alleviate hunger in several drought-stricken villages by shipping grain.
cloze: New policies were designed to {{alleviate}} traffic congestion in the downtown core.
mnemonic: ALLEVIATE: levi- means light; make a burden LIGHT.

definition: to give out or set aside resources for a particular purpose
examples: The city allocated extra funds to repair roads damaged by the floods.
Researchers must allocate their limited time carefully during field seasons.
cloze: The university plans to {{allocate}} half of the grant to student scholarships.
mnemonic: ALL-O-CATE: give ALL of it to each CATegory.

definition: to refer to something indirectly
examples: In his speech he alluded to the scandal without naming anyone.
The poem alludes to several ancient myths familiar to educated readers.
cloze: Without mentioning her name directly, the speaker seemed to {{allude}} to the former director.
mnemonic: ALLUDE: playing (ludere) around a subject without naming it.

definition: distant and unwilling to engage with others
examples: He remained aloof at the party, standing apart from the crowd and speaking to no one.
Her aloof manner made her new colleagues think she disliked everyone in the office.
cloze: The {{aloof}} professor rarely spoke to students outside of class.
mnemonic: ALOOF: a LOOF-ty person standing apart.

definition: to change in character or form, usually slightly
examples: Heavy mining has altered the landscape of the region for generations.
The author altered the ending of the novel after her editor suggested revisions.
cloze: Even small shifts in temperature can {{alter}} the behavior of migratory birds.
mnemonic: ALTER sounds like ALTERnative: make another version.

definition: selfless concern for the well-being of other people
examples: The nurse's altruism led her to volunteer in disaster zones every summer without any payment.
True altruism expects nothing in return for the help that one person gives to others.
cloze: His quiet {{altruism}} showed in the anonymous donations he made to local hospitals.
mnemonic: ALTRUISM: 'all-true-ism', all for others (alter = other).

definition: a mixture or blend of different elements
examples: The city's culture is an amalgam of Asian, European, and African traditions.
The dental filling was an amalgam of mercury and silver.
cloze: The novel is an {{amalgam}} of mystery, romance, and historical fact.
mnemonic: AMALGAM: 'a-mal-gam', many metals gummed together.

definition: to accumulate a large quantity over time
examples: Over decades, the collector amassed a vast library of rare books.
She amassed a fortune by investing wisely in real estate.
cloze: The army began to {{amass}} troops along the northern border.
mnemonic: AMASS: gather into a MASS.

definition: having more than one possible meaning; unclear
examples: The ambiguous wording of the contract led to a dispute over payment.
Her ambiguous reply left him unsure whether she had accepted or declined.
cloze: Because the instructions were {{ambiguous}}, the students interpreted them in several different ways.
mnemonic: AMBI = both; two ways to go.

definition: having mixed or contradictory feelings about something
examples: He felt ambivalent about moving abroad, excited yet afraid to leave home.
Voters remained ambivalent about the candidate, liking her ideas but doubting her experience.
cloze: She was {{ambivalent}} about the job offer, attracted by the salary but dreading the long commute.
mnemonic: AMBI + VALENT: two strengths pulling at once.

definition: able to walk; relating to walking
examples: Ambulatory patients were allowed to leave their beds and walk the hospital corridors.
The clinic offers ambulatory care, so most patients go home the same day.
cloze: After the operation, she was {{ambulatory}} within a day and soon left the hospital.
mnemonic: AMBULatory: AMBle, walk; 'ambulance' moves.

definition: to make a bad situation better
examples: New drainage systems helped ameliorate the flooding in the lower district.
The company hoped a pay raise would ameliorate low morale among staff.
cloze: Reforms were introduced to {{ameliorate}} conditions in the overcrowded prisons.
mnemonic: A-MELIORATE: 'meliorate' sounds like 'better' (Latin melior).

definition: open and responsive to suggestion; willing to cooperate
examples: The committee was amenable to changing the schedule to suit everyone.
She is amenable to advice and often adjusts her plans after feedback.
cloze: The usually stubborn manager proved {{amenable}} to the proposal after hearing the data.
mnemonic: AMENABLE: willing to say 'AMEN' to a suggestion.

definition: having a pleasant, friendly manner
examples: The amiable neighbor often shared fresh vegetables from his garden with everyone on the street.
Their amiable conversation over tea continued late into the evening without a single argument.
cloze: Everyone liked the {{amiable}} new teacher, who greeted students by name each morning.
mnemonic: AMIABLE: Latin amicus = friend.

definition: having no clear shape or structure
examples: The amorphous cloud drifted across the sky without any definite outline or form.
Her amorphous plans for the future never became specific enough to act upon.
cloze: The {{amorphous}} blob of clay on the table had no recognizable form yet.
mnemonic: A-MORPH-ous: without morph (form).

definition: to a full or more than sufficient degree
examples: The volunteers were amply rewarded with food, music, and heartfelt thanks from the town.
Her careful research amply supports the conclusion that the bridge needs repair.
cloze: The festival's budget was {{amply}} covered by ticket sales, leaving a large surplus.
mnemonic: AMPLY sounds like AMPLE: more than enough.

definition: in a wild, uncontrolled, destructive manner (as in 'run amuck')
examples: The unsupervised puppies ran amuck through the garden, uprooting every seedling.
When the power failed, panic ran amuck among the crowd in the stadium.
cloze: Without a firm leader, the committee's spending ran {{amuck}} and the budget collapsed.
mnemonic: A MUCK of mess: things run amuck make a muck.

definition: something placed in the wrong historical period
examples: A wristwatch in the Roman epic was a glaring anachronism in the film.
The ancient ritual seemed an anachronism in the modern, tech-driven city.
cloze: The sword-wielding duelist in the 1990s novel struck readers as a comical {{anachronism}}.
mnemonic: ANA-CHRONO: against time, like a clock in the wrong century.

definition: comparable in certain respects; similar in function
examples: The heart is analogous to a pump because both move fluid.
Their situation was analogous to that of earlier settlers facing a harsh winter.
cloze: A bird's wing and an insect's wing are {{analogous}}, since both serve the function of flight.
mnemonic: ANALOGous: like an ANALOGy.

definition: something or someone intensely disliked or detested
examples: Corruption is anathema to anyone who believes in honest public service.
To the strict traditionalist, any change in the ritual was anathema.
cloze: Censorship was {{anathema}} to the editor, who believed every voice deserved a hearing.
mnemonic: ANATHEMA: Greek 'accursed thing'; a-NATHEMA, cursed.

definition: a person or organism from whom later ones are descended
examples: Biologists believe whales evolved from a land-dwelling ancestor that resembled a small wolf.
Many families preserve photographs and letters from ancestors who immigrated a century ago.
cloze: The common {{ancestor}} of humans and chimpanzees lived millions of years ago.
mnemonic: ANCESTOR: ANCIENT SISTER/brother line before you.

definition: a short, amusing, or revealing story about a real event
examples: The speaker opened with an anecdote about her first day at work.
He told an anecdote about his grandfather that made everyone laugh.
cloze: The biographer included an {{anecdote}} to illustrate the general's sense of humor.
mnemonic: AN-ECDOTE: 'a nec-dote', a little unpublished tale.

definition: lacking vigor, strength or vitality; weak and feeble
examples: The anemic recovery left thousands of workers still searching for jobs a year later.
Critics dismissed the film's anemic plot as too thin to sustain two hours.
cloze: After an {{anemic}} showing at the polls, the party's leaders called for a complete rethink.
mnemonic: Anemia means thin blood; an ANEMIC argument has no blood in it.

definition: strong hostility or ill will
examples: Years of animosity between the two families finally ended at the wedding of their children.
He felt no animosity toward his rival, only respect for the way she competed.
cloze: The debate was marked by open {{animosity}} between the candidates.
mnemonic: ANIMOSITY: animal-like hatred.

definition: to declare something officially invalid
examples: The court moved to annul the contract because it had been signed under severe pressure.
Their marriage was annulled after only three months, as if it had never happened legally.
cloze: The judge refused to {{annul}} the election results despite the allegations.
mnemonic: AN-NUL: make it NULL, nothing.

definition: deliberately bland and inoffensive; also, something that soothes pain
examples: The senator gave an anodyne speech that avoided every controversial topic and offended nobody.
Critics called the film anodyne, a safe story with no real edge or risk.
cloze: The committee's {{anodyne}} statement said nothing of substance and was designed to upset no one.
mnemonic: AN-odyne sounds like 'an-ODD-ine': not odd, no pain, nothing to react to.

definition: deviating from what is standard or normal
examples: The anomalous readings suggested that the sensor had malfunctioned during the overnight test.
Scientists puzzled over the anomalous warm spell that arrived in the middle of winter.
cloze: The lone {{anomalous}} result in an otherwise consistent experiment demanded an explanation.
mnemonic: A-NOMALOUS: 'not the norm' (a-nomal).

definition: something that deviates from what is normal or expected
examples: The single warm day in January was an anomaly in an otherwise freezing month.
Researchers puzzled over the anomaly in the data that no model could explain.
cloze: A student who fails every quiz yet aces the final exam is a statistical {{anomaly}}.
mnemonic: ANOMALY: A NOrMAL-less thing, not normal.

definition: to provoke hostility in someone
examples: He antagonized his coworkers by constantly criticizing their work in front of the whole team.
The new tax law antagonized small business owners all across the country.
cloze: She tried not to {{antagonize}} the guard by asking too many questions.
mnemonic: ANTAGONIZE: turn someone into an ANTagonist, an enemy.

definition: came before in time; preceded
examples: The ancient temple antedated the nearby city by several centuries.
Her interest in birds antedated her formal training in biology by many years.
cloze: Fossil evidence shows that these tools {{antedated}} the earliest known farming settlements.
mnemonic: ANTE = before; the date came before.

definition: playfully odd, absurd, or ridiculous (the noun means a silly prank)
examples: The comedian's antic gestures had the entire audience laughing within seconds.
His antic behavior at the formal dinner embarrassed his more serious colleagues.
cloze: The puppy's {{antic}} leaps and spins across the lawn made the children giggle.
mnemonic: ANTIC sounds like 'antics' — clownish behavior.

definition: to expect or predict something and prepare for it
examples: Economists anticipate that demand for renewable energy will grow rapidly over the next decade.
The architects anticipated heavy snowfall and designed the roof with a steep slope.
cloze: Meteorologists did not {{anticipate}} that the storm would strengthen so quickly.
mnemonic: ANTI-CIPATE: act BEFORE (ante) it happens.

definition: a remedy that counteracts something harmful
examples: The doctor quickly administered an antidote to the poison before it could damage the organs.
Laughter can be a powerful antidote to stress, worry, and the weight of a hard day.
cloze: Travel proved the perfect {{antidote}} to his years of routine and boredom.
mnemonic: ANTI + DOTE (given): something given against harm.

definition: a strong dislike or aversion
examples: He felt a deep antipathy toward anyone who flattered the boss.
Their mutual antipathy was obvious from the way they avoided each other.
cloze: Her {{antipathy}} for crowded spaces kept her away from festivals and concerts.
mnemonic: ANTI + PATHy (feeling): feeling against.

definition: outdated; too old to be useful or fashionable
examples: The office still relied on an antiquated filing system that nobody understood anymore.
Critics called the law antiquated, since it ignored the realities of modern technology.
cloze: Her {{antiquated}} views on education belonged to a century that had long passed.
mnemonic: ANTIQUE + ated: so old it belongs in an antique shop.

definition: directly opposed; the exact opposite in nature
examples: Her calm, methodical style is antithetical to his impulsive, chaotic approach.
Cruelty is antithetical to everything the charity stands for.
cloze: A policy of secrecy is {{antithetical}} to the principles of open government.
mnemonic: ANTI + thesis: a thesis set against another.

definition: showing little interest, concern, or emotion
examples: Voters grew apathetic after years of broken promises, and turnout fell sharply.
The apathetic student stared out the window while the teacher pleaded for participation.
cloze: Despite the urgent appeals, the council remained {{apathetic}} about the crumbling school roof.
mnemonic: A-PATH-etic: no path of feeling leads anywhere.

definition: lack of interest, enthusiasm, or concern
examples: Voter apathy kept turnout below thirty percent in the local election.
The students' apathy frustrated teachers who tried every method to engage them.
cloze: Years of failed promises bred {{apathy}} among citizens who no longer expected change.
mnemonic: A-PATHY: without feeling (pathos).

definition: the highest point or peak
examples: The apex of the mountain was hidden in thick clouds throughout the entire expedition.
His career reached its apex when he won the Nobel Prize in his early fifties.
cloze: At the {{apex}} of its power, the empire controlled most of the known world.
mnemonic: APEX: sounds like 'a peak' (ape on top of a peak).

definition: a short, memorable statement expressing a general truth
examples: "A stitch in time saves nine" is an aphorism many children learn early.
The author's essays were studded with aphorisms that readers copied into notebooks.
cloze: Her grandfather spoke mostly in {{aphorism}}, each pithy line packing a lesson into a few words.
mnemonic: APHORISM: 'a far ISM' of wisdom, packed into one line.

definition: expressing ideas in short, memorable, wise sayings
examples: His aphoristic style filled the essays with quotable one-line observations about human folly.
The novelist's aphoristic wit made her conversation easy to remember and repeat.
cloze: Franklin's {{aphoristic}} prose packed whole lessons into a single pithy sentence.
mnemonic: APHORISM: a short saying that 'sets apart' a truth in a nutshell.

definition: calm self-assurance and poise, especially under pressure
examples: The speaker handled the hostile questions with remarkable aplomb.
She walked onto the stage with aplomb despite the broken microphone.
cloze: The young diplomat displayed great {{aplomb}} when the talks suddenly turned confrontational.
mnemonic: A PLOMB line hangs straight and steady; so does a person with aplomb.

definition: of doubtful authenticity; widely circulated but probably untrue
examples: The story that Washington chopped down a cherry tree is apocryphal.
Many of the famous quotations attributed to him are apocryphal.
cloze: The tale of the hidden treasure is likely {{apocryphal}}, since no record of it exists.
mnemonic: APOCRYPHAL: hidden (crypt) texts nobody can confirm.

definition: the highest point; peak of success or development
examples: The empire reached its apogee in the second century, controlling vast territories.
The singer's career hit its apogee when she sold out three stadiums in one week.
cloze: For the satellite, the {{apogee}} is the farthest point of its orbit from Earth.
mnemonic: APO-GEE: A Peak On GEE-whiz heights.

definition: a person who abandons a former faith, cause, or loyalty
examples: Once a fierce party loyalist, he was branded an apostate after criticizing its leaders.
The community shunned the apostate who renounced the beliefs he had preached for decades.
cloze: The movement treated every former member as an {{apostate}} deserving contempt.
mnemonic: A-POST-ate: he left his post and abandoned his faith.

definition: a terse, pointed saying; a short instructive maxim
examples: The general's apothegm, "Fortune favors the prepared," was posted in every barracks.
His speeches ended with an apothegm that the press quoted the next morning.
cloze: The editor prized the crisp {{apothegm}}, which said in six words what the chapter took pages to argue.
mnemonic: APOTHEGM sounds like 'a pot of gems' - a small pot of wisdom gems.

definition: the highest point of development; the perfect example or glorification of something
examples: The cathedral represents the apotheosis of Gothic architecture.
For many fans, that final concert was the apotheosis of the band's career.
cloze: The symphony's closing movement was the {{apotheosis}} of the composer's lifelong search for harmony.
mnemonic: APO-THEO-sis: raising someone to a god (theos), the ultimate peak.

definition: clearly visible or understood; seeming real but maybe not
examples: It soon became apparent that the old bridge could not support heavy trucks.
The apparent calm of the lake hid dangerous currents beneath the surface.
cloze: The benefits of regular exercise are {{apparent}} to anyone who tracks their health over time.
mnemonic: A-PARENT: appears, like a parent in plain view.

definition: to calm someone by giving in to their demands
examples: The government tried to appease the protesters by lowering fuel taxes for the whole winter.
He offered a bouquet of flowers to appease his angry host after arriving very late.
cloze: The company agreed to some demands in order to {{appease}} the striking workers.
mnemonic: APPEASE: bring to PEACE with a gift.

definition: large enough to be noticed or measured
examples: The new insulation made an appreciable difference in the monthly heating bill.
There was no appreciable change in the patient's condition overnight.
cloze: Even a small tax can have an {{appreciable}} effect on spending among low-income households.
mnemonic: Appreciable = you can appreciate (notice) it.

definition: anxious fear that something bad may happen
examples: She felt a growing apprehension as the test date approached.
The villagers watched the darkening sky with apprehension.
cloze: He signed the contract with some {{apprehension}}, unsure whether the risks were worth it.
mnemonic: Apprehension: your mind GRABS (apprehend) trouble before it arrives.

definition: anxious or fearful that something bad will happen
examples: She felt apprehensive before her first day at the new school.
The apprehensive passengers gripped their seats as the plane shook.
cloze: He was {{apprehensive}} about the surgery and asked the doctor many questions.
mnemonic: APPREHENSIVE: your mind is 'grabbing' (apprehend) at fears.

definition: expressing approval or praise
examples: The critic's approbatory review sent ticket sales soaring for the little play.
She gave an approbatory nod as the apprentice finished the delicate repair.
cloze: The coach's {{approbatory}} remarks after the match lifted the whole team's spirits.
mnemonic: Approbatory contains 'approb' = approve.

definition: to take something for one's own use, often without permission
examples: The dictator appropriated farmland and gave it to his supporters.
Critics accused the designer of appropriating motifs from indigenous cultures without credit.
cloze: The treasurer was jailed for having {{appropriated}} charity funds for his own luxuries.
mnemonic: Make it your OWN PROPERty: appropriate = take as proper(ty).

definition: close to the actual value but not exact
examples: The approximate age of the fossil is sixty million years, according to radiometric dating.
Guides gave an approximate length of the trail, but hikers found it slightly longer.
cloze: An {{approximate}} count suggests that about ten thousand birds nest on the island.
mnemonic: APPROXIMATE = APPROaching exact.

definition: belonging to or attached to something larger as an accessory
examples: The deed transferred the house and all rights appurtenant to the land.
A well and a small barn are appurtenant to the farmhouse.
cloze: The fishing rights were {{appurtenant}} to the estate and passed to each new owner.
mnemonic: Appurtenant sounds like 'appertain': it pertains to the main property.

definition: appropriate or suitable for the situation
examples: The poem's title is apt, since it describes autumn leaves falling.
Her apt remark summed up the mood of the entire room.
cloze: The comparison of the economy to a ship in a storm seemed {{apt}} to most listeners.
mnemonic: APT: perfect fit, like an 'adapt'ed shape.

definition: based on random choice rather than reason
examples: The judge's arbitrary decision seemed to have no basis in law.
Choosing a name felt arbitrary, so we picked the first one on the list.
cloze: The rules seemed {{arbitrary}} because no one could explain the reasons behind them.
mnemonic: ARBITRARY: the ARBiter does as he pleases.

definition: known or understood by only a few; secret
examples: Only a few scholars understood the arcane rituals of the ancient order.
The tax code is filled with arcane rules that baffle ordinary taxpayers.
cloze: The wizard's {{arcane}} lore was guarded in a library few were permitted to enter.
mnemonic: ARCANE hides in an ARK: sealed and secret.

definition: deliberately playful or mischievous, often in a knowing, teasing way
examples: She gave him an arch look, clearly amused by his clumsy attempt at secrecy.
His arch remarks about the committee made everyone laugh while still stinging a little.
cloze: With an {{arch}} smile, the host hinted that she knew exactly who had sent the flowers.
mnemonic: Raised eyebrow forms an ARCH: a sly, knowing look.

definition: belonging to an earlier time; outdated
examples: The contract was full of archaic phrases that few modern readers understood.
Using a quill pen seems archaic in an age of tablets and smartphones.
cloze: Lawyers criticized the {{archaic}} statute for ignoring how people live today.
mnemonic: ARCH-aic sounds like ancient ARCHes: old stuff.

definition: enthusiastic and passionate
examples: She was an ardent supporter of the local football team.
His ardent desire to become a doctor motivated him to study every night.
cloze: The senator, an {{ardent}} defender of free speech, spoke for three hours without notes.
mnemonic: ARDENT: burning (Latin ardere, to burn).

definition: intense enthusiasm or passion
examples: He pursued his studies with ardor, often reading until dawn.
The young couple's ardor cooled after several years of marriage.
cloze: The crowd's {{ardor}} grew as the candidate delivered the final lines of her speech.
mnemonic: ARDOR: 'ardent' burning inside.

definition: involving great effort; difficult and tiring
examples: The arduous climb to the summit took nearly twelve hours.
Writing the dissertation was an arduous task that lasted three years.
cloze: After an {{arduous}} journey across the desert, the travelers collapsed in exhaustion.
mnemonic: ARDUOUS: ARDent work you DO is hard.

definition: having little or no rain; extremely dry
examples: The arid desert receives less than five inches of rain per year.
Few crops can grow in such arid soil without irrigation.
cloze: Cacti thrive in the {{arid}} climate where most plants would quickly die.
mnemonic: ARID: 'a rid of water'.

definition: complete and utter; used to intensify something bad
examples: He was an arrant liar who had never told the truth about his past.
The mayor dismissed the claim as arrant nonsense, without a shred of evidence.
cloze: Only an {{arrant}} fool would invest his life savings in a scheme that obviously collapsed.
mnemonic: ARRANT sounds like ERRANT, but means absolute: an arrant knave is a total knave.

definition: an impressive or wide-ranging display or collection
examples: The shop offers an array of cheeses from around the world.
She was stunned by the array of options on the restaurant menu.
cloze: A dazzling {{array}} of colors greeted visitors at the flower market.
mnemonic: ARRAY: items lined up in ARRAY.

definition: a person who has recently gained power or status, often seen as pushy
examples: Old-money families sneered at the arriviste who had bought the estate next door.
The club's members treated the flashy newcomer as a vulgar arriviste.
cloze: Despite his fortune, the {{arriviste}} was never fully accepted by the city's established elite.
mnemonic: French 'arrive': he has just ARRIVED and wants everyone to notice.

definition: having an exaggerated sense of one's own importance
examples: The arrogant executive ignored the advice of everyone around him.
Her arrogant tone made it clear that she saw herself as superior.
cloze: The {{arrogant}} young actor assumed the role was his before the audition had even begun.
mnemonic: ARROGANT: 'a rogue giant' puffed up.

definition: to claim or seize without right
examples: The director arrogated to himself powers that the charter reserved for the board.
Critics said the president had arrogated authority that belongs to the legislature.
cloze: It is presumptuous to {{arrogate}} the credit for a victory that the whole crew earned.
mnemonic: ARROGAte: an ARROGANT person grabs what is not theirs.

definition: clever, skillful, and often sly in achieving one's aims
examples: The artful negotiator got everything she wanted while seeming to concede much.
With an artful remark, he steered the conversation away from his mistake.
cloze: The child's {{artful}} excuses nearly convinced his parents that the vase had broken by itself.
mnemonic: ARTful = full of ART, the art of trickery.

definition: able to express ideas clearly and effectively
examples: The articulate young lawyer explained the complex case in plain language.
She was so articulate that audiences always understood her points immediately.
cloze: As a gifted and {{articulate}} speaker, he could make difficult ideas accessible to anyone.
mnemonic: ARTICULATE: parts joined clearly, like a jointed limb of words.

definition: clever trickery or cunning used to deceive; a crafty device
examples: The spy gained entry to the embassy through an elaborate artifice.
Her charm was not artifice; it flowed naturally from real warmth.
cloze: The salesman's friendly manner was merely {{artifice}} meant to lower our guard.
mnemonic: ARTIFICE: ART + make (fic) = something crafted to fool.

definition: natural and without deceit or pretense
examples: The child's artless questions made the adults laugh because they were so direct and innocent.
Her artless honesty, free from any trick or pretense, made her a favorite among friends.
cloze: He gave an {{artless}} reply, never suspecting that it might embarrass anyone.
mnemonic: ARTLESS: lacking ART, no tricks.

definition: natural simplicity; lack of cunning or pretense
examples: The child's artlessness made everyone in the room smile at her honest questions.
Critics admired the artlessness of the poems, which seemed untouched by calculation.
cloze: Her {{artlessness}} was so complete that she never suspected anyone of lying to her.
mnemonic: Art-less: no art, no tricks.

definition: a position of dominant power or influence
examples: The company's ascendancy in the market lasted until cheaper rivals appeared.
Over the decade, the reformists gained ascendancy over the old guard in parliament.
cloze: After the victory, the northern faction held {{ascendancy}} over all neighboring territories.
mnemonic: ASCEND + ancy: climbing to the top and staying there.

definition: to find out something for certain
examples: Investigators worked to ascertain the exact cause of the fire in the warehouse.
It is difficult to ascertain the truth when witnesses give conflicting accounts.
cloze: Before signing, you should {{ascertain}} that the figures in the contract are accurate.
mnemonic: ASCERTAIN: make CERTAIN.

definition: practicing severe self-discipline and avoiding luxury
examples: The monk led an ascetic life, eating little and owning almost nothing.
His ascetic habits, including cold showers and fasting, impressed his followers.
cloze: She chose an {{ascetic}} lifestyle, giving up comfort and possessions to focus on spiritual practice.
mnemonic: ASCETIC: 'a sick-tic' of denying yourself pleasures.

definition: to attribute something to a cause or source
examples: Historians ascribe the poem to a monk who lived in the tenth century.
She ascribed her success to hard work and good mentors.
cloze: Doctors {{ascribe}} the sudden fatigue to a lack of sleep rather than to any illness.
mnemonic: A-SCRIBE: write it down to someone's account.

definition: with suspicion or disapproval (as in looking sideways)
examples: Neighbors looked askance at the stranger who photographed every house on the street.
He viewed the sudden offer askance, wondering what the catch might be.
cloze: The old professor looked {{askance}} at the student's wildly ambitious thesis proposal.
mnemonic: Ask-ANCE: you ask 'is this OK?' with a sideways look.

definition: not straight or level
examples: The picture hung askew on the wall after the earthquake shook the entire building.
His tie was askew and his hair was messy after the long, windy walk.
cloze: The crooked sign was {{askew}}, tilting dangerously to one side.
mnemonic: ASKEW: 'a skew' from straight.

definition: a particular part or feature of a situation or idea
examples: Climate scientists study every aspect of the atmosphere, from temperature to humidity.
One interesting aspect of the study was how participants' moods affected their memory.
cloze: Economic factors are only one {{aspect}} of the complex problem of urban poverty.
mnemonic: ASPECT: a face you SPECT (see) from one side.

definition: harshness of tone or manner
examples: He spoke with asperity, clearly annoyed by the repeated interruptions during his presentation.
The asperity of her reply surprised those who had always known her as gentle.
cloze: The teacher's {{asperity}} disappeared whenever the children behaved well.
mnemonic: ASPERITY: rough like sandpaper (asper).

definition: to direct one's hopes toward a lofty goal
examples: Many young athletes aspire to compete in the Olympics someday.
She aspired to become a renowned scientist like her idol.
cloze: Students who {{aspire}} to leadership positions often volunteer for extra responsibilities.
mnemonic: ASPIRE: breathe (spirare) toward a dream.

definition: to attack violently, whether physically or with words
examples: Protesters assailed the senator with questions about his vote on the bill.
Waves of doubt assailed her as the deadline drew closer.
cloze: Critics continued to {{assail}} the policy, calling it reckless and unfair to the poor.
mnemonic: To ASSAIL is to send a SAIL of arrows at someone.

definition: to agree to a proposal or opinion
examples: The board assented to the plan after a brief discussion.
He nodded to assent when asked if he understood the terms.
cloze: Rather than argue, she chose to {{assent}} to the committee's decision.
mnemonic: AS-SENT: you 'sent' a yes in reply.

definition: to judge or estimate the quality, value, or amount of something
examples: Geologists assessed the damage to the dam after the earthquake.
Teachers assess students' progress through exams, projects, and class participation.
cloze: Before building the road, engineers must {{assess}} its impact on nearby wildlife.
mnemonic: ASSESS: sit beside (as-sess) and judge.

definition: showing great care and persistent effort
examples: The assiduous student reviewed her notes every single evening for the entire school year.
His assiduous attention to every small detail prevented a very costly error in the final report.
cloze: Thanks to {{assiduous}} research, the historian uncovered documents that no one had seen before.
mnemonic: ASSIDUOUS: you SIT (sedere) at your desk to work.

definition: with constant, careful, and persistent effort
examples: She studied assiduously for months, rarely missing a single day of practice.
The gardener worked assiduously to remove every weed before the competition began.
cloze: Having promised to finish the report, he {{assiduously}} checked every figure twice.
mnemonic: ASSIDUOUSLY: you SIT ('sid') at your desk and keep at it.

definition: to soothe or make less severe
examples: The nurse's calm voice helped assuage the patient's fears before the operation began.
Nothing could assuage her grief after the sudden loss of her beloved older brother.
cloze: The mayor tried to {{assuage}} residents' worries by promising a full investigation.
mnemonic: ASSUAGE sounds like 'a sweet-age': sweetens pain.

definition: to accept as true without proof
examples: Early astronomers assumed that the Earth stood still at the center of the universe.
Researchers should not assume that results from mice will apply to humans.
cloze: Many people {{assume}} that heavier objects fall faster, but experiments show otherwise.
mnemonic: ASSUME: you take UP (sume) an idea without proof.

definition: having sharp judgment, especially in practical matters
examples: The astute investor sold his shares just before the market crashed, avoiding huge losses.
Her astute observation revealed the hidden flaw in a plan that everyone else had approved.
cloze: An {{astute}} politician, he sensed the shift in public opinion before the polls did.
mnemonic: ASTUTE: 'a stew-tea' wit, quick and sharp.

definition: the reappearance of a trait or behavior from distant ancestors; a throwback
examples: His sudden urge to hunt wild game seemed an atavism from a distant, primitive past.
Biologists saw the baby's tiny tail-like growth as an atavism.
cloze: The mob's brutality struck observers as a frightening {{atavism}} in a supposedly civilized city.
mnemonic: ATAVISM: ATAVus is Latin for ancestor - your great-great-grandfather resurfacing.

definition: to make amends for a wrong
examples: He volunteered at the shelter for years to atone for his past mistakes.
The king sought to atone for his cruelty by building a hospital.
cloze: She wanted to {{atone}} for her harsh words by apologizing in person.
mnemonic: AT-ONE-ment: being 'at one' again with the person wronged.

definition: to waste away through lack of use
examples: Muscles atrophy when a limb is kept in a cast for several months without exercise.
Without regular practice, his once fluent language skills began to atrophy and fade.
cloze: If the program loses funding, the institution's research capacity will {{atrophy}} within a few years.
mnemonic: A-TROPHY: no food (trophe), so it shrinks.

definition: to make weaker, thinner, or less intense
examples: Thick walls attenuate the sound from the busy street outside.
The drug is designed to attenuate the symptoms of the virus.
cloze: Distance will {{attenuate}} the signal until it becomes too faint to detect.
mnemonic: ATTENUATE: tenuis = thin; make thin.

definition: to regard something as caused by or belonging to someone or something
examples: Historians attribute the decline of the empire to economic problems and civil wars.
The painting was attributed to a Dutch artist, though experts still debate its origin.
cloze: Scientists {{attribute}} the rise in sea levels mainly to melting ice and warming oceans.
mnemonic: ATTRIBUTE = ad + tribute: pay credit to a source.

definition: showing a bold willingness to take risks
examples: The audacious plan to cross the Atlantic in a rowboat attracted worldwide attention.
Her audacious proposal startled the board, but it was approved in the end.
cloze: It was an {{audacious}} move to challenge the champion in his own hometown.
mnemonic: AUDACIOUS: has AUDience-grabbing GUTS.

definition: bold daring, sometimes to the point of rudeness or recklessness
examples: He had the audacity to ask for a raise on his first day.
The explorers' audacity astonished onlookers, who thought the voyage was certain suicide.
cloze: It took considerable {{audacity}} to challenge the champion in front of her own fans.
mnemonic: AUDACITY sounds like 'odd-ass-city': an oddly bold nerve.

definition: to make greater by adding to it
examples: She took a second job to augment her modest income.
The museum plans to augment its collection with works from local artists.
cloze: He hoped to {{augment}} his savings by investing in a small business.
mnemonic: AUGMENT: 'August' gets bigger each day in summer; auge = increase.

definition: conducive to success; favorable
examples: The sunny weather was an auspicious start to the festival.
It was an auspicious time to open a business, with the economy growing.
cloze: The new company enjoyed an {{auspicious}} beginning, selling out its first product in a week.
mnemonic: AUSPICIOUS: birds (aves) seen as good signs.

definition: severe or strict; without comfort or ornament
examples: The austere room held only a narrow bed and a wooden chair.
He was an austere judge who rarely smiled and never joked.
cloze: The monastery's {{austere}} design reflected the monks' simple, disciplined way of living.
mnemonic: AUSTERE sounds like 'Austria in a stern winter'.

definition: strict economy or severe self-discipline
examples: The government imposed austerity measures that cut public spending sharply.
The monks lived in austerity, eating only bread and water.
cloze: Years of {{austerity}} left schools short of books and hospitals short of staff.
mnemonic: AUSTERITY: noun of austere; sternly sparse.

definition: ruling with absolute power; domineering and unwilling to consult others
examples: The autocratic king dismissed his advisers and made every decision alone.
Employees resented the manager's autocratic habit of ignoring their suggestions entirely.
cloze: Under the {{autocratic}} regime, citizens had no say in how the country was run.
mnemonic: AUTO + crat: one person drives the whole car by himself.

definition: self-governing; independent
examples: The region became autonomous after years of negotiation with the central government.
Autonomous vehicles use sensors to navigate without a human driver.
cloze: Each department operates as an {{autonomous}} unit, free from direct control by headquarters.
mnemonic: AUTO + NOMOS: self-law.

definition: independently, without outside control or direction
examples: The rover navigated autonomously, choosing its own path across the rocky terrain.
Each branch of the company operates autonomously, setting its own budgets and hiring policies.
cloze: The research team worked {{autonomously}}, free from supervision by the central office.
mnemonic: AUTO (self) + nomos (law): making your own laws.

definition: extreme greed for wealth
examples: His avarice drove him to cheat even his closest business partners.
The miser's avarice left him rich in gold but poor in friends.
cloze: Stories about dragons guarding treasure are often warnings about {{avarice}} and its dangers.
mnemonic: AVARICE: 'AVA wants RICHES' always.

definition: extremely greedy for wealth
examples: The avaricious landlord raised rents again, though he already owned half the town.
Her avaricious uncle counted every coin and begrudged each gift he gave.
cloze: The {{avaricious}} executive demanded a larger bonus even as the company laid off workers.
mnemonic: AVARICE: a VERY RICH wish - 'a very rich' appetite.

definition: to state firmly that something is true
examples: The witness averred that she had seen the defendant at the scene of the crime.
He continued to aver his innocence despite the mounting evidence against him in court.
cloze: The scientist will {{aver}} that her findings are accurate, even if critics doubt them.
mnemonic: AVER: sounds like 'a verity': claim the truth.

definition: a strong dislike or reluctance
examples: She has an aversion to heights and avoids tall buildings.
His aversion to risk kept him from investing in stocks.
cloze: The child showed a strong {{aversion}} to vegetables and pushed them aside at every meal.
mnemonic: AVERSION: you turn (vert) AWAY (a-).

definition: to prevent something undesirable from happening
examples: Quick action by the pilot averted a disaster when both engines failed over the sea.
Diplomats worked through the night in a last attempt to avert a war between the neighbors.
cloze: The new safety system helped {{avert}} what might have been a serious accident.
mnemonic: A-VERT: turn (vert) away.

definition: having a keen enthusiasm for something
examples: She is an avid reader who finishes a novel every week.
The avid collector traveled across the country to find rare stamps.
cloze: As an {{avid}} gardener, he spends every weekend tending his roses.
mnemonic: AVID: sounds like 'a video-addict': can't get enough.

definition: off course; amiss
examples: Her plans went awry when the train was delayed by a storm.
Something had gone awry in the experiment, and the results made no sense.
cloze: The project went {{awry}} when two key engineers resigned in the same week.
mnemonic: AWRY: sounds like 'a-wry', twisted off course.

definition: a statement accepted as self-evidently true
examples: It is an axiom of economics that resources are limited.
The mathematician began with a few simple axioms and built the whole theory from them.
cloze: The idea that all people deserve fair treatment is an {{axiom}} of the legal system.
mnemonic: AXIOM: a basic 'axe' to chop at everything else; foundation.

definition: to pester or harass persistently
examples: The reporters badgered the senator with questions until he finally left the room.
She badgered her brother for weeks until he agreed to lend her the car.
cloze: Stop trying to {{badger}} me into signing; I need more time to read the contract.
mnemonic: Badgers dig and nag at a burrow; you BADGER someone nonstop.

definition: threatening harm; menacing
examples: The cat fixed a baleful glare on the dog that wandered into its yard.
A baleful light glowed in the windows of the abandoned house.
cloze: The villain cast a {{baleful}} look at the hero, clearly promising revenge.
mnemonic: BALE of fire: a threatening, harmful look.

definition: to refuse or hesitate to proceed, as if stopped by an obstacle
examples: Investors balked at the high price and withdrew their offers.
The horse balked at the narrow bridge and would not cross.
cloze: Many employees {{balk}} whenever management proposes yet another round of reorganization.
mnemonic: A horse BALKs at a wall and will not take another step.

definition: lacking originality; boringly predictable or overused
examples: The film's banal dialogue, full of stock phrases, put half the audience to sleep.
Critics dismissed the novel as banal, a collection of clichés about love and loss.
cloze: His speech was so {{banal}} that listeners could predict each line before he finished it.
mnemonic: Banal sounds like "bland" — flat, ordinary talk.

definition: the quality of being dull and unoriginal; a trite remark
examples: The banality of the greeting-card verse made the audience groan.
He grew tired of the banality of small talk about the weather.
cloze: Critics complained about the {{banality}} of the dialogue, which was full of tired clichés.
mnemonic: BAN-ality: you'd BAN such a boring cliché.

definition: a source of continual harm or distress
examples: Weeds are the bane of every gardener, returning no matter how often they are pulled.
Constant traffic became the bane of her daily commute and her patience.
cloze: Poor record keeping was the {{bane}} of the small clinic, causing endless errors and delays.
mnemonic: Bane rhymes with pain — it is what causes you pain.

definition: to send away or force to leave, often officially
examples: The king chose to banish the traitor from the kingdom forever.
She tried to banish her doubts by reviewing the plan one more time.
cloze: Villagers voted to {{banish}} the thief from the town after repeated offenses.
mnemonic: BAN + ISH: ban someone from the land.

definition: playful, friendly teasing conversation
examples: The easy banter between the two comedians made the show feel spontaneous.
Their friendly banter filled the kitchen as they cooked together.
cloze: The team enjoyed the light-hearted {{banter}} that filled the locker room before the game.
mnemonic: Banter sounds like "bantam" — small light playful sparring.

definition: morally low, ignoble, or contemptible
examples: He was driven by base motives, hoping only to profit from his neighbors' misfortune.
The novel's villain commits a base act of betrayal against his oldest friend.
cloze: Betraying a friend for a small bribe is a {{base}} deed that no excuse can soften.
mnemonic: BASE = at the bottom, low in morals.

definition: the corruption or debasement of something by adding inferior elements
examples: Purists denounced the film as a bastardization of the beloved novel.
The restaurant's cheap fusion dish was a bastardization of traditional paella.
cloze: Linguists lament the {{bastardization}} of the language by careless slang and jargon.
mnemonic: A bastard form: not the pure original, a lesser mixed copy.

definition: showing blissful happiness or serene joy
examples: A beatific smile spread across the child's face as she tasted the ice cream.
The monk's beatific expression suggested a peace that no worry could disturb.
cloze: After the long journey, she sank into the chair with a {{beatific}} look of contentment.
mnemonic: BEATIFIC: like 'beatitude', the blessed bliss of saints.

definition: attractive on the wearer; or fitting and appropriate
examples: The deep green dress was very becoming and brought out her eyes.
Such rude outbursts are not becoming in a person of your position.
cloze: She wore a hat that was most {{becoming}}, flattering her face and complementing her coat.
mnemonic: A becoming outfit is one you BECOME - it suits what you are.

definition: to ask earnestly or to dodge (as in beg the question: assume what must be proved)
examples: The analyst's claim begs the question, since it assumes what it should prove.
Critics say the argument begs the question by treating its conclusion as already true.
cloze: Saying the law is just because it is lawful seems to {{beg}} the question.
mnemonic: Begging the question = begging you to accept the conclusion for free.

definition: to resent someone for having or receiving something; to give reluctantly
examples: I don't begrudge her the promotion; she worked harder than anyone.
He begrudged every dollar spent on the repairs, complaining constantly about the cost.
cloze: Nobody could {{begrudge}} the team its victory after such a grueling season.
mnemonic: Hold a GRUDGE: be-GRUDGE.

definition: to charm or deceive someone, often cleverly
examples: The con artist beguiled elderly investors with promises of enormous returns.
Beguiled by the sweet melody, the sailors steered straight toward the rocks.
cloze: The storyteller could {{beguile}} children for hours with tales of dragons and hidden treasure.
mnemonic: BE-GUILE: using guile (cunning) to charm.

definition: is necessary or proper for (someone to do)
examples: It behooves any traveler to learn a few local customs before arriving.
It behooves the committee to read the report carefully before voting.
cloze: With the deadline looming, it {{behooves}} every team member to double-check the figures.
mnemonic: It BE-HOOVES you: a hoof-stamp telling you what you must do.

definition: to explain or discuss excessively; to go on about
examples: I won't belabor the point; you all know why the deadline matters.
The professor belabored the same example until students stopped paying attention.
cloze: There is no need to {{belabor}} the obvious; everyone already agrees the plan failed.
mnemonic: BE-LABOR: work a point to death.

definition: to give a false impression of; to contradict
examples: His calm voice belied the panic he felt as the plane shook violently.
The company's cheerful ads belie the grim working conditions inside its factories.
cloze: Her youthful appearance {{belies}} her age; she is actually nearly seventy.
mnemonic: BE-LIE: it makes you believe a lie about the truth.

definition: to make someone or something seem unimportant
examples: Good leaders never belittle their staff in front of colleagues, because it destroys trust and morale.
He belittled her achievement by claiming that her promotion was nothing more than a lucky accident.
cloze: It is unkind to {{belittle}} a child's efforts when she has worked so hard.
mnemonic: BE-LITTLE: make someone seem little.

definition: eager to fight; aggressively hostile
examples: The bellicose senator urged immediate war and rejected every peace proposal.
His bellicose tone at the meeting turned a routine disagreement into a shouting match.
cloze: The dictator's {{bellicose}} speeches alarmed neighbouring nations, who began preparing for conflict.
mnemonic: Latin bellum = war; think of a war BELL ringing.

definition: hostile and eager to fight
examples: The belligerent customer shouted at the cashier and slammed his fist on the counter.
Tension grew as the belligerent nation massed troops along the border.
cloze: His {{belligerent}} tone only made the negotiators less willing to compromise.
mnemonic: Bell + 'gerent': a bell rings for war (bellum = war).

definition: to express deep regret or sorrow about something
examples: Farmers bemoan the lack of rain that has withered their crops this year.
He spent the evening bemoaning his bad luck instead of fixing the problem.
cloze: Older residents often {{bemoan}} the disappearance of the neighborhood shops they grew up with.
mnemonic: BE-MOAN: you literally moan about it.

definition: an advantage or good result
examples: One benefit of bilingual education is improved memory and problem-solving.
Researchers examined the long-term health benefits of a plant-based diet among thousands of volunteers.
cloze: The main {{benefit}} of the new vaccine is long-lasting protection.
mnemonic: BENE = good: benefit is something good.

definition: kind and generous; well-meaning
examples: The benevolent donor quietly paid tuition for dozens of struggling students each year.
A benevolent ruler, she lowered taxes and funded hospitals for the poor.
cloze: The {{benevolent}} old man gave away most of his fortune to local charities.
mnemonic: Bene = good, volent = wishing: wishing good.

definition: ignorant, unenlightened; living in intellectual or moral darkness
examples: Reformers viewed the isolated village as a benighted place that needed schools.
Only a benighted ruler would ban books and imprison the scholars who wrote them.
cloze: The traveler's {{benighted}} host insisted that the earth was flat and refused to hear otherwise.
mnemonic: BE-NIGHTed: caught in the NIGHT, no light of knowledge.

definition: gentle and harmless; not threatening, especially of a tumor
examples: The doctor reassured him that the growth was benign and required no surgery.
Her benign smile put the nervous new employees at ease on their first day.
cloze: Fortunately the tumor proved {{benign}}, so no aggressive treatment was necessary.
mnemonic: Benign = "be nice": good, not harmful.

definition: to leave to someone in a will; to hand down
examples: She bequeathed her entire collection of rare books to the town library when she died.
The ancient empire bequeathed its laws and architecture to the many civilizations that followed it.
cloze: The retired captain chose to {{bequeath}} his sailing boat to his youngest grandson.
mnemonic: Be-QUEATH: sounds like "be quiet" and leave a will.

definition: deprived of something; lacking, especially after a loss
examples: After the fire, the family was bereft of nearly all its possessions.
The speech was bereft of any new ideas and sounded like a recycled one.
cloze: She was {{bereft}} after her closest friend moved away, and the house felt achingly empty.
mnemonic: Bereft sounds like "robbed" — something has been taken.

definition: to surround and attack; to overwhelm with requests or troubles
examples: The army besieged the fortress for six months until supplies ran out.
Reporters besieged the actor with questions as he left the courthouse.
cloze: After the scandal, the senator's office was {{besieged}} by angry phone calls.
mnemonic: BE-SIEGE: put a siege around someone.

definition: to damage the reputation of; to stain
examples: The scandal threatened to besmirch the senator's otherwise spotless reputation among voters in her home district.
Rivals spread false rumors in an attempt to besmirch her good name before the election.
cloze: He sued the tabloid for trying to {{besmirch}} his honor with unfounded accusations.
mnemonic: SMIRCH is like smear: you smear someone's name.

definition: so infatuated that one cannot think clearly; also, drunk
examples: The besotted young man wrote poems about her every day and ignored his friends.
She was besotted with her new puppy and photographed it constantly.
cloze: He was so {{besotted}} with his fiancée that he overlooked every obvious warning sign.
mnemonic: Like a SOT (drunkard), drunk on love.

definition: to be disloyal to; to reveal unintentionally or expose
examples: He betrayed his friends by selling their secrets to a rival.
Her trembling hands betrayed how nervous she really was.
cloze: A faint smile {{betrayed}} the juror's true opinion before the verdict was read.
mnemonic: BE-TRAY: handing someone on a TRAY to the enemy.

definition: an unfair preference for or against something, leading to distorted judgment
examples: Researchers use blind trials to prevent personal bias from influencing the outcome.
Some critics detected a political bias in the newspaper's coverage of the election.
cloze: A reviewer with a strong {{bias}} against new methods may reject good research unfairly.
mnemonic: BIAS leans (like a BIAS-cut fabric) to one side.

definition: to divide into two branches or parts
examples: The road bifurcates just past the old mill, with one branch toward the coast.
Researchers bifurcate the sample into two groups so that they can compare the results.
cloze: The river will {{bifurcate}} near the delta, forming two separate channels to the sea.
mnemonic: BI = two + FURCA = fork: split in two.

definition: bad-tempered and irritable (literally, suffering from excess bile)
examples: The bilious old critic dismissed every new play as worthless trash.
His bilious mood darkened whenever anyone mentioned his rival's success.
cloze: The editor's {{bilious}} comments about younger writers made the staff dread her notes.
mnemonic: BILE in the liver makes you BILIOUS: sour and grumpy.

definition: to cheat or swindle someone out of money
examples: The fraudster bilked hundreds of retirees out of their savings with a fake investment scheme.
Tourists were bilked by a taxi driver who charged ten times the normal fare.
cloze: The scheme was designed to {{bilk}} unsuspecting customers of their deposits before the company vanished overnight.
mnemonic: BILK sounds like "milk" — they milk your money.

definition: flattering or coaxing words used to persuade
examples: Despite the salesman's blandishments, she refused to sign the contract without reading it.
The prince was immune to the blandishments of courtiers who wanted favours.
cloze: He resisted every {{blandishment}} offered by lobbyists hoping to win his vote with sweet talk.
mnemonic: Sounds like "bland dish meant" to soften you with sugar.

definition: completely obvious in an offensive or shameless way
examples: The senator told a blatant lie that anyone could disprove in seconds.
His blatant disregard for the rules angered the whole team.
cloze: The company's {{blatant}} copying of its rival's design led to an immediate lawsuit.
mnemonic: BLAT-ant sounds like a bleating blare: loud and obvious.

definition: gloomy and without hope; bare and cheerless
examples: The economic forecast looked bleak for the region, with layoffs expected in nearly every sector.
A cold wind swept across the bleak, treeless moor, and not a single bird sang.
cloze: After months of failed experiments, the researcher's outlook grew increasingly {{bleak}}.
mnemonic: BLEAK sounds like 'bleach': drained of color and hope.

definition: having a narrow, limited outlook that ignores other views
examples: His blinkered attitude kept him from seeing any merit in the proposal.
Only a blinkered observer could ignore such overwhelming evidence.
cloze: The company's {{blinkered}} focus on short-term profit blinded it to changing markets.
mnemonic: Horse BLINKERS limit sight to straight ahead; so does a blinkered mind.

definition: carefree and cheerful; casually indifferent
examples: With blithe confidence, he ignored every warning and walked onto the thin ice.
Her blithe optimism annoyed colleagues who were buried in problems.
cloze: The tourists strolled along the cliff edge with {{blithe}} unconcern for the dangers below.
mnemonic: Blithe sounds like "blissful" — happy and unworried.

definition: to talk loudly and aggressively with little effect
examples: The manager blustered about firing everyone but never actually took any action.
He blustered his way through the interview, hiding his lack of knowledge behind loud claims.
cloze: Instead of answering the question, the minister began to {{bluster}} and threaten the reporters.
mnemonic: Blustery wind is loud but harmless, like a blusterer.

definition: to support or strengthen
examples: New evidence bolstered the defense attorney's argument that her client was elsewhere.
The coach tried to bolster the team's confidence before the final match.
cloze: The government introduced subsidies to {{bolster}} the struggling farming sector.
mnemonic: A BOLSTER is a long pillow that props you up.

definition: pompous; using grand words with little meaning
examples: The candidate's bombastic speeches were full of grand promises but short on details.
Tired of his bombastic style, the editor cut half the adjectives from his article.
cloze: The {{bombastic}} orator filled the hall with lofty phrases that meant almost nothing.
mnemonic: BOMB-astic: a speech that explodes with noise but no substance.

definition: a helpful benefit or blessing
examples: The new highway proved a boon to the once isolated mountain town.
Free tutoring was a boon for students who could not afford private lessons.
cloze: Rain at the end of the long drought was a {{boon}} to every farmer in the valley.
mnemonic: BOON sounds like 'bonus': a welcome extra benefit.

definition: rude, rough, and insensitive in manner
examples: His boorish habit of interrupting guests embarrassed his wife at every dinner party.
The boorish fan shouted insults at the players and spilled drink on his neighbours.
cloze: Her {{boorish}} table manners, including loud chewing and grabbing food, shocked the hosts.
mnemonic: A BOAR eating at the table is boorish.

definition: to remove offensive or improper parts from a text
examples: Victorian editors chose to bowdlerize Shakespeare so families could read it aloud.
The network bowdlerized the film, cutting every scene with strong language.
cloze: The publisher decided to {{bowdlerize}} the novel before releasing it to schools.
mnemonic: Named for Thomas BOWDLER, who published a cleaned-up Shakespeare.
