definition: boldly shameless; without embarrassment
examples: The brazen thief walked in daylight past security and took a painting off the wall.
She made a brazen attempt to take credit for her colleague's research.
cloze: His {{brazen}} lie, told to the judge's face, stunned everyone in the courtroom.
mnemonic: BRASS face: a tough face that never blushes.

definition: an important discovery or achievement
examples: The discovery of penicillin was a breakthrough in modern medicine.
Scientists announced a breakthrough in the development of clean energy.
cloze: The team made a major {{breakthrough}} after years of failed experiments.
mnemonic: BREAK through a wall of difficulty.

definition: the quality of being brief and concise
examples: The brevity of her letter surprised him; it contained only three short sentences.
Poets prize brevity, saying a great deal in very few words.
cloze: "{{Brevity}} is the soul of wit," Polonius says, ironically before rambling on at length.
mnemonic: Brev- like "abbreviate": make it short.

definition: to show resentment or anger, often by drawing oneself up
examples: She bridled at the suggestion that she had copied her colleague's work.
The senator bridled when reporters questioned her motives in front of the crowd.
cloze: Employees {{bridle}} at being micromanaged by a supervisor who trusts none of them.
mnemonic: A horse tosses its head against the BRIDLE: you resist and bristle.

definition: to react angrily or defensively, as if hackles raised
examples: She bristled at the suggestion that she had needed help with the project.
The cat bristled when the strange dog wandered into the yard.
cloze: Employees {{bristle}} whenever the manager lectures them about punctuality, since they feel unfairly singled out.
mnemonic: A BRISTLE is a stiff hair; an angry person's hair stands up like a brush.

definition: a forceful verbal attack; originally a ship's side or a volley from it
examples: The editorial was a broadside against the mayor's handling of the budget.
In his memoir, the retired general delivered a broadside against his former rivals.
cloze: The senator launched a {{broadside}} against the bill, denouncing every provision in turn.
mnemonic: A ship's broad side firing all its cannons at once.

definition: a trite, unoriginal remark meant to soothe
examples: Telling a grieving friend that time heals all wounds can sound like an empty bromide.
The speech was full of bromides about hard work and never giving up.
cloze: Instead of offering real solutions, the mayor repeated the same old {{bromide}} about patience.
mnemonic: Bromide was a sedative; a BROMIDE remark puts you to sleep.

definition: to tolerate or allow, usually used in the negative
examples: The strict coach would brook no excuses for lateness.
The general could not brook any challenge to his authority.
cloze: The headmaster will not {{brook}} bullying of any kind in his school.
mnemonic: You can't BROOK a brook of nonsense; you'd rather dam it.

definition: to intimidate with stern or overbearing talk
examples: The lawyer tried to browbeat the witness into changing her testimony.
Bullies often browbeat quieter classmates into handing over their lunch money.
cloze: He would {{browbeat}} his employees until they agreed with every decision he made.
mnemonic: Beat down with your BROW: a scowl that cows.

definition: abrupt and curt in manner, often rudely so
examples: The brusque receptionist answered our questions in single words and barely looked up.
His brusque dismissal of her idea left the whole meeting feeling uncomfortable and tense.
cloze: Though not unkind, the surgeon's {{brusque}} manner made nervous patients feel rushed and unimportant.
mnemonic: BRUSQUE sounds like "brusk" — a brush-off.

definition: in an abrupt, curt, and somewhat rude manner
examples: The clerk brusquely waved the customer away without hearing the question.
"Sit down," the doctor said brusquely, and began scribbling notes.
cloze: He answered so {{brusquely}} that the nervous applicant was too intimidated to ask a follow-up.
mnemonic: BRUSQUE sounds like BRUSH-off - a quick brush-off reply.

definition: to resist or go against, especially a trend or authority
examples: The company bucked the industry trend by hiring more workers during the recession.
Few employees dared to buck the boss's policy on remote work.
cloze: Few investors were willing to {{buck}} the market and buy when everyone else was selling.
mnemonic: A bucking horse throws off its rider: it resists control.

definition: relating to pleasant country life; pastoral
examples: The painting shows a bucolic scene of shepherds and sheep beneath a golden sky.
They left the noisy city for a bucolic village surrounded by meadows and orchards.
cloze: The poet's {{bucolic}} verses celebrate peaceful farms, grazing cattle, and quiet rural evenings.
mnemonic: Sounds like "buck" — deer in a peaceful countryside.

definition: clumsy and awkward in a foolish, inept way
examples: The bumbling waiter dropped the tray and then apologized to the wrong table.
His bumbling attempts at fixing the sink flooded the entire kitchen.
cloze: The film's {{bumbling}} detective stumbles into clues by accident and never realizes it.
mnemonic: BUMBLING bumps and fumbles: a bumblebee bumping into things.

definition: irritatingly self-assertive or conceited
examples: The bumptious young manager lectured veterans about methods he had never actually tried himself.
His bumptious confidence annoyed colleagues who knew how little he had actually accomplished at work.
cloze: Everyone avoided the {{bumptious}} newcomer, who bragged constantly and assumed his opinion mattered most.
mnemonic: BUMP into everyone with your ego.

definition: to grow or increase rapidly; to flourish
examples: Tech startups began to burgeon in the city once cheap office space became available.
Her interest in astronomy burgeoned after she looked through a real telescope.
cloze: As the population continued to {{burgeon}}, the town had to build new schools every year.
mnemonic: Burgeon sounds like "burger on" — it swells and grows.

definition: to support or reinforce, as with an argument or structure
examples: The lawyer buttressed her claim with letters and sworn testimony.
Thick stone walls buttress the old cathedral against the strong winds.
cloze: The researchers presented new data to {{buttress}} their controversial theory.
mnemonic: A BUTT-ress: leaning your butt on a wall for support.

definition: excessively complicated and secretive, like a labyrinth
examples: The byzantine rules for getting a permit baffled even the lawyers.
He struggled through the byzantine bureaucracy to renew his passport.
cloze: The company's {{byzantine}} organizational chart left nobody certain who was responsible for what.
mnemonic: Byzantium's court was famous for intricate intrigue.

definition: a harsh, jarring mixture of sounds
examples: A cacophony of car horns and sirens filled the street at rush hour.
The orchestra's tuning produced a cacophony before the conductor raised his baton.
cloze: The {{cacophony}} of barking dogs and shouting vendors made the market impossible to ignore.
mnemonic: CACA-phony: it sounds like crows, "caw caw" — ugly noise.

definition: extremely thin, pale, and gaunt like a corpse
examples: The cadaverous prisoner could barely stand after months in the dungeon.
Her cadaverous face, sunken and gray, alarmed the doctors at the clinic.
cloze: The illness left him {{cadaverous}}, with hollow cheeks and skin the color of paper.
mnemonic: CADAVER = corpse; looks like one.

definition: to persuade by flattery or gentle urging
examples: He cajoled his reluctant friend into lending him the car with compliments and promises of free lunches.
She gently cajoled the shy boy onto the dance floor with smiles and constant encouragement.
cloze: Despite all the managers' efforts to {{cajole}} the client, she refused to change her mind.
mnemonic: CAJOLE sounds like "cage a jolly" — coax a bird out sweetly.

definition: emotionally hardened; insensitive to others' suffering
examples: The callous landlord evicted the family in the middle of winter without a moment's pity or concern.
His callous joke about the disaster offended every listener, many of whom had lost friends in it.
cloze: It was {{callous}} of them to ignore the pleas of the starving villagers.
mnemonic: CALLOUS sounds like "callus" — hardened skin means a hardened heart.

definition: immature and inexperienced
examples: The callow recruit had never left his village and trusted everyone he met.
Critics dismissed the novel as the work of a callow writer with little real experience.
cloze: The {{callow}} intern, fresh from college, made several embarrassing mistakes in his first week on the job.
mnemonic: CALLOW: like a bird with bald (callow) fledgling skin.

definition: a false statement made to damage someone's reputation; slander
examples: The rival's calumny, claiming she had stolen funds, nearly ruined the candidate's campaign.
He sued the paper for repeating the calumny after it had been disproved.
cloze: Spreading {{calumny}} about a colleague may win you a promotion briefly, but it ruins your name.
mnemonic: CALUMNY sounds like 'column' - lies printed in a column about someone.

definition: a false or misleading story deliberately spread as if true
examples: The rumor that the mayor had fled the city was a canard invented by rivals.
Historians long ago exposed the story as a canard, though it still circulates online.
cloze: Fact-checkers quickly dismissed the {{canard}} about the bank's imminent collapse.
mnemonic: Canard is French for 'duck': a story as quacky as a duck.

definition: truthful and straightforward, even if awkward
examples: In a candid interview, the actor admitted that his first film was a failure.
I appreciate your candid feedback, even though it was hard to hear.
cloze: The teacher gave a {{candid}} assessment of the student's weak performance.
mnemonic: CANDID: like "candle" light on the truth.

definition: frankness and sincerity in speech
examples: I appreciated the doctor's candidness about my chances of recovery.
His candidness sometimes shocked colleagues who preferred polite evasions.
cloze: The interviewer praised the actress for her {{candidness}} about the failures in her career.
mnemonic: CANDID camera shows the truth; candidness = being the same.

definition: honesty and openness in speech
examples: Her candor about her mistakes earned the respect of her team.
The patient appreciated the doctor's candor regarding the risks of surgery.
cloze: He answered the reporters with disarming {{candor}}, admitting every error without excuse.
mnemonic: CANDOR looks like candid: straight talk.

definition: shrewd and careful, especially in money or politics
examples: The canny investor sold his shares just before the market fell.
A canny negotiator, she let the other side speak first.
cloze: With {{canny}} timing, the senator released her statement just before the news cycle ended.
mnemonic: Sounds like "can-do" plus clever: a person who knows how to win.

definition: bad-tempered, argumentative, and difficult
examples: The cantankerous old man complained about everything from the soup to the weather.
A cantankerous colleague, she disputed every suggestion in the meeting.
cloze: Our {{cantankerous}} neighbor argues with everyone who walks past his gate.
mnemonic: CAN-TANK-erous: a grouchy man in a tank.

definition: having a lot of room; spacious
examples: The capacious bag held all her books, a laptop, and her lunch.
A capacious closet ran the whole length of the hall.
cloze: The {{capacious}} hall could seat well over two thousand people.
mnemonic: CAPACIOUS: has great capacity.

definition: the maximum amount something can hold or produce; the ability to do something
examples: The reservoir's capacity is enough to supply the city for two years.
Human beings have a remarkable capacity for learning languages in early childhood.
cloze: The stadium reached full {{capacity}} an hour before the match began.
mnemonic: CAPACITY: a CAP holds a certain amount.

definition: to surrender or give in after resistance
examples: After months of siege and hunger, the city finally capitulated to the powerful invading army.
The company refused to capitulate to the union's demands and chose to endure a long and costly strike.
cloze: Facing certain defeat, the general chose to {{capitulate}} rather than lose more troops.
mnemonic: CAPITULATE: lower your head (caput) in surrender.

definition: a sudden unpredictable change of mood or behavior
examples: On a caprice, he abandoned his career and moved to a farm.
The king's decisions were governed by caprice rather than law.
cloze: She bought the expensive car on a mere {{caprice}}, regretting it the next day.
mnemonic: CAPRICE sounds like "capricious" goat jumps.

definition: given to sudden, unpredictable changes of mood or behavior
examples: The capricious king rewarded his servants one day and punished the same people the next.
Capricious weather made it impossible for the organizers to plan an outdoor picnic with any confidence.
cloze: Her {{capricious}} decisions confused her staff, who never knew what she would want next.
mnemonic: CAPRI goats leap unpredictably.

definition: of chief importance; fundamental
examples: Honesty is the cardinal virtue in a scientific career, the professor told us.
The cardinal rule of the lab is to label every sample immediately.
cloze: Ignoring customer feedback is a {{cardinal}} error for any new business.
mnemonic: Cardinals are the chief officers of the church; cardinal = chief.

definition: to complain or find fault in a petty way
examples: Stop carping about the cold coffee and be grateful you have a job.
Critics carped at minor flaws while ignoring the film's real achievements.
cloze: She would {{carp}} endlessly about the tiniest details of the arrangements.
mnemonic: A fish "carp" opens its mouth and keeps nagging.

definition: tending to find fault in a petty, annoying way
examples: The carping reviewer complained about the font, the margins, and even the paper.
Tired of her mother-in-law's carping remarks, she finally left the room.
cloze: Constant {{carping}} from the audience made it hard for the speaker to continue.
mnemonic: A CARP fish nips and nips: a carper nitpicks.

definition: to criticize or punish severely
examples: The coach castigated his players in the locker room for their lazy and careless performance.
Newspapers castigated the mayor for ignoring repeated warnings about the flooding that damaged hundreds of homes.
cloze: The judge did not hesitate to {{castigate}} the company for its reckless disregard of safety.
mnemonic: CASTIGATE sounds like "cast a gate" — you cast out the guilty with harsh words.

definition: a violent upheaval or disaster that causes great change
examples: The earthquake was a cataclysm that destroyed the old city in under a minute.
Historians describe the world war as a cataclysm that redrew the map of Europe.
cloze: Ecologists warn that a single {{cataclysm}}, such as a massive volcanic eruption, could end a species.
mnemonic: CATA-CLYSM: a flood crashing down (Greek kluzein, to wash over).

definition: something that triggers or speeds up change
examples: The president's speech was the catalyst for massive public protests.
In chemistry, a catalyst speeds up a reaction without being consumed.
cloze: The scandal served as a {{catalyst}} for long-overdue reform of the industry.
mnemonic: CATA-LYST: lets a reaction go fast, like "list" of things sparking.

definition: providing emotional release or relief
examples: Writing about her grief in a journal was a cathartic experience that finally released months of pent-up sorrow.
He found a long, hard cry cathartic after the stressful week and felt much calmer afterward.
cloze: The ending of the play was {{cathartic}}, releasing the audience from the tension that had built up.
mnemonic: CATHARSIS cleans you out: tears or laughter purge the emotion.

definition: broad and wide-ranging, as in tastes or interests (lowercase sense)
examples: She has catholic tastes in music, enjoying everything from opera to punk.
His catholic interests ranged from astronomy to medieval poetry and cooking.
cloze: With her {{catholic}} curiosity, she read widely across history, science, and fiction.
mnemonic: Greek katholikos: 'universal', taking in the whole.

definition: sarcastic and biting; able to burn or corrode
examples: Her caustic wit left the audience laughing and the unfortunate target of her jokes squirming.
Caustic chemicals such as drain cleaner must be handled carefully with gloves and protective goggles.
cloze: The critic's {{caustic}} review, full of stinging sarcasm, wounded the playwright deeply.
mnemonic: Think of caustic soda: it burns.

definition: showing a lack of proper concern; dismissive
examples: His cavalier attitude to safety rules put the entire crew at risk.
She was cavalier about deadlines and often submitted work days late.
cloze: The manager's {{cavalier}} treatment of customer complaints cost the company many clients.
mnemonic: CAVALIER: a horseman looking down on others.

definition: to raise petty objections; to quibble
examples: It is easy to cavil at small flaws in an otherwise excellent performance by the cast.
Critics cavilled over the film's length but admitted that its story was gripping.
cloze: She tends to {{cavil}} at every minor detail of the plan instead of offering a better one.
mnemonic: CAVIL sounds like "cave in" — trivial objections.

definition: to stop or come to an end
examples: Production at the factory ceased when the main supplier went out of business.
The volcano has not ceased erupting since it first awakened last spring.
cloze: Fish populations may {{cease}} to reproduce if water temperatures rise too far.
mnemonic: CEASE-fire: stop shooting.

definition: to give up or surrender (territory, rights, or power)
examples: After the war, the defeated country ceded a strip of land to its neighbor.
The founder reluctantly ceded control of the company to a new board.
cloze: Neither side was willing to {{cede}} even a small point during the negotiations.
mnemonic: CEDE = 'seed' it away; give it up.

definition: swiftness of movement or action
examples: The firefighters responded with remarkable celerity, reaching the burning building within three minutes.
With great celerity, the clerk processed the entire stack of forms before lunchtime arrived.
cloze: The courier delivered the package with such {{celerity}} that the customer received it the same morning.
mnemonic: CELERITY resembles "accelerate" — speed.

definition: to examine and remove objectionable material from books, films, or letters
examples: The regime censored newspapers, cutting any article that criticized the government.
Editors were pressured to censor the scene before the film aired.
cloze: Authorities tried to {{censor}} the book, deleting every passage that questioned official policy.
mnemonic: A CENSOR makes things SENSible by cutting - or so he claims.

definition: to criticize harshly and officially
examples: The committee voted to censure the senator for misusing funds.
Parents censured the school for its slow response to the safety problem.
cloze: The board voted to publicly {{censure}} the director for misleading shareholders.
mnemonic: CENSURE sounds like "sensor": a sensor judging your faults.

definition: intellectual rather than emotional
examples: The professor's cerebral approach to poetry, all analysis and theory, left little room for feeling or enjoyment.
It was a cerebral film that rewarded careful thought but bored audiences hoping for fast action.
cloze: Known for his {{cerebral}} style, the chess master rarely showed emotion at the board.
mnemonic: CEREBRAL: cerebrum is the brain.

definition: distress or embarrassment caused by failure or humiliation
examples: To her chagrin, she realized she had been wearing mismatched shoes all day.
He read the harsh review with deep chagrin.
cloze: Much to his {{chagrin}}, the proof he was so proud of contained a glaring error.
mnemonic: CHAGRIN sounds like 'sha-GRIN' - a sheepish grin hiding embarrassment.

definition: to support or defend a cause or person strongly
examples: She championed the rights of workers throughout her long career.
The mayor championed the plan to build new public libraries in every district.
cloze: For decades the senator {{championed}} educational reform, fighting for funding in every budget.
mnemonic: A champion fights for a side; to champion is to fight for a cause.

definition: a person falsely claiming skill or knowledge
examples: The charlatan sold bottles of colored water as a cure for every disease.
He was exposed as a charlatan with no medical training.
cloze: The self-proclaimed financial guru turned out to be a {{charlatan}} who lost clients' money.
mnemonic: CHARLATAN: "charl" for chatter plus fraud — a talker with nothing.

definition: cautious and wary about doing something
examples: After being cheated once, she was chary of lending money to anyone, even close friends and relatives.
Investors remain chary of risky ventures after the crash and keep most of their money in safe bonds.
cloze: Voters are {{chary}} of promises from politicians who have failed before.
mnemonic: CHARY sounds like "cherry" — be careful with it.

definition: to scold or rebuke severely
examples: The coach chastised the whole team after the game for its sloppy play and lack of effort.
She chastised her son for lying about his homework and told him to apologize to his teacher.
cloze: The principal will {{chastise}} any student who bullies others.
mnemonic: CHASTISE contains "chaste": you make someone pure by scolding.

definition: fanatical belief in the superiority of one's own group or sex
examples: His chauvinism led him to dismiss every idea that came from another country.
Male chauvinism in the workplace kept many talented women from promotion.
cloze: Economists warned that national {{chauvinism}} could poison trade relations with neighbors.
mnemonic: Named for Chauvin, a soldier absurdly devoted to Napoleon.

definition: a person with aggressive, prejudiced belief in the superiority of their own group or sex
examples: The chauvinist insisted that his country's customs were superior to all others.
As a male chauvinist, he refused to take seriously any suggestion from women on the team.
cloze: The senator was branded a {{chauvinist}} for dismissing every foreign product as inferior.
mnemonic: Named for Chauvin, a fanatical soldier devoted to his own side.

definition: to restrain, curb, or hold back
examples: The government introduced tariffs to check the flow of cheap imports.
She tried to check her anger before replying to the insult.
cloze: Strong laws are needed to {{check}} the spread of corruption in public office.
mnemonic: Chess: a CHECK stops the king in his tracks.

definition: marked by ups and downs, often including disreputable episodes
examples: The mayor had a checkered past that included bankruptcy and a brief jail term.
The company's checkered history of success and scandal made investors cautious.
cloze: Despite a {{checkered}} career, the old detective was still respected for his instincts.
mnemonic: A checkerboard has dark and light squares: good and bad mixed.

definition: trickery used to deceive, especially in legal or political matters
examples: Through legal chicanery, the firm avoided paying the money it owed.
Voters grew weary of political chicanery and demanded honest government.
cloze: The contract was a product of clever financial {{chicanery}} designed to confuse the auditors.
mnemonic: CHICKEN-ery: a sneaky chicken that tricks you.

definition: an unrealistic dream or illusion; a wild fanciful notion
examples: His plan to get rich overnight turned out to be a chimera.
For years, peace in the region seemed a chimera that no treaty could make real.
cloze: Perfect efficiency is a {{chimera}}: every real system loses some energy along the way.
mnemonic: The CHIMERA was a mythical monster: imaginary, not real.

definition: courteous, honorable, and considerate, especially toward women
examples: The chivalrous stranger gave up his umbrella and walked home in the storm.
Medieval tales praise chivalrous knights who protected the weak and kept their word.
cloze: It was a {{chivalrous}} gesture when he offered his coat to the shivering stranger.
mnemonic: CHIVALROUS: a CHEVALIER, a French knight on horseback.

definition: easily angered; bad-tempered
examples: The choleric general exploded in rage at the smallest mistake and often threw papers across the room.
His choleric temper made him extremely hard to work for, and many employees quit within a month.
cloze: The {{choleric}} landlord shouted at tenants who were even a day late with rent.
mnemonic: CHOLERA-ic: sick and furious.

definition: to laugh in a breathy, gleeful way
examples: The children began to chortle as the clown tripped over his oversized shoes.
He chortled with delight when he saw his rival's embarrassing mistake.
cloze: She could not help but {{chortle}} at the absurd headline in the morning paper.
mnemonic: Blend of CHUCKLE + SNORT, coined by Lewis Carroll.

definition: rude and surly; bad-mannered
examples: It would be churlish to refuse such a generous gift after the host went to so much trouble.
His churlish reply to the waiter embarrassed his date and ruined the mood of the evening.
cloze: The {{churlish}} clerk grunted at customers and never once looked up from his phone.
mnemonic: Churl = peasant; churlish people behave like boors.

definition: indirect and roundabout
examples: We took a circuitous route through the hills to avoid the heavy traffic on the main road.
His circuitous explanation wandered through a dozen unrelated stories and never actually got to the point.
cloze: The river followed a {{circuitous}} path before eventually reaching the sea.
mnemonic: CIRCUIT: going around in a circle.

definition: the use of many words where fewer would do; roundabout speech
examples: The minister's circumlocution avoided the question while using nearly five hundred words.
Legal documents are famous for circumlocution, burying simple ideas inside lengthy and tangled phrases.
cloze: Rather than say he was fired, he used {{circumlocution}}, talking about "changes in his professional direction."
mnemonic: CIRCUM = around, LOCUTION = speaking: talking around the point.

definition: to restrict within limits, or to draw a boundary around
examples: Strict rules circumscribe what the interns are allowed to do without supervision.
Her options were circumscribed by a tiny budget and a rapidly approaching deadline.
cloze: The new law will {{circumscribe}} the powers of the agency and prevent future abuses.
mnemonic: CIRCUM (around) + scribe (write): draw a circle around.

definition: cautious, careful to consider consequences
examples: The circumspect lawyer reviewed every clause before advising her client.
Being circumspect about money, he saved for years before buying a house.
cloze: Investors were {{circumspect}} after the crash and examined every proposal with great care.
mnemonic: CIRCUM + SPECT: look around before acting.

definition: a condition or fact connected with an event or situation
examples: Under normal circumstances, the river floods only in early spring.
The researchers studied how economic circumstances influence a family's access to education.
cloze: Given the {{circumstance}} of the drought, the government rationed water across the region.
mnemonic: CIRCUM = around: things standing AROUND an event.

definition: to avoid or get around an obstacle or rule, often cleverly
examples: The company circumvented the regulations by registering overseas.
Drivers circumvented the roadblock by taking a farm track.
cloze: Clever lawyers found a way to {{circumvent}} the new restrictions without technically breaking the law.
mnemonic: CIRCUM = around, VENT = go: go around.

definition: to quote or mention as evidence or an example
examples: Scholars cite the study as proof that early reading improves later achievement.
The essay cites several historical documents to support its argument.
cloze: Students must {{cite}} their sources whenever they use another author's ideas.
mnemonic: CITE sounds like SITE: point to the source site.

definition: kept secret, often because illegal or improper
examples: The two leaders held a clandestine meeting in a remote mountain cabin, far from the press.
Police uncovered a clandestine laboratory hidden beneath the warehouse where illegal drugs were being produced.
cloze: The spies communicated through {{clandestine}} messages hidden inside ordinary newspapers.
mnemonic: CLAN + DESTINE: a clan with its own destined secrets.

definition: to make something easier to understand
examples: The professor clarified the difficult concept with a simple diagram on the board.
Scientists published additional data to clarify the confusion about the earlier results.
cloze: Please {{clarify}} what you mean by that term, because it has several possible definitions.
mnemonic: CLARify = make CLEAR.

definition: mercy shown in punishing someone
examples: The governor granted clemency to the prisoner after twenty years.
The defense lawyer pleaded for clemency on account of his client's youth.
cloze: The judge showed {{clemency}}, reducing the sentence because of the defendant's remorse.
mnemonic: CLEMENCY: "clement" weather is mild; mild justice.

definition: excessively sweet or sentimental to the point of disgust
examples: The cloying perfume filled the small elevator and gave everyone riding in it an instant headache.
Critics found the film's cloying sentimentality hard to stomach and described its ending as sickly sweet.
cloze: The dessert was so {{cloying}} that I could manage only a single bite.
mnemonic: Cloying = "clogging" with sweetness.

definition: to come together to form one whole
examples: Small, scattered protest groups coalesced into a powerful national movement within the space of a single year.
The scattered clouds slowly coalesced into a dark and threatening storm front over the valley.
cloze: Disparate ideas began to {{coalesce}} into a clear plan as the discussion continued.
mnemonic: CO + ALESCE (grow): grow together.

definition: to treat with excessive care and indulgence
examples: Parents who coddle their children, protecting them from every difficulty, may stunt their growing independence.
The pampered prince was coddled by his servants and rarely heard anything but praise or good news.
cloze: It does no good to {{coddle}} athletes who need to be challenged.
mnemonic: CODDLE: like cuddle too much.

definition: to force someone to act by threats or pressure
examples: The gang tried to coerce the shopkeeper into paying them money every month for so-called protection.
No suspect should ever be coerced, by threats or force, into signing a confession against their will.
cloze: The dictator used fear to {{coerce}} the citizens into supporting his regime.
mnemonic: CO-ERCE: sounds like "coax" but by force.

definition: clear, logical, and convincing
examples: She presented a cogent argument, clear and logical, that persuaded even the most doubtful members of the board.
The report offered several cogent reasons for delaying the project until the funding was secure.
cloze: His {{cogent}} analysis of the data left the committee with no grounds for disagreement.
mnemonic: COGENT: your COGs click together neatly in your mind.

definition: to think deeply about something; to ponder
examples: The philosopher sat by the fire for hours, cogitating on the meaning of freedom.
Give me a day to cogitate on your offer before I give you an answer.
cloze: The jury needed several hours to {{cogitate}} before delivering a carefully considered verdict.
mnemonic: COGITATE: "cogito ergo sum" — I think, therefore I am.

definition: aware or fully informed
examples: She was cognizant of the risks but went ahead anyway.
The manager is well cognizant of the problems on the factory floor.
cloze: Being {{cognizant}} of the deadline, the team worked through the weekend.
mnemonic: COGNIZANT: cognition = knowing.

definition: logical, consistent, and easy to follow as a whole
examples: The essay presented a coherent argument supported by clear evidence in every paragraph.
Researchers struggled to form a coherent picture from the scattered fragments of pottery.
cloze: A {{coherent}} theory must explain all the observations without contradicting any of them.
mnemonic: CO-HERE: ideas stick (cohere) together.

definition: sticking together; forming a unified whole
examples: The cohesive team worked together seamlessly during the crisis, each member trusting the others completely.
A cohesive essay links every paragraph logically to the next so that the argument flows smoothly.
cloze: The mayor hoped to build a more {{cohesive}} community from the city's many neighborhoods.
mnemonic: COHESIVE: like glue "adhesive".

definition: to happen at the same time, or to match exactly
examples: The arrival of the migratory birds coincides with the first warm weeks of spring.
The artist's interests coincided with those of the museum, so the exhibition was a success.
cloze: Peak tourist season tends to {{coincide}} with the school holidays in many countries.
mnemonic: CO + INCIDENT: two incidents together.

definition: to fall down suddenly or fail completely
examples: The roof of the ancient temple collapsed during a severe earthquake.
Several powerful civilizations collapsed within a few decades because of drought and warfare.
cloze: If the bee population continues to {{collapse}}, many crops will lose their natural pollinators.
mnemonic: COLLAPSE: all LAPSE (fall) down.

definition: a person who works in the same profession or organization
examples: The biologist shared her results with colleagues at an international conference.
He asked a colleague in the history department to read his draft before submission.
cloze: A fellow {{colleague}} at the university helped her design the survey.
mnemonic: COLLEAGUE: a friend you work with, like a team-LEAGUE.

definition: informal, characteristic of everyday conversation
examples: The author's colloquial style makes the book read like a friendly chat over coffee.
Words like "gonna" are colloquial and should be avoided in formal academic essays.
cloze: The speaker used a {{colloquial}} phrase, which some in the audience found too casual for the occasion.
mnemonic: COLLOQUIAL contains "loqu" = speak; spoken casually.

definition: secret cooperation for an illegal or deceitful purpose
examples: The two rival firms were fined millions for collusion to fix prices and cheat their customers.
Investigators found strong evidence of collusion between corrupt officials and the contractors who won the city's building projects.
cloze: The inspectors, acting in {{collusion}} with the factory owners, hid the safety violations.
mnemonic: COLLUDE: "collide" secretly working together.

definition: extremely large; gigantic
examples: The explorers stood before a colossal statue carved out of the mountainside.
The company announced a colossal loss that wiped out ten years of profit.
cloze: Building the dam was a {{colossal}} undertaking requiring thousands of workers and a decade of labor.
mnemonic: The COLOSSEUM was colossal.

definition: to begin or start
examples: Construction on the new science building will commence early next spring.
The ceremony commenced with a short speech by the university president.
cloze: Classes will {{commence}} on the first Monday of September.
mnemonic: COMMENCE: Come and 'mence' is the start of a course.

definition: deserving praise
examples: Her commendable honesty in admitting the error earned the respect of her colleagues.
The volunteers did commendable work after the flood, sleeping little for days.
cloze: The firefighters showed {{commendable}} courage in rescuing the trapped family.
mnemonic: COMMEND + able: able to be commended.

definition: proportionate; matching in size or degree
examples: Salary will be commensurate with the experience and qualifications of the successful applicant, the advertisement explained.
The punishment was not commensurate with the minor offense, and many observers thought it far too harsh.
cloze: He insisted that the reward be {{commensurate}} with the great risk he had taken.
mnemonic: COM + MENSURE: measured together, same measure.

definition: to make up for a loss or give payment for something
examples: The government compensated farmers whose crops had been destroyed by the flood.
Some animals compensate for poor eyesight with an exceptionally sharp sense of smell.
cloze: The company agreed to {{compensate}} workers for the extra hours they put in.
mnemonic: COM-PENSATE: pay (pens) back to balance.

definition: to collect and arrange information from various sources
examples: The librarian compiled a list of rare books held in the university archives.
Researchers compiled data from twenty years of weather records to study long-term trends.
cloze: Her task was to {{compile}} the survey results into a single report.
mnemonic: COMPILE: pile things together.

definition: smugly satisfied with oneself and unaware of dangers
examples: The champions grew complacent and were shocked by a surprise defeat.
A complacent attitude toward safety can lead to terrible accidents.
cloze: Because sales had been strong for years, the management became {{complacent}} and ignored new competitors.
mnemonic: COMPLACENT = comfortably PLACID with yourself.

definition: eager to please; willing to go along with others' wishes
examples: The complaisant host rearranged the dinner three times to suit every guest's taste.
A complaisant assistant, he never questioned the boss's odd instructions.
cloze: The {{complaisant}} committee approved every proposal without debate, eager not to cause any friction.
mnemonic: COMPLAISANT: COMPLY + PLEASANT - he complies to please.

definition: to complete or improve by adding something that goes well with it
examples: Modern surveys complement traditional interviews by reaching a larger number of people.
The soft lighting complemented the warm colors of the paintings in the gallery.
cloze: A diet rich in vegetables can {{complement}} regular exercise to improve overall health.
mnemonic: comPLEment = completes (not compliment, praise).

definition: completing or enhancing each other; supplying what the other lacks
examples: The two partners had complementary skills: one designed, the other sold.
Wine and cheese are complementary, each bringing out the best in the other.
cloze: Their talents were {{complementary}}, so the project succeeded where solo efforts had failed.
mnemonic: COMPLEMENT with an E completes; 'compliment' with I praises.

definition: involved with others in wrongdoing
examples: Officials who looked away were as complicit in the fraud as those who profited directly.
She refused to remain silent and become complicit in the cover-up of the accident.
cloze: By staying silent, the board members became {{complicit}} in the scheme to hide the company's losses.
mnemonic: COMPLICIT sounds like "accomplice".

definition: one of the parts that make up a larger whole
examples: Water is a key component of nearly every living cell.
Each component of the machine must be tested before the final assembly.
cloze: The most important {{component}} of the plan is a reliable source of funding.
mnemonic: COMPONENT: parts that COMPOSE a thing.

definition: to make worse by adding to existing difficulties
examples: Heavy rains compounded the flood damage caused by the earlier storm.
He compounded his error by lying about it afterward.
cloze: The delay was {{compounded}} by a strike that shut down the shipping port.
mnemonic: Compound interest piles more on top; compound problems pile up too.

definition: to consist of or be made up of
examples: The country comprises twenty-six states, each with its own regional government.
A typical cell comprises a nucleus, cytoplasm, and an outer membrane.
cloze: The committee will {{comprise}} experts from biology, chemistry, and engineering.
mnemonic: COMPRISE = COMPlete set, includes all parts.

definition: a feeling of guilt about doing something wrong
examples: He lied to his friend without a shred of compunction.
She felt no compunction about leaving early to avoid the speech.
cloze: The thief took the money without {{compunction}}, though he knew the family needed it.
mnemonic: COM-PUNCTION: a puncture in your conscience.

definition: to admit something is true after first resisting; to yield
examples: The candidate was forced to concede that her earlier forecast had been wrong.
After hours of debate, he finally conceded the point to his opponent.
cloze: The champion was too proud to {{concede}} defeat, even when the score was hopeless.
mnemonic: CON + CEDE: cede the point to the other side.

definition: to form an idea in the mind, or to imagine
examples: Einstein conceived the theory of relativity while working as a patent clerk.
It is difficult to conceive how enormous the universe really is.
cloze: Engineers first had to {{conceive}} a new design before they could build the bridge.
mnemonic: CON-CEIVE: take in (receive) an idea.

definition: to win over or calm an angry person or settle a dispute
examples: The mediator tried to conciliate the two factions with a series of compromises.
He sent flowers to conciliate his offended neighbor after the noisy party.
cloze: The manager worked to {{conciliate}} the angry customers by offering refunds and apologies.
mnemonic: CON (with) + CIL (council): sit at a council together and make peace.

definition: intended to calm anger or make peace
examples: The president adopted a conciliatory tone, hoping to end the dispute.
She offered a conciliatory gesture by inviting her rival to lunch.
cloze: After the argument, he sent a {{conciliatory}} note apologizing and proposing a compromise.
mnemonic: CONCILIATORY: CONCILE sounds like "reconcile".

definition: to reach a decision or opinion based on evidence; to end
examples: After reviewing the data, the researchers concluded that the drug was effective.
The author concludes the chapter with a summary of her main argument.
cloze: From the fossil evidence, scientists {{conclude}} that dinosaurs were warm-blooded.
mnemonic: CON-CLUDE: shut (close) the argument with a decision.

definition: occurring together with something else, naturally accompanying
examples: Rapid growth brought concomitant problems of traffic and rising rents.
The drug's benefits come with concomitant risks that patients must weigh.
cloze: Fame and its {{concomitant}} loss of privacy were more than the young singer expected.
mnemonic: CON (with) + COMITANT (company): comes along with.

definition: to agree
examples: All three medical experts concurred that the painting was a clever forgery and not a genuine work.
The appeals judges concurred with the lower court's decision and rejected the company's lengthy objections.
cloze: I {{concur}} with your assessment that the plan needs more funding.
mnemonic: CON + CUR: running together in agreement.

definition: happening at the same time
examples: The study ran concurrent experiments in three different laboratories across Europe and North America.
Concurrent revolts in several provinces weakened the central government of the ancient empire.
cloze: Students may take two {{concurrent}} courses as long as the schedules do not overlap.
mnemonic: CON + CURRENT: running along together.

definition: to accept or overlook behavior regarded as wrong
examples: The school does not condone bullying in any form and punishes students who are caught engaging in it.
By saying nothing, he seemed to condone his friends' dishonest scheme, though he privately disapproved of it.
cloze: Few leaders would openly {{condone}} corruption among their own advisers.
mnemonic: CON + DONE: act as if the wrong is done and forgiven.

definition: making a certain outcome likely or possible
examples: A quiet library is conducive to the kind of concentrated study that exams demand.
Warm, humid weather is conducive to the rapid growth of mold.
cloze: Loud construction noise is hardly {{conducive}} to a restful afternoon nap.
mnemonic: CON-DUCE: leads to (like 'produce') a result.

definition: to carry out or organize an activity
examples: Marine biologists conducted a survey of coral reefs along the northern coast.
The professor conducted an experiment to test how temperature affects plant growth.
cloze: Scientists plan to {{conduct}} further tests before publishing their findings.
mnemonic: CON-DUCT: lead (duct) an activity through.

definition: to keep within limits or restrict to a place
examples: Early experiments were confined to small laboratories because the equipment was bulky.
The disease was confined to a small area thanks to rapid quarantine measures.
cloze: The rules attempt to {{confine}} fishing to certain months of the year.
mnemonic: CON-FINE: keep it within a fine (limit) line.

definition: to establish that something is true
examples: Laboratory tests confirmed that the sample was far older than first believed.
The archaeologist's discovery confirmed the legend of the lost city.
cloze: Further experiments are needed to {{confirm}} the results.
mnemonic: CON-FIRM: make FIRM.

definition: a large, destructive fire
examples: A conflagration swept through the old harbor district and destroyed dozens of wooden warehouses.
The match dropped carelessly in the dry forest ignited a conflagration that burned for weeks.
cloze: The tiny spark grew into a {{conflagration}} that devoured the village within hours.
mnemonic: CON + FLAG: flames flagging across a field.

definition: to merge two or more distinct things into one, confusing them
examples: Many people conflate weather with climate, though they differ greatly.
The report conflates correlation with causation, weakening its argument.
cloze: Do not {{conflate}} confidence with competence; loud people are not always skilled ones.
mnemonic: CON + FLAte: blow things together into one lump.

definition: to comply with rules, standards, or expectations
examples: All buildings in the district must conform to strict safety regulations.
Some scientists feared that young researchers would conform to prevailing theories rather than question them.
cloze: Students are expected to {{conform}} to the university's code of academic honesty.
mnemonic: CON-FORM: take the same form as others.

definition: to confuse or surprise; to prove wrong
examples: The sudden change in the rules confounded the beginners, who could no longer follow how the game worked.
The surprising results confounded the experts, whose careful predictions had turned out to be completely wrong.
cloze: The riddle will {{confound}} even clever students who think they know the answer.
mnemonic: CON-FOUND: found something that makes you perplexed.

definition: secretly plotting or scheming, often cooperating in wrongdoing
examples: The two clerks were conniving to hide the missing funds from the auditors.
She suspected her cousin was conniving with the lawyer to take over the estate.
cloze: Rather than face the board, the director kept {{conniving}} behind closed doors to protect himself.
mnemonic: CON-niving: planning a CON behind everyone's back.

definition: an expert judge in matters of taste or art
examples: As a wine connoisseur, he could identify a vintage with a single sip.
The gallery attracted connoisseurs willing to pay high prices for rare prints.
cloze: A true {{connoisseur}} of cheese, she could tell the region of origin from the aroma alone.
mnemonic: Connoisseur: "con-a-sewer" who knows fine things — sounds French "to know".

definition: to make or declare sacred; to dedicate solemnly to a purpose
examples: The bishop consecrated the new cathedral in a ceremony attended by thousands.
She consecrated her life to the care of orphans.
cloze: The community chose to {{consecrate}} the battlefield as a memorial, treating the ground as holy.
mnemonic: CON-SECRATE contains SACRed - to make sacred.

definition: following one after another without a break
examples: The region suffered three consecutive years of drought, devastating local farms.
The team won five consecutive championships between 2010 and 2015.
cloze: Students who miss two {{consecutive}} classes may be dropped from the course.
mnemonic: CONSECUTIVE: SEQUEL after SEQUEL in a row.

definition: as a result; therefore
examples: The soil was poor; consequently, the settlers struggled to grow enough food.
The dam failed, and consequently, the town downstream was flooded.
cloze: The library's funding was cut; {{consequently}}, it had to reduce its opening hours.
mnemonic: CONSEQUENCE + ly = as a result.

definition: fairly large in amount, size, or importance
examples: The new policy had a considerable impact on rural employment.
A considerable amount of ice has disappeared from the glacier in only two decades.
cloze: The expedition required {{considerable}} planning and a large amount of equipment.
mnemonic: CONSIDERable = worth considering because it is big.

definition: to be made up of; to have as the basic element
examples: The Earth's atmosphere consists mainly of nitrogen and oxygen, with traces of other gases.
The course consists of weekly lectures, small group discussions, and a final research project.
cloze: A healthy ecosystem will {{consist}} of many interdependent species.
mnemonic: CON-SIST: all parts sit (sist) together.

definition: clearly visible; attracting attention
examples: Wearing a bright red coat, she was conspicuous in the crowd.
He made a conspicuous effort to avoid looking at his former boss.
cloze: The ugly new tower is {{conspicuous}} against the old skyline of the city.
mnemonic: CON + SPICUOUS: spic = see; easily seen.

definition: anxiety or dismay caused by something unexpected
examples: News of the sudden resignation caused consternation among the staff.
To his consternation, the door was locked and his keys were inside.
cloze: The announcement filled the passengers with {{consternation}} as the plane lost altitude.
mnemonic: CONSTERNATION: your stomach turns over in a stern shock.

definition: a component part; also a voter represented by an official
examples: Hydrogen is a key constituent of water and of nearly all organic compounds.
The senator answered letters from every constituent, whether they had voted for her or not.
cloze: Salt is the main {{constituent}} of the brine, with traces of other minerals.
mnemonic: CONSTITUENT: helps CONSTITUTE the whole thing.

definition: to form or make up a whole; to be equal to
examples: Women constituted nearly half of the factory workforce by the end of the war.
Scientists debate what constitutes evidence of intelligent behavior in animals.
cloze: Leaves {{constitute}} the main part of the diet of these large herbivores.
mnemonic: CONSTITUTE: constitution = what a thing is made of.

definition: to limit or restrict someone or something
examples: Limited funds constrained the museum's ability to expand its collection.
Mountains constrained the early settlers to a narrow strip of fertile land.
cloze: Government regulations can {{constrain}} the growth of small businesses.
mnemonic: CON-STRAIN: strain tightly against freedom.

definition: a limit or restriction on what one can do
examples: Budget constraints forced the school to cancel the field trip.
Working under tight time constraints, the engineers could not test every feature.
cloze: The lack of funds was the main {{constraint}} on the project's expansion.
mnemonic: CONSTRAIN: like a strain that holds you tight.

definition: to interpret the meaning of something in a particular way
examples: Her silence was construed as consent, though she had never agreed.
Don't construe my honesty as hostility; I only want to help.
cloze: Lawyers will {{construe}} the vague clause in whichever way best serves their clients.
mnemonic: CONSTRUE: CONSTRUct a meaning from the words.

definition: complete or perfect in skill; supremely accomplished (the verb means to complete)
examples: She was a consummate professional who never lost her composure under pressure.
The violinist's consummate artistry left the audience speechless.
cloze: Only a {{consummate}} diplomat could have calmed both furious delegations in one afternoon.
mnemonic: CON + SUM: the sum total; all of the skill.

definition: belonging to the present time; living or happening at the same time
examples: The museum displays both ancient pottery and contemporary sculpture in its largest gallery.
Contemporary accounts of the plague describe the terror felt in the crowded medieval cities.
cloze: The author uses {{contemporary}} language to make the old story easier for modern readers.
mnemonic: CON-TEMPO-rary: with the same TEMPO of time.

definition: showing scorn and a sense that someone is beneath one
examples: She gave the amateur's attempt a contemptuous glance and walked away.
His contemptuous tone made it clear he thought the proposal worthless.
cloze: The champion was {{contemptuous}} of his weaker opponents and refused even to shake hands.
mnemonic: Contempt: you look DOWN your nose - 'con-TEMPT-uous' tempts no respect.

definition: to assert; to compete or struggle
examples: Scientists contend that the climate is changing faster than earlier models had predicted, and urge immediate action.
Several strong teams will contend for the national championship this season, so the outcome is hard to predict.
cloze: The lawyer will {{contend}} that her client was not even in the city that night.
mnemonic: CONTEND: tend to fight with words.

definition: causing or likely to cause disagreement; argumentative
examples: The contentious debate over the new tax law divided the city council for the entire spring.
She avoided contentious topics like politics at family dinners to keep the peace among her relatives.
cloze: The {{contentious}} issue of water rights has divided the two regions for decades.
mnemonic: CONTENTious: a contest of tents? fights over everything.

definition: the circumstances or surrounding words that give meaning to something
examples: Readers can often guess a word's meaning from the context of the sentence.
Historians must understand the political context of a document before judging its message.
cloze: Taken out of {{context}}, the quote seems to say the opposite of what the speaker intended.
mnemonic: CON-TEXT: what goes with the text.

definition: a group of people representing or sharing a common feature; also, adjective: dependent on
examples: A large contingent of fans traveled across the country to support the team.
The delegation included a small contingent of scientists and a dozen journalists.
cloze: A strong {{contingent}} of volunteers arrived from the neighboring town to help with the cleanup.
mnemonic: CON + TENd: those who hold together as a group; also 'it depends'.

definition: to state the opposite of; to be inconsistent with
examples: The new evidence contradicts the earlier theory that the climate was stable.
Her findings contradicted those of previous studies, prompting further investigation.
cloze: Witnesses sometimes {{contradict}} one another when describing the same event.
mnemonic: CONTRA-DICT: speak (dict) against.

definition: a striking difference between two things
examples: The contrast between the dry plains and the green river valley was striking.
In contrast to earlier periods, the twentieth century saw rapid population growth.
cloze: The painter used a bold {{contrast}} of light and dark to create drama.
mnemonic: CONTRA-ST: stand against each other.

definition: to give something toward a common result; to help cause
examples: Volunteers contributed thousands of hours to restoring the wetland after the oil spill.
Deforestation contributes to soil erosion and the loss of habitats for many native animals.
cloze: Many factors may {{contribute}} to the success of a business startup.
mnemonic: CON-TRIBUTE: give a tribute together.

definition: feeling or showing remorse for wrongdoing
examples: The contrite thief wept openly in court and returned everything he had stolen from the shop.
She offered a contrite apology for forgetting her friend's birthday and promised to make up for it.
cloze: Looking {{contrite}}, the boy admitted he had broken the window.
mnemonic: CONTRITE: "con-trite" — you feel crushed (Latin terere, to rub).

definition: deep remorse for having done wrong
examples: The boy's tearful contrition convinced his parents that he truly regretted the lie.
He showed no contrition for the harm he had caused, which angered the judge.
cloze: She wrote a letter of {{contrition}}, admitting her mistake and begging forgiveness.
mnemonic: CONTRITION: a heart ground down (triturated) by guilt.

definition: to devise or bring about by clever planning, often artificially
examples: The prisoners contrived a way to signal each other through the pipes.
She contrived to meet him 'by accident' outside his office.
cloze: The author {{contrived}} an unlikely coincidence to bring the lovers back together.
mnemonic: CONTRIVE - 'con' + 'trive': con a plan into being.

definition: a prolonged public disagreement about something
examples: The dam project sparked controversy among environmentalists and local residents.
Scholars still debate the controversy over how the pyramids were built.
cloze: The new law has caused much {{controversy}} among teachers and parents.
mnemonic: CONTROVERSY: CONTRA + VERSE = verses against each other.

definition: stubbornly disobedient to authority
examples: The contumacious witness refused to answer the judge's questions and was held in contempt of court at once.
Contumacious students ignored every instruction from the dean and openly mocked the rules of the school.
cloze: The {{contumacious}} prisoner defied his guards at every turn.
mnemonic: Contumacious = contempt + tenacious: stubbornly contemptuous of authority.

definition: a confusing and difficult problem or puzzle
examples: The ethical conundrum left the committee deadlocked for weeks, since every option seemed equally unacceptable to someone.
How to cut costs without losing staff is a conundrum that troubles nearly every manager today.
cloze: The riddle was a real {{conundrum}}, and none of the students could solve it.
mnemonic: CONUNDRUM sounds like "can't understand rum".

definition: to come together for a meeting, or to call people to meet
examples: Delegates from forty nations convened in Geneva to discuss the climate agreement.
The dean convened a special committee to review the new curriculum.
cloze: The scientists will {{convene}} next month to share their latest research findings.
mnemonic: CON-VENE: come (ven) together.

definition: to change from one form or use to another
examples: Plants convert sunlight into chemical energy through the process known as photosynthesis.
The old factory was converted into an art museum that attracts thousands of visitors each year.
cloze: Engineers developed a machine that can {{convert}} ocean waves into electricity.
mnemonic: CON-VERT: turn (vert) into something else.

definition: friendly, lively and fond of good company
examples: The host's convivial manner put nervous guests at ease right away.
A convivial crowd filled the tavern, laughing and sharing stories.
cloze: The reunion dinner had a {{convivial}} atmosphere, full of toasts and laughter.
mnemonic: CON + VIV (live): living it up together.

definition: extremely complex and difficult to follow
examples: The convoluted plot of the film confused even devoted fans.
He gave a convoluted explanation that only made things less clear.
cloze: The tax code's {{convoluted}} rules require an expert to understand them.
mnemonic: CON-VOLUTE: coiled, twisting like a spiral.

definition: to work together toward a shared goal
examples: Scientists from many nations cooperate to monitor the polar ice caps.
The two villages cooperated to build a dam that protected both from flooding.
cloze: Birds in the colony {{cooperate}} to defend their nests from predators.
mnemonic: CO-OPERATE: operate together.

definition: abundant; plentiful
examples: The student took copious notes during the lecture and filled three entire notebooks by the end of term.
Copious rainfall turned the dry, dusty valley bright green within just a few weeks of spring.
cloze: The chef used {{copious}} amounts of butter, so the sauce was extremely rich.
mnemonic: COPIOUS contains "copy" — lots of copies.

definition: warm, friendly, and polite
examples: The host gave us a cordial welcome and offered tea at once.
Relations between the neighboring countries remain cordial despite trade disputes.
cloze: Despite their rivalry, the two founders maintained a {{cordial}} relationship.
mnemonic: CORD = heart in Latin; a heartfelt greeting.

definition: an abundant supply of good things
examples: The market was a cornucopia of fruit, cheese, bread, and fresh flowers.
The library offers a cornucopia of resources for anyone curious about local history.
cloze: Her garden produced a {{cornucopia}} of tomatoes, beans, and squash by late summer.
mnemonic: CORN + copia: the horn of plenty overflowing with food.

definition: a natural consequence or result that follows from something
examples: A corollary of the new tax is that small shops will raise their prices.
In geometry, the corollary follows directly from the theorem just proved.
cloze: Rising sea levels have an unwelcome {{corollary}}: more frequent flooding of coastal towns.
mnemonic: Corollary = 'little gift' after a proof: a free extra result.

definition: to confirm or support with evidence
examples: Two eyewitnesses corroborated the defendant's account of where he had been on the night in question.
Later experiments corroborated the scientist's original hypothesis and silenced many of her early critics.
cloze: Fingerprints on the glass helped to {{corroborate}} the detective's suspicion that the suspect had been present.
mnemonic: CO + ROBORATE (robust): make a claim strong together.

definition: worldly and sophisticated; at home in many countries and cultures
examples: The cosmopolitan city drew artists and traders from every continent.
Having lived on four continents, she had a cosmopolitan outlook and spoke five languages.
cloze: The restaurant's menu, with dishes from a dozen nations, reflected the owner's {{cosmopolitan}} tastes.
mnemonic: COSMOS + politan: a citizen of the whole cosmos.

definition: pampered; treated with excessive care and protection
examples: The only grandchild was cosseted by relatives who never let her lift a finger.
Having been cosseted all his life, he was shocked by the discomforts of camp.
cloze: The royal heir was {{cosseted}} by servants who anticipated his every wish.
mnemonic: COSSET sounds like 'cozy set': wrapped up in comfort.

definition: having the same boundaries or extent in space, time, or meaning
examples: The county is coterminous with the old kingdom's borders.
Her term of office was coterminous with the president's, ending the same day.
cloze: In ancient times the city and the state were {{coterminous}}, since the walls enclosed the whole country.
mnemonic: CO + TERMINus: sharing the same END or boundary.

definition: to tolerate or approve of
examples: The headmaster would not countenance cheating in any form and expelled students who were caught doing it.
The government could not countenance such flagrant abuse of power and quickly dismissed the officials involved.
cloze: We cannot {{countenance}} violence against peaceful protesters, whatever the reason.
mnemonic: COUNT + ENANCE: you "count" it as acceptable.

definition: to cancel or reverse an order already given
examples: The general countermanded the order to attack when scouts reported a trap.
Only the director could countermand the instructions issued by her deputy.
cloze: The captain was forced to {{countermand}} his earlier command when the weather suddenly turned.
mnemonic: COUNTER + MAND(ate): a command that counters a command.

definition: to desire strongly something belonging to another
examples: She coveted her neighbor's beautiful garden and its blooming roses, and secretly wished that it were hers.
Many athletes covet the gold medal above all else and spend their whole lives training for it.
cloze: He secretly began to {{covet}} his friend's job and the status that came with it.
mnemonic: COVET: love it so, you "cover" it with your eyes.

definition: to frighten into submission; intimidate
examples: The dictator tried to cow his critics with threats of imprisonment.
The bully's size and loud voice were enough to cow the younger students.
cloze: Refusing to be {{cow}}ed by the powerful firm, the small shop kept fighting in court.
mnemonic: A big COW looming over you makes you cower.

definition: to crouch or shrink away in fear
examples: The frightened puppy cowered in the corner whenever anyone raised their voice.
Villagers cowered in their homes as the soldiers marched noisily through the streets.
cloze: Rather than {{cower}} before the bully, she stood tall and calmly demanded that he stop.
mnemonic: COWER sounds like "cow-er": a scared cow ducks.

definition: insensitive, tactless, and lacking refinement
examples: It was crass of him to brag about his bonus in front of laid-off colleagues.
Her crass jokes at the funeral shocked the mourners and offended the family.
cloze: The advertisement was {{crass}} in its use of a tragedy to sell expensive cars.
mnemonic: CRASS sounds like "grass" — rough, not manicured.

definition: contemptibly cowardly
examples: The craven soldier threw down his weapon and ran at the first shot.
Critics condemned the craven refusal of leaders to oppose injustice.
cloze: It was a {{craven}} act to blame an innocent colleague to avoid punishment.
mnemonic: CRAVEN sounds like "crave in" — hiding like a crow.

definition: acceptance of something as true; belief
examples: The detective gave no credence to the suspect's unlikely alibi.
New evidence lent credence to the theory that the painting was a forgery.
cloze: The unsupported rumor deserved no {{credence}}, since nobody could name its source.
mnemonic: CREDit, CREDible: Latin credere, to believe.

definition: deserving praise or respect, though not outstanding
examples: The rookie turned in a creditable performance in her first major race.
Finishing second in such a strong field is a creditable result.
cloze: The team's {{creditable}} showing in the finals earned them polite applause from the crowd.
mnemonic: CREDITable: earns you credit.

definition: willingness to believe things too readily
examples: Con artists prey on the credulity of lonely, trusting people.
The tale was so absurd that it strained even the audience's credulity.
cloze: His {{credulity}} was legendary; he believed every chain letter that landed in his inbox.
mnemonic: CREDulity: too much CREDit given to claims.

definition: too ready to believe things; gullible
examples: Credulous investors believed every promise the swindler made, and most lost their life savings to him.
The credulous child accepted her brother's tall tale about a talking dog living in the attic.
cloze: Only a {{credulous}} person would believe that a stranger wants to give away millions for free.
mnemonic: CRED = believe (credit); credulous believes too much.

definition: sad and disappointed after a setback
examples: The team trudged off the field crestfallen after losing the final.
She looked crestfallen when she learned her application had been rejected.
cloze: The boy's {{crestfallen}} face told us the surprise party had been spoiled.
mnemonic: A rooster's CREST FALLs when it loses a fight.

definition: extremely important, or involving careful judgment
examples: Critical thinking allows students to question assumptions and evaluate evidence.
Water is critical to survival in the harsh desert environment.
cloze: The hospital faced a {{critical}} shortage of blood donors.
mnemonic: CRITICAL = CRITIC judges carefully.

definition: extremely important; decisive
examples: Water is crucial to the survival of every living organism.
Her crucial discovery transformed the way scientists understand the immune system.
cloze: Accurate measurements are {{crucial}} in any scientific experiment.
mnemonic: CRUCIAL = CRUX (the central point).

definition: the decisive or most important point
examples: The crux of the problem is that the funding is simply inadequate.
She went straight to the crux of the matter in her opening statement.
cloze: The {{crux}} of the dispute is who actually owns the land.
mnemonic: CRUX is like cross — the crossing point.

definition: having a hidden or puzzling meaning
examples: She left behind a cryptic message that nobody in the family was able to decipher.
The detective puzzled for hours over the cryptic clue scrawled on the wall in red chalk.
cloze: His {{cryptic}} reply left everyone wondering what he actually meant.
mnemonic: CRYPT: a hidden, dark chamber with secrets.

definition: to take clear, definite form; to become concrete
examples: Her vague ideas began to crystallize into a workable business plan.
Public opposition crystallized after the council announced the plan to close the park.
cloze: After the debate, my opinions seemed to {{crystallize}} into one firm conclusion.
mnemonic: Like liquid becoming a crystal: shape appears.

definition: to select from a large group; to remove unfit members
examples: The editor culled the best stories from hundreds of submissions to create a short, strong anthology.
Farmers were forced to cull the infected herd in order to stop the disease from spreading further.
cloze: The researcher spent months trying to {{cull}} reliable data from hundreds of old records.
mnemonic: CULL sounds like "pull" — pull out the best.

definition: to reach a final or highest point
examples: Years of grueling training culminated in her winning the gold medal at the national championships.
The tense negotiations, which dragged on for months, culminated in a historic peace agreement between the two nations.
cloze: The festival will {{culminate}} in a spectacular fireworks show on the final night.
mnemonic: CULMEN = top; reach the peak.

definition: responsibility for wrongdoing; guilt
examples: The long investigation established the driver's culpability in the accident beyond any reasonable doubt.
He denied culpability, insisting that the mistake was made by a colleague.
cloze: The memo shows the manager's {{culpability}} in covering up the safety defects.
mnemonic: CULPrit + ability to be blamed: culpable = guilty.

definition: deserving blame for wrongdoing
examples: The inquiry found the captain culpable for ignoring the storm warnings.
She felt culpable for the accident, though she had not caused it directly.
cloze: The court held the manufacturer {{culpable}} in the deaths because it knew of the fault.
mnemonic: CULPABLE contains "culprit" — the guilty one.

definition: clumsy and awkward to carry or use
examples: The cumbersome old computer took up half the desk and made a terrible noise whenever it started.
The cumbersome approval process, requiring seven signatures, delayed the project by several months and frustrated everyone involved.
cloze: Carrying the {{cumbersome}} suitcase up three flights of stairs exhausted her.
mnemonic: CUMBER-some: it burdens you with some weight.

definition: increasing gradually by successive additions
examples: The cumulative effect of small changes in temperature can alter an entire ecosystem.
Learning is cumulative: new knowledge builds on what students already understand.
cloze: The {{cumulative}} rainfall over the season was higher than in any previous year.
mnemonic: CUMULATIVE: CUMULUS clouds pile up.

definition: extreme greed, especially for money
examples: The cupidity of the landlords drove rents beyond what families could pay.
Their cupidity was aroused by rumors of gold in the hills.
cloze: His {{cupidity}} was obvious as he eyed the open safe filled with jewels.
mnemonic: CUPID wants things — wanting wealth, not love.

definition: to restrict or keep within limits
examples: Governments introduced taxes to curb the use of fossil fuels.
The treatment helped curb the spread of the infection through the village.
cloze: Strict measures were taken to {{curb}} illegal fishing in the protected waters.
mnemonic: CURB the dog like a curb holds the road edge.

definition: a bad-tempered, difficult person, often old
examples: The curmudgeon next door complained whenever children played in the street, whatever the time of day.
Beneath the grumpy exterior of the old curmudgeon lay a surprisingly warm heart and a dry sense of humor.
cloze: The {{curmudgeon}} grumbled about the noise, the weather, and the price of bread.
mnemonic: CURMUDGEON: a "cur" (mean dog) and "mudgeon" mud-grumpy.

definition: hasty and superficial; done without attention to detail
examples: He gave the long contract only a cursory glance before signing it, and later regretted his haste.
A cursory inspection of the wall missed the deep crack hidden behind the old wallpaper.
cloze: After a {{cursory}} review of the report, she realized she had overlooked several errors.
mnemonic: CURSORY: cursor racing over the page quickly.

definition: to reduce or cut short
examples: The company curtailed overtime hours across all departments in an effort to save money this year.
Heavy snow forced the airline to curtail its flights and strand thousands of travelers overnight.
cloze: Budget cuts will {{curtail}} the library's opening hours starting next month.
mnemonic: CURT + TAIL: cut the tail short.

definition: according to the usual habit or tradition
examples: It is customary in many cultures to remove shoes before entering a home.
Customary law, passed down orally, governed the village for centuries.
cloze: In academic writing, it is {{customary}} to cite previous research on the topic.
mnemonic: CUSTOMary = following CUSTOM.

definition: distrustful of people's motives; believing selfishness drives all
examples: The cynical reporter assumed every politician was lying for personal gain.
Her cynical remark that charity is just show offended the organizers.
cloze: He grew {{cynical}} about public service after seeing how many officials accepted bribes.
mnemonic: CYNIC: sounds like "sin-ic" — sees sin everywhere.

definition: a scarcity or lack of something
examples: A dearth of rainfall left the reservoirs nearly empty by August.
The town suffered a dearth of skilled nurses after the hospital cut salaries.
cloze: Because of a {{dearth}} of reliable data, the economists hesitated to publish any forecast.
mnemonic: DEARth sounds like DEAR: when something is dear (costly), there is little of it.

definition: a sudden, humiliating failure or collapse
examples: The merger turned into a debacle that cost the firm millions and its reputation.
After the election debacle, the party's leaders resigned in disgrace.
cloze: The product launch was a complete {{debacle}}: the website crashed, shipments were lost, and customers demanded refunds.
mnemonic: DEBACLE: the dam BREAKS (French débâcle, a breaking up of ice) and everything collapses.

definition: to lower the quality, value, or dignity of something
examples: Critics said that constant advertising debased the once-noble tradition of the festival.
Rulers who debased the coinage mixed cheap metal into silver to fund their wars.
cloze: Politicians who lie so openly {{debase}} public discourse for everyone.
mnemonic: DE-BASE: send something down to the base, the bottom.

definition: to weaken seriously; to sap the strength of
examples: The long illness debilitated him so badly that he could barely climb the stairs without help.
Years of drought debilitated the region's farming economy and forced many families to leave.
cloze: A {{debilitating}} fever kept the explorer in bed for weeks and drained all his strength.
mnemonic: DEBILITate contains ABILITY with a 'de-' prefix: it removes your ability.

definition: charming, stylish, and confident in manner
examples: The debonair actor strolled into the party in a perfectly tailored suit.
With his easy smile and polished manners, the diplomat seemed utterly debonair.
cloze: He remained {{debonair}} even when the car broke down on the way to the gala.
mnemonic: French 'de bon air': of good air, so he looks smooth.

definition: to expose a claim or myth as false
examples: Scientists worked to debunk the myth that we use only ten percent of our brains.
The documentary debunks several popular legends about the famous explorer.
cloze: A single clear experiment was enough to {{debunk}} the so-called miracle cure.
mnemonic: Remove the BUNK (nonsense).

definition: the destruction of a large portion of a population or group
examples: The plague caused the decimation of the town's population within a single year.
Economists feared the decimation of small businesses during the long recession.
cloze: The disease brought about the {{decimation}} of the island's amphibians, leaving only a few survivors.
mnemonic: DECI = ten: Romans killed one in ten, now it means massive loss.

definition: to become smaller, weaker, or less; to refuse politely
examples: Populations of some amphibians have declined sharply over the past thirty years.
Trade along the old caravan route declined once ships began carrying goods by sea.
cloze: If funding continues to {{decline}}, the research station may have to close.
mnemonic: DE-CLINE: slope (cline) downward.

definition: polite, proper, and in good taste
examples: The guests were decorous throughout dinner, speaking softly and waiting their turns.
Her decorous manner at the funeral earned the respect of even the stern elders.
cloze: In a {{decorous}} voice, he asked if anyone minded his opening the window.
mnemonic: DECORous: good DECOR and good manners.

definition: polite, dignified behavior that fits a formal occasion
examples: Even in the heated debate, the senator maintained perfect decorum.
The students were reminded that courtroom decorum forbids talking or eating during the trial.
cloze: The children's loud shouting at the funeral offended mourners who expected quiet {{decorum}}.
mnemonic: DECORum: DECORated manners, neat and proper like a decorated room.

definition: to publicly condemn or denounce
examples: Environmental groups decried the plan to drain the wetlands.
Teachers decried the budget cuts as a betrayal of students.
cloze: Many economists {{decry}} the policy, arguing it will deepen inequality and slow growth.
mnemonic: DE-CRY: to cry out against.

definition: to reach a conclusion by reasoning from evidence
examples: From the layers of rock, geologists deduced the sequence of ancient volcanic eruptions.
Detectives deduce the identity of a thief from small clues left at the scene.
cloze: Scientists can {{deduce}} the age of a tree by counting the rings in its trunk.
mnemonic: DE-DUCE: lead (duce) down from evidence.

definition: respectful submission to another's judgment or wishes
examples: The young lawyer spoke with deference to the veteran judge.
Out of deference to her grandfather's age, they let him choose the restaurant.
cloze: In {{deference}} to the host's customs, the guests removed their shoes at the door.
mnemonic: DEFER to someone: you put their wishes first.

definition: showing polite respect and submission to another's wishes or authority
examples: The deferential junior lawyer waited for the partner to finish before speaking.
He gave a deferential bow when the elder entered the room.
