examples: The poem exalts the courage of ordinary soldiers who defended the town.
The king exalted his loyal general to the rank of duke.
cloze: Fans continued to {{exalt}} the singer, calling her the greatest voice of her generation.
mnemonic: EXALT: ALTitude - lift UP high.

definition: to irritate intensely; to infuriate
examples: The constant delays exasperated the passengers, who had waited for hours.
Her teenage son's refusal to answer questions exasperated her.
cloze: It can {{exasperate}} even a patient teacher when students ignore the same instructions daily.
mnemonic: EX + ASPER (rough): rubbing someone the rough way.

definition: to dig out carefully, especially to uncover remains
examples: Archaeologists excavated the ruins of an ancient city buried under volcanic ash.
Workers excavated a deep trench before laying the pipes beneath the street.
cloze: The team plans to {{excavate}} the burial site next summer.
mnemonic: EX-CAVATE: take out of the CAVE/cavity.

definition: to go beyond a limit or be greater than something
examples: Annual rainfall in the region can exceed three meters during the monsoon season.
The results exceeded the researchers' expectations by a wide margin.
cloze: The number of visitors began to {{exceed}} the capacity of the national park.
mnemonic: EX-CEED: go out (ex) beyond the limit.

definition: to keep out or leave out of consideration
examples: The study excluded participants who had a history of heart disease.
Historians have often excluded women's stories from accounts of the past.
cloze: Researchers must {{exclude}} other possible causes before they can identify the true source.
mnemonic: EX-CLUDE: shut (clude) out.

definition: to criticize very harshly; to strip off skin
examples: Reviewers excoriated the film as dull, confusing and badly acted.
The editorial excoriated the mayor for ignoring the flooded neighborhoods.
cloze: Critics were quick to {{excoriate}} the company for hiding the defects from customers.
mnemonic: EX + CORIUM (hide): rip the skin off verbally.

definition: intensely painful or agonizing
examples: The patient endured excruciating pain before the surgery.
Waiting for the verdict was an excruciating experience for the whole family.
cloze: The comedian's joke fell flat, and the silence that followed was {{excruciating}}.
mnemonic: EX-CRUCI: from the cross (crux) - crucifying pain.

definition: to clear from blame or guilt
examples: New DNA evidence exculpated the prisoner after twenty years behind bars, proving that he had not committed the crime.
The investigation exculpated the pilot, blaming faulty equipment rather than any mistake on his part.
cloze: The video footage helped to {{exculpate}} the driver, proving he was not at fault.
mnemonic: EX-CULP-ate: out of CULPability, take away the blame.

definition: to feel or express great loathing for; to curse
examples: Crowds execrated the dictator and cheered when his statue fell.
She execrated the thief who had stolen her late father's watch.
cloze: Fans began to {{execrate}} the owner who had sold their best players to rivals.
mnemonic: EXECUTE the person's name with curses: EXECRATE.

definition: a detailed critical explanation or interpretation, especially of a text
examples: The scholar's exegesis of the poem uncovered layers of meaning that earlier critics missed.
His long exegesis of the ancient manuscript filled three volumes.
cloze: The seminar was devoted to careful {{exegesis}} of a single, difficult passage from the Bible.
mnemonic: EXEGESIS: EXit the text with a GESture of explanation - leading meaning out.

definition: a perfect or typical model worth imitating
examples: She was an exemplar of integrity, admired by colleagues and rivals alike.
The ancient temple is considered an exemplar of classical design.
cloze: The nurse became an {{exemplar}} of compassion, the model other staff were urged to follow.
mnemonic: EXAMPLE + ar: an example to follow.

definition: serving as an excellent model; worthy of imitation
examples: Her exemplary conduct earned the praise of the entire school.
He received an award for exemplary service to the community.
cloze: The nurse's {{exemplary}} dedication made her a model for younger staff.
mnemonic: EXEMPLARY: an EXAMPLE to follow.

definition: to be a typical example of; to illustrate by example
examples: Her generosity toward strangers exemplifies the warm spirit of the whole community.
The painting exemplifies the style of the early Renaissance, with its calm balance and careful perspective.
cloze: Her quiet courage during the crisis will {{exemplify}} true leadership for years to come.
mnemonic: EXAMPLE + ify: make into an example.

definition: to show or display clearly
examples: Many species exhibit complex social behavior when living in groups.
The museum exhibited rare pottery from the early Bronze Age.
cloze: Patients with the illness often {{exhibit}} symptoms such as fever and fatigue.
mnemonic: EX-HIBIT: hold (hib) out to show.

definition: to urge strongly, to encourage earnestly
examples: The coach exhorted the players to give their best in the final, urging them with passionate words.
Leaders exhorted citizens to conserve water during the drought, appealing to them on radio and television every day.
cloze: The preacher began to {{exhort}} the congregation to be more charitable.
mnemonic: EX-HORT: sounds like 'EXPORT'; push people out into action.

definition: urgent; demanding immediate attention
examples: The exigent crisis, with water rising by the hour, forced officials to act within a few hours.
Under exigent circumstances, such as a fire or an immediate threat to life, police may enter without a warrant.
cloze: The {{exigent}} needs of the flood victims required immediate action from the government.
mnemonic: EXIGENT: EXITS now! It's urgent.

definition: the quality of being scanty or meager
examples: The exiguity of their savings forced the couple to postpone the wedding.
Reviewers lamented the exiguity of evidence supporting the author's grand claim.
cloze: Given the {{exiguity}} of his salary, he could barely afford a single room.
mnemonic: EXIGUITY sounds like 'exit': little is left, nearly gone.

definition: to officially clear of blame or wrongdoing
examples: The official inquiry exonerated the manager of any wrongdoing, ending months of rumor and suspicion about his honesty.
Fingerprint evidence found at the scene eventually exonerated the accused man, and the court set him free.
cloze: The investigation will either condemn or {{exonerate}} the accused officers.
mnemonic: EX-ONERATE: remove the ONUS (burden) of guilt.

definition: unreasonably high, especially of prices
examples: Hotels charge exorbitant rates during the festival, sometimes ten times their normal price for a small room.
He refused to pay the exorbitant fee demanded by the lawyer, which was far more than the service was worth.
cloze: Tourists were shocked at the {{exorbitant}} prices charged for a simple sandwich.
mnemonic: EX-ORBIT-ant: goes out of ORBIT, beyond limits.

definition: to become larger or make something larger
examples: The empire expanded rapidly after its armies conquered the neighboring kingdoms.
Metals expand when heated and contract again when they cool, so bridges include small gaps.
cloze: The company plans to {{expand}} its research center to include a new laboratory.
mnemonic: EX-PAND: pan (spread) out.

definition: extensive in scope; or open, friendly, and talkative
examples: The estate had expansive lawns that stretched to the horizon.
In an expansive mood after dinner, he told stories for hours.
cloze: The professor, {{expansive}} after the success of his book, spoke warmly to every student.
mnemonic: EXPAND: it opens out wide, in space and in manner.

definition: convenient and practical, though possibly not principled
examples: It was expedient to blame the supplier, though the fault was the company's own.
The mayor chose the most expedient solution rather than the wisest.
cloze: Politicians often choose the {{expedient}} course, even if it is not the most ethical.
mnemonic: EXPEDIENT: EXPEDITES the job, quick and practical.

definition: stated clearly and in detail, leaving no doubt
examples: The teacher gave explicit instructions about how to format the final report.
The law makes an explicit ban on dumping chemicals into the river.
cloze: The author makes an {{explicit}} comparison between the two historical periods.
mnemonic: EX-PLICIT: unfolded (plicit) for all to see.

definition: to make full use of a resource, often unfairly
examples: Early industries exploited the region's forests, cutting down trees faster than they could regrow.
Some predators exploit the habits of their prey to catch them easily.
cloze: Companies that {{exploit}} cheap labor often face criticism from human rights groups.
mnemonic: EX-PLOIT: a feat that uses everything.

definition: a product sent to another country for sale
examples: Coffee has been the country's main export for over a century.
Exports of electronic goods rose sharply after the factories were modernized.
cloze: The nation's largest {{export}} is timber, shipped across the Pacific.
mnemonic: EX-PORT: goes OUT of the port.

definition: to uncover or leave unprotected against something
examples: Erosion has exposed layers of ancient rock along the cliffs.
Children exposed to music at an early age often develop stronger language skills.
cloze: Fossils are often {{exposed}} when heavy rain washes away the surface soil.
mnemonic: EX-POSE: put out into view.

definition: to explain in detail
examples: The professor expounded on his theory for over an hour.
She expounded the rules of the game to the new players.
cloze: He was invited to {{expound}} on his theory before the committee.
mnemonic: EXPOUND: you set out (ponere) the argument piece by piece.

definition: to erase or remove completely
examples: The court agreed to expunge the old conviction from his record.
Editors expunged every mention of the scandal from the official history.
cloze: The senator demanded that the offensive remarks be {{expunged}} from the public transcript.
mnemonic: EX + PUNCH (point): remove the marked points.

definition: to remove offensive or objectionable material from a text
examples: The censor expurgated the novel, removing every crude or offensive passage before it could reach schools.
Older editions of the play were expurgated for schoolchildren, with the rude jokes and violent scenes cut out.
cloze: The publisher decided to {{expurgate}} the book, cutting passages thought unsuitable for young readers.
mnemonic: EX-PURGE: PURGE out the bad parts.

definition: still existing; not destroyed or lost
examples: Only three extant copies of the ancient manuscript survive today, and all are kept in locked museum vaults.
The oldest extant temple in the region, still standing after seventeen centuries, dates from the third century.
cloze: Few {{extant}} manuscripts of the ancient play remain in libraries today.
mnemonic: EXTANT = still STANDing; opposite of extinct.

definition: making a fault or crime seem less serious by offering excuses
examples: The judge reduced the sentence after hearing the extenuating circumstances of the case.
Illness was an extenuating factor that explained why the report arrived late.
cloze: Given the {{extenuating}} circumstances, the committee decided not to punish the late applicant.
mnemonic: EXTENUATE: make a crime THIN (tenuis) and slighter.

definition: no longer existing; having died out
examples: The dodo became extinct in the seventeenth century after sailors hunted it to the last bird.
Scientists debate whether a sudden asteroid impact made the dinosaurs extinct.
cloze: Many large mammals went {{extinct}} at the end of the last ice age.
mnemonic: EX-TINCT: the fire is out (extinguished).

definition: to praise enthusiastically
examples: The reviewers extolled the film as a masterpiece, praising its acting, music, and the courage of its director.
Teachers constantly extolled the virtues of reading every day, promising that it would improve vocabulary and focus.
cloze: Critics continue to {{extol}} the novel as the finest work of its decade.
mnemonic: EX-TOLL: raise up with a bell toll of praise.

definition: to remove or take out, often with effort
examples: Miners extract copper and gold from deep underground using powerful drilling machines.
Scientists extracted DNA from the ancient bones to learn more about the extinct animal.
cloze: The factory uses special machines to {{extract}} oil from the seeds.
mnemonic: EX-TRACT: pull (tract) out.

definition: irrelevant; not part of the subject at hand
examples: Please remove all extraneous details from your essay, keeping only the facts that support your main argument.
Extraneous noise from the street outside made it hard for the audience to hear the soft-spoken speaker.
cloze: The editor cut every {{extraneous}} detail that did not support the main argument.
mnemonic: EXTRA + NEOUS: EXTRA, outside what is needed.

definition: to infer unknown values by projecting known facts
examples: Scientists extrapolated future sea levels from current measurements, assuming that the present rate of change would continue.
You cannot extrapolate a nationwide trend from the results of one small town, however carefully it was surveyed.
cloze: Analysts tried to {{extrapolate}} next year's sales from the numbers of the previous three years.
mnemonic: EXTRA-POLATE: stretch the line OUTside the known data.

definition: full of energy, excitement, and cheerfulness
examples: The exuberant crowd, shouting and waving flags, cheered wildly for the winning team all through the night.
Her exuberant laugh, full of energy and delight, filled the whole room whenever she entered.
cloze: The children's {{exuberant}} shouts rang through the playground as the snow began to fall.
mnemonic: EX-UBER-ant: UBER-full, overflowing with energy.

definition: treating serious matters with inappropriate humor
examples: His facetious remark about the funeral shocked the mourners, who thought it deeply disrespectful.
She made a facetious suggestion that the team should simply ask the rival to lose.
cloze: Annoyed by the {{facetious}} tone of the memo, the director demanded a serious reply.
mnemonic: Contains all five vowels in order: a-e-i-o-u, a playful word for playful speech.

definition: too easy and superficial; lacking depth
examples: Reducing a complex war to a facile tale of good versus evil ignores history.
The critic dismissed the novel's ending as facile, resolving every conflict too conveniently.
cloze: He offered a {{facile}} answer that avoided the real complexities of the problem.
mnemonic: FACILE sounds like 'facility': too easy, with no real depth.

definition: to make an action or process easier
examples: New roads facilitated trade between the coastal towns and the mountain villages.
Technology can facilitate learning by giving students access to a wide range of information.
cloze: A teacher's role is to {{facilitate}} discussion rather than simply deliver lectures.
mnemonic: FACILitate: FACILE = easy.

definition: given to forming rival groups; causing internal conflict
examples: The factious council split into three camps that rarely agreed on anything.
Rebuilding the party was difficult because its factious members distrusted each other.
cloze: A {{factious}} legislature cannot pass major reforms, because each bloc fights to protect its own interests.
mnemonic: FACTIOUS = full of FACTIONs.

definition: artificial; created or manufactured rather than natural or genuine
examples: The company created a factitious sense of urgency to push customers to buy.
Opponents accused him of stirring up factitious outrage over a minor issue.
cloze: The group's {{factitious}} support was really the work of paid actors posing as ordinary citizens.
mnemonic: FACT-itious: FACTory-made, manufactured (not fictitious, not factual).

definition: based on a mistaken belief or faulty reasoning
examples: The senator's fallacious argument ignored the fact that correlation does not prove causation.
Scientists dismissed the claim as fallacious because it relied on a single flawed experiment.
cloze: Her conclusion was {{fallacious}}, since it assumed that every successful company must have a charismatic founder.
mnemonic: FALLACY is inside FALLACious: a false idea.

definition: left unused or inactive, especially of land
examples: Farmers left the field fallow for a year to restore the soil.
After a fallow period of several years, the poet suddenly began writing again.
cloze: The land lay {{fallow}} for a season so that the exhausted soil could recover its nutrients.
mnemonic: FALL-OW: let the field fall asleep for a season.

definition: very careful about accuracy and detail; hard to please
examples: The fastidious editor checked every comma and citation before approving the manuscript.
He was so fastidious about cleanliness that he wiped the table after every guest left.
cloze: A {{fastidious}} tailor, she rejected three bolts of cloth for tiny flaws no customer would ever notice.
mnemonic: FAST-IDIOUS: fussy about every little thing, even a FAST glance must be perfect.

definition: extreme tiredness resulting from effort or illness
examples: Researchers found that mental fatigue reduces students' accuracy on long tests.
Workers on night shifts often suffer from fatigue and lose concentration.
cloze: Hikers experienced severe {{fatigue}} after climbing for ten hours.
mnemonic: FATIGUE sounds like FAT-EEG: so tired you can't move.

definition: silly and pointless, especially in a smug way
examples: The host's fatuous remarks about the weather filled the awkward silence.
Critics mocked the fatuous plot of the film, which made no sense whatsoever.
cloze: Rather than address the budget crisis, the mayor offered a {{fatuous}} slogan that solved nothing.
mnemonic: FATuous: a FAT-headed, empty-minded remark.

definition: helpful, advantageous, or approving
examples: Favorable weather helped farmers produce a record harvest this year.
The new book received favorable reviews from critics around the world.
cloze: The company enjoyed {{favorable}} conditions for trade after the treaty was signed.
mnemonic: FAVORable: you FAVOR it.

definition: to flatter and act servilely to gain favor
examples: Courtiers would fawn over the king, praising even his worst jokes.
The new intern tended to fawn over the director, agreeing with everything she said.
cloze: Rather than {{fawn}} over powerful donors, the candidate spoke frankly about their influence on policy.
mnemonic: A FAWN (deer) follows its mother; a FAWNing person follows the powerful.

definition: possible and practical to do
examples: Engineers concluded that building a tunnel under the bay was technically feasible.
It is not feasible to test every individual plant in such a large forest.
cloze: The committee decided that the plan was not {{feasible}} given the limited budget.
mnemonic: FEASIBLE = FEAT is possible.

definition: lacking initiative or strength of character; irresponsible
examples: The feckless young heir squandered his inheritance within two years.
Her feckless brother never held a job for more than a month.
cloze: The {{feckless}} manager ignored every warning, leaving the project to collapse without any plan to save it.
mnemonic: FECK-less: has no FEct, no effect, useless.

definition: fertile; producing abundant offspring, growth, or ideas
examples: The river valley's fecund soil produced rich harvests year after year.
The novelist had a fecund imagination and published a book almost every year.
cloze: In the {{fecund}} marshes, frogs and insects multiplied by the thousands each spring.
mnemonic: FECUND sounds like 'fee-kind': kind with fruit and babies.

definition: well chosen or apt; pleasing
examples: Her felicitous phrasing captured the mood of the occasion perfectly.
The architect made a felicitous choice of materials, blending the building into the hillside.
cloze: The speaker's {{felicitous}} remark neatly summed up the mood of the entire audience.
mnemonic: FELICITY means happiness; a felicitous phrase gives happy results.

definition: cruel, fierce, and deadly
examples: The hero fought the fell dragon that terrorized the kingdom.
A fell disease swept through the village, leaving few survivors.
cloze: In one {{fell}} swoop, the hawk seized the rabbit and vanished into the sky.
mnemonic: FELL = fierce as hell; think 'one fell swoop'.

definition: to search out and discover by persistent investigation
examples: The reporter ferreted out the truth about the secret payments.
Auditors ferreted out hidden errors that others had overlooked.
cloze: It took patient detectives to {{ferret}} the key witness out of hiding after months of searching.
mnemonic: A FERRET burrows into holes to flush things out.

definition: able to produce abundant crops or offspring
examples: The Nile valley was fertile land where ancient Egyptians grew wheat and barley.
Volcanic ash makes the soil fertile, so farmers settle near active volcanoes despite the risks.
cloze: Only a small portion of the island is {{fertile}} enough to support crops.
mnemonic: FERTILE: FERT = bring forth fruit.

definition: showing intense and sincere feeling
examples: She made a fervent plea for donations to rebuild the flooded school.
The team's fervent supporters sang through the entire match despite the pouring rain.
cloze: His {{fervent}} devotion to the cause led him to give up his career and travel the country speaking about it.
mnemonic: FERVent sounds like FEVER: feelings running hot.

definition: to honor or celebrate someone with a party or public festivities
examples: The town feted the returning champions with a parade and fireworks.
The author was feted at a gala dinner after winning the major prize.
cloze: The city prepared to {{fete}} the astronauts with a grand parade through downtown.
mnemonic: Sounds like FÊTE = festival, party.

definition: changing often, especially in loyalty or affection
examples: The fickle public abandoned the singer as soon as a new star appeared.
Spring weather here is fickle: sunshine at noon may become hail by evening.
cloze: Voters in the district are {{fickle}}, switching their support from one party to another every election.
mnemonic: FICKLE sounds like TICKLE: it never stays still.

definition: violently intense or aggressive
examples: Fierce competition among species for scarce water shaped the entire desert ecosystem over centuries.
The fierce storm ripped the roof from the barn and scattered the hay across the field.
cloze: The region faced {{fierce}} winds that destroyed crops.
mnemonic: FIERCE sounds like PIERCE: sharp and strong.

definition: to get by trickery or clever maneuvering
examples: He finagled his way into the sold-out concert by pretending to be a reporter.
She finagled an extra week of vacation out of her unsuspecting manager.
cloze: The clever clerk managed to {{finagle}} a free upgrade without paying a cent.
mnemonic: FINAGLE sounds like 'finesse' + 'angle': work an angle.

definition: skill and delicacy in handling a delicate situation
examples: The diplomat handled the tense negotiation with great finesse, soothing both angry sides without giving offense.
She played the difficult piece with great finesse, making every note seem effortless.
cloze: Resolving the dispute required more {{finesse}} than force, and the mediator proved remarkably tactful.
mnemonic: FINE + ESSE: a fine touch.

definition: a person who stirs up unrest or passionate action
examples: The young firebrand rallied thousands to protest the new tax.
Once a quiet student, she became a firebrand whose speeches inspired the whole movement.
cloze: The party feared the {{firebrand}} whose fiery speeches kept provoking unrest in the capital.
mnemonic: A burning stick (brand) that sets others aflame.

definition: relating to government money, especially taxes and spending
examples: The government announced a new fiscal policy to reduce its debt.
Fiscal responsibility requires careful balancing of public income and spending.
cloze: The university's {{fiscal}} year begins in July and ends the following June.
mnemonic: FISCAL: FISC = purse of the state.

definition: to grow tired or weak; to lose energy or interest
examples: The runner began to flag near the end, her stride shortening with every step.
Enthusiasm for the project flagged once the early excitement faded.
cloze: As the long meeting dragged on, the audience's attention started to {{flag}}.
mnemonic: A flag droops when the wind dies: energy FLAGS.

definition: new and inexperienced; just starting to develop
examples: The fledgling company struggled to compete with larger, established rivals in its first difficult year.
She offered advice to fledgling writers who were nervous about their first novels.
cloze: The {{fledgling}} democracy faced many challenges in its first few years of independence.
mnemonic: A baby bird with new FLEDGE feathers is just learning to fly.

definition: to swindle someone out of money
examples: Dishonest contractors fleeced the elderly couple out of their life savings.
Tourists are often fleeced by overcharging taxi drivers.
cloze: The con man tried to {{fleece}} investors with a fake gold mine.
mnemonic: Shear the sheep: take the FLEECE off a victim.

definition: able to change or bend easily
examples: Bamboo is flexible enough to bend in strong winds without breaking.
The university offers flexible schedules for students who work part time.
cloze: A {{flexible}} approach is necessary when plans change unexpectedly.
mnemonic: FLEX your muscle: it bends.

definition: not showing proper seriousness or respect
examples: His flippant reply to the judge's question earned him a stern warning.
She regretted making a flippant comment about a topic that was painful for her friend.
cloze: The student's {{flippant}} attitude toward the safety rules worried the lab supervisor.
mnemonic: FLIP-pant: FLIPping a question away without thought.

definition: overly elaborate or ornate; reddish in color
examples: The author's florid prose buried a simple story under layers of decoration.
The orator's florid language impressed some listeners but exhausted others.
cloze: His {{florid}} style, crowded with adjectives and metaphors, made even a simple letter hard to read.
mnemonic: FLORid: covered in FLOWERs, over-decorated.

definition: to struggle clumsily; to proceed in confusion
examples: The new manager floundered for months, unsure what the job really required of her.
A swimmer floundered in the shallow water, splashing wildly and gasping for breath.
cloze: Without a clear plan, the project began to {{flounder}} and drift off course.
mnemonic: A flat FLOUNDER fish flapping helplessly on the deck.

definition: to grow or develop successfully; to thrive
examples: Trade and the arts flourished in the city during the golden age of the republic.
Coral reefs flourish in warm, shallow, sunlit waters far from the polluted coastlines.
cloze: Small businesses often {{flourish}} when the local economy is strong.
mnemonic: FLOURISH sounds like FLOWER-ish: blooming.

definition: to openly disregard a rule or convention with scorn
examples: Drivers who flout the speed limit endanger everyone on the road.
The young artist loved to flout tradition by painting on bare concrete walls.
cloze: Several companies chose to {{flout}} the new regulations, confident that inspectors would rarely visit.
mnemonic: To FLOUT is to FLAUNT disrespect for the rule.

definition: to rise and fall irregularly
examples: Temperatures in the desert fluctuate widely between day and night.
Prices of agricultural goods fluctuate according to weather conditions and demand.
cloze: The population of the lake's fish tends to {{fluctuate}} from one year to the next.
mnemonic: FLUCT: like FLUid waves going up and down.

definition: able to speak or write a language smoothly and easily
examples: After living abroad for five years, she became fluent in three languages.
The professor's fluent explanation helped even beginners follow the complicated theory.
cloze: Students who read widely tend to become more {{fluent}} writers.
mnemonic: FLUENT: words FLOW like a river.

definition: to confuse or perplex completely
examples: The tricky riddle flummoxed even the most experienced puzzle solvers.
Her unexpected question flummoxed the candidate, who had no answer ready.
cloze: Complex tax forms can {{flummox}} even educated adults who are used to solving difficult problems.
mnemonic: FLUMMOX sounds like a funny word for being thrown in a muddle.

definition: having plenty of money; also level with a surface
examples: Flush from a big commission, the broker treated the whole office to dinner.
The cabinet door sat flush with the wall, leaving no visible gap.
cloze: Because the company was {{flush}} with cash, it could buy its rival outright.
mnemonic: Your wallet is FLUSH: pressed full, filled to the brim.

definition: constant change; a state of continual movement
examples: Prices remained in a state of flux throughout the unstable year.
Her plans were in flux, changing with each new piece of news.
cloze: With the economy in constant {{flux}}, forecasting next year's sales was nearly impossible.
mnemonic: FLUX = FLOW: always flowing, never still.

definition: a minor weakness or eccentricity in character
examples: Her only foible was a habit of arriving twenty minutes early to everything.
The biographer treated his subject's foibles with gentle humor.
cloze: Friends tolerated his {{foible}} of rereading the same joke at every dinner, since he was otherwise kind.
mnemonic: FOIBLE sounds like FEEBLE - a small weakness.

definition: to stir up or instigate trouble or rebellion
examples: Agitators tried to foment unrest among the unpaid factory workers.
The pamphlets were designed to foment revolt against the colonial governor.
cloze: The rumor was spread deliberately to {{foment}} distrust between the two allied nations.
mnemonic: FOMENT sounds like FERMENT: trouble bubbling up like brewing.

definition: recklessly bold; taking risks without sensible thought
examples: It was foolhardy to swim in the river during the flood.
The foolhardy climber ignored the storm warnings and set out alone.
cloze: Investing every cent in one risky venture was a {{foolhardy}} decision that cost him everything.
mnemonic: FOOL + HARDY: a fool who is hardy... bold without brains.

definition: patient self-control; restraint in the face of provocation
examples: The teacher showed great forbearance when the class repeatedly interrupted her.
Thanks to the bank's forbearance, the farmer was given extra time to repay his loan.
cloze: She thanked her colleagues for their {{forbearance}} during the long, difficult months of the renovation.
mnemonic: FORBEAR = bear with: forBEARance is bearing with others calmly.

definition: to prevent or delay by acting beforehand
examples: The government cut interest rates to forestall a looming recession.
He raised his hand to forestall any further objections from the committee.
cloze: The company hired extra security guards to {{forestall}} any attempt at theft during the sale.
mnemonic: FORE (before) + STALL: stop it before it happens.

definition: pitifully sad, lonely, and abandoned
examples: The forlorn puppy waited by the door long after its owner had gone.
A forlorn figure stood on the empty platform as the last train left.
cloze: After the friends departed, she felt {{forlorn}} in the quiet, deserted house.
mnemonic: FOR-LORN: lorn means lost; entirely lost and alone.

definition: inspiring fear or awe because of size, power, or difficulty
examples: The champion was a formidable opponent who had not lost in five years.
Climbing the icy peak without oxygen is a formidable challenge even for experts.
cloze: The new team faces a {{formidable}} task: catching up with competitors who have a decade's head start.
mnemonic: FORM-idable: a huge FORM looming over you.

definition: to create or express carefully a plan, idea, or statement
examples: Newton formulated the laws of motion after studying falling objects.
The research team formulated a hypothesis to explain the sudden drop in bee populations.
cloze: Scientists must {{formulate}} a clear question before beginning any experiment.
mnemonic: FORM-ULATE: give a FORM to an idea.

definition: willing to give information; also about to appear
examples: The witness was not forthcoming about where she had been that night.
Funds for the project are forthcoming once the permits are approved.
cloze: Asked about the merger, the CEO was surprisingly {{forthcoming}} and answered every question.
mnemonic: FORTH + COMING: information coming forth.

definition: direct, honest, and outspoken
examples: The forthright witness answered every question plainly, without evasion.
Her forthright criticism stung, but it helped the writer improve.
cloze: I appreciate a {{forthright}} manager who tells me the truth, even when it is unwelcome.
mnemonic: FORTH-right: speaks forth, right out.

definition: courage in pain or adversity
examples: She bore her long and painful illness with remarkable fortitude and never once complained to her nurses.
It took great fortitude to rebuild the farm after the flood had destroyed every building on it.
cloze: The explorers showed {{fortitude}} through months of cold, hunger, and uncertainty.
mnemonic: FORTitude: a FORT of inner strength.

definition: happening by chance, often luckily
examples: Their meeting at the airport was entirely fortuitous; neither had planned to travel that day.
A fortuitous discovery of old letters allowed the historian to complete her book.
cloze: By a {{fortuitous}} coincidence, the two friends booked the same flight without knowing it.
mnemonic: FORTUne-ous: it happened by FORTUNE.

definition: to encourage the development of
examples: Good teachers foster curiosity in their students rather than simply demanding that they memorize facts.
The program aims to foster cooperation between rival communities that have distrusted each other for years.
cloze: The new library will {{foster}} a love of reading among children in the neighborhood.
mnemonic: FOSTER parents help a child grow.

definition: irritable and quarrelsome; hard to control
examples: The fractious committee argued over every minor detail for hours.
The teacher struggled to calm the fractious children after the long bus ride.
cloze: The coalition proved too {{fractious}} to agree on a single policy, and it soon fell apart.
mnemonic: FRACTious: breaking into FRACTions, groups that fight.

definition: easily broken or damaged; delicate
examples: The fragile ecosystem of the island was damaged by the arrival of invasive species.
Ancient manuscripts are fragile and must be handled with great care.
cloze: Coral reefs are {{fragile}} and can be destroyed by even slight changes in temperature.
mnemonic: FRAGILE = FRAGment easily.

definition: a basic structure that supports something or guides thinking
examples: The scientist developed a theoretical framework to explain the behavior of the cells.
Engineers built a steel framework before adding the walls and roof of the stadium.
cloze: The treaty provides a legal {{framework}} for protecting endangered species.
mnemonic: FRAME + WORK: the frame holds the work.

definition: not serious; lacking sense or importance
examples: The court dismissed the frivolous lawsuit within minutes, since it had no serious legal basis whatsoever.
She spent her entire bonus on frivolous gadgets that she never used after the first week.
cloze: Critics called the proposal {{frivolous}}, noting that it ignored the city's urgent problems.
mnemonic: FRIVOLous: FRILLy and light.

definition: careful and sparing with money or resources
examples: Growing up poor made her a frugal shopper who always compared prices.
The frugal family reused jars and mended clothes instead of buying new ones.
cloze: Despite his wealth, he led a {{frugal}} life, eating simple meals and driving an old car.
mnemonic: FRUGAL sounds like FRUGAL-ity: saving every FRUit and penny.

definition: to prevent from succeeding; to cause annoyance by blocking
examples: Heavy storms frustrated all attempts to reach the stranded hikers.
The constant delays frustrated the engineers, who wanted to launch on schedule.
cloze: Bad weather will {{frustrate}} our plans to hold the festival outdoors.
mnemonic: Frustrate is 'in vain': efforts made useless.

definition: excessively flattering or effusive, to the point of insincerity
examples: The ambassador's fulsome praise of the host's cooking made the other guests squirm with discomfort.
Tired of fulsome compliments, the chef preferred honest criticism from his colleagues.
cloze: She distrusted the {{fulsome}} flattery of the salesman, which seemed far too eager to be sincere.
mnemonic: FULSOME = FULL of SOME-too much praise; it is overfull.

definition: the purpose or role of something
examples: The main function of the liver is to filter toxins from the blood.
Scientists studied the function of each part of the cell using powerful microscopes.
cloze: The {{function}} of the tower was to warn ships of dangerous rocks.
mnemonic: FUNCTION: what a thing does when it is working.

definition: forming the basic or most important part of something
examples: Photosynthesis is a fundamental process that sustains almost all life on Earth.
Many historians argue that the printing press brought fundamental changes to European society.
cloze: Reading carefully is a {{fundamental}} skill for success in every university course.
mnemonic: FUNDAMENTAL: the FOUNDation.

definition: in addition; moreover
examples: The treatment is inexpensive; furthermore, it has few side effects.
The soil is poor; furthermore, rainfall is unreliable in this region.
cloze: The proposal is too costly; {{furthermore}}, it would take years to complete.
mnemonic: FURTHER + MORE: adds more.

definition: secretive; done in a stealthy way to avoid notice
examples: He cast a furtive glance at the answers on his neighbor's desk.
The furtive movements of the stranger near the door caught the guard's attention.
cloze: With {{furtive}} steps, the burglar crept along the hall, pausing at every creak of the floor.
mnemonic: FURry cat moving quietly: FURtive.

definition: incapable of producing any useful result
examples: All efforts to rescue the sinking ship proved futile, and the crew finally abandoned it.
It is futile to argue with someone who refuses to listen to any evidence.
cloze: After years of {{futile}} attempts to repair the machine, the engineers finally decided to replace it.
mnemonic: FUTILE sounds like FOOT-tile: stamping your foot achieves nothing.

definition: an embarrassing blunder, especially a social one
examples: Calling the host by the wrong name was an awkward gaffe.
The candidate's gaffe at the debate dominated the news for days.
cloze: The ambassador's careless joke was a serious diplomatic {{gaffe}} that required a public apology.
mnemonic: GAFFE sounds like 'gaffe-aw!', an embarrassed gasp.

definition: to deny or contradict
examples: No one could gainsay the evidence presented in court, since every document had been verified.
It is hard to gainsay the achievements of a scientist who has won three major prizes.
cloze: Few critics would {{gainsay}} her talent, though many questioned her character.
mnemonic: GAIN-SAY: say against what is gained or claimed.

definition: bold, rude impudence
examples: She had the gall to ask for a refund after eating the entire meal.
I could not believe the gall of a stranger who cut ahead and then complained.
cloze: It took real {{gall}} to criticize the chef while stuffing a second plate of his dessert.
mnemonic: GALL bladder bitterness: bitter, bold rudeness.

definition: to shock or excite into taking action
examples: The tragedy galvanized the community into demanding safer streets and better lighting at night.
A rousing speech from the coach galvanized the weary players in the final quarter.
cloze: The scandal was enough to {{galvanize}} voters who had previously ignored politics altogether.
mnemonic: Luigi GALVANI used electricity to make frog legs jump: shock into action.

definition: a calculated opening move or ploy designed to gain advantage
examples: The chess player's opening gambit sacrificed a pawn to gain control of the center.
Offering free samples was a clever gambit to win over cautious shoppers.
cloze: The senator's surprise resignation was a political {{gambit}} meant to force a quick election.
mnemonic: In chess, a GAMBIT sacrifices a piece to GAMBLE on gain.

definition: to gather or collect, especially information or approval
examples: The new film garnered praise from critics across the country and filled theaters for months.
Researchers worked for months to garner support for the new project.
cloze: The candidate hoped to {{garner}} enough votes in the northern districts to win the election.
mnemonic: GARNER sounds like GRANARY: to store up grain.

definition: excessively talkative, especially about trivial things
examples: The garrulous neighbor kept us on the porch for an hour discussing his garden.
A garrulous passenger chatted all through the flight, though no one answered him.
cloze: Normally quiet, he became {{garrulous}} after a glass of wine and talked about everything and nothing.
mnemonic: GARRULOUS sounds like GARGLE: words endlessly pouring out of the throat.

definition: lacking social grace; awkward
examples: The gauche newcomer loudly criticized the food at his host's dinner.
His gauche attempt at flattery embarrassed everyone at the table.
cloze: Though brilliant, he was {{gauche}} in company and often said exactly the wrong thing.
mnemonic: GAUCHE is French for left, the clumsy hand.

definition: to produce or bring something into existence
examples: Wind turbines generate electricity without burning fossil fuels.
The new exhibit helped generate public interest in local history.
cloze: Volcanic vents can {{generate}} enough heat to support unusual deep-sea ecosystems.
mnemonic: GENERATor makes power: it GENERATEs.

definition: friendly, cheerful, and pleasant in manner
examples: Our genial host welcomed every guest with a warm handshake.
The genial old shopkeeper chatted with everyone who came in.
cloze: Despite his stern reputation, the judge was {{genial}} in private and told jokes at lunch.
mnemonic: GENIAL - a GENIe who is jolly and kind.

definition: polite and refined, sometimes in an affected way
examples: The genteel hostess served tea in her finest porcelain cups.
They lived in a genteel neighborhood where everyone spoke softly and dressed well.
cloze: The retired teacher spoke in a {{genteel}} manner that made rudeness seem unthinkable.
mnemonic: GENTEEL ~ GENTLE-man: elegant manners.

definition: relevant to the subject under consideration
examples: The judge ruled that the witness's remarks were not germane to the case.
Please keep your comments germane to the topic we are discussing.
cloze: Only facts {{germane}} to the central question of the inquiry were allowed into the report.
mnemonic: GERMANE is a GERM of the same idea, related to the matter.

definition: to redraw electoral districts unfairly to favor one party
examples: The party gerrymandered the map to secure a majority with fewer votes.
Lawmakers were accused of gerrymandering districts to dilute minority voting power.
cloze: Critics say legislators {{gerrymander}} the boundaries so that politicians pick their voters.
mnemonic: Named for Governor GERRY and a district shaped like a SALAMANDER.

definition: to gather information or facts bit by bit
examples: From the scattered letters, historians glean details about daily life in the village.
It was hard to glean the truth from such vague and contradictory reports.
cloze: Reporters tried to {{glean}} hints about the merger from the executive's brief remarks.
mnemonic: Like gleaning leftover grain from a field, piece by piece.

definition: fluent but insincere or superficial
examples: The salesman's glib patter hid the product's many defects until it was too late for buyers.
Her glib answer failed to address the complex problem the reporter raised.
cloze: Beware the {{glib}} politician who offers an easy solution to every difficult problem.
mnemonic: GLIB: words that GLIde out without thought.

definition: an excessive supply; also, to fill beyond capacity
examples: A glut of oil on the market sent prices tumbling.
The harvest produced a glut of tomatoes, and farmers could barely sell them.
cloze: A {{glut}} of new graduates competing for the same few openings drove wages down.
mnemonic: GLUT sounds like GULP - too much swallowed at once.

definition: to provoke or urge someone into action
examples: His friends tried to goad him into entering the dangerous race.
The bully would goad smaller students until they lost their tempers.
cloze: Rather than {{goad}} the angry crowd, the officer spoke softly and asked everyone to step back.
mnemonic: A GOAD is a pointed stick; GO! the ox is prodded.

definition: extremely light, thin, and delicate
examples: The bride wore a gossamer veil that floated in the breeze.
Morning dew made the spider's gossamer threads shine in the grass.
cloze: She draped a {{gossamer}} scarf across her shoulders, so thin that it seemed made of mist.
mnemonic: Goose-summer: floating spider silk drifting in autumn air.

definition: happening slowly and in small steps
examples: The gradual erosion of the canyon took millions of years.
Historians describe a gradual shift from farming to factory work.
cloze: A {{gradual}} warming of the oceans has altered where many fish species live.
mnemonic: GRADUAL: by GRADEs, step by step.

definition: dishonest gain, especially by political corruption
examples: The mayor was voted out amid charges of graft in city contracts.
Investigators uncovered graft in the highway department, where officials took bribes.
cloze: The city's budget was drained by {{graft}}, with officials pocketing public money.
mnemonic: Greedy hands GRAB the cash: graft.

definition: using pompous, lofty language
examples: The grandiloquent speaker used big words where simple ones would do.
His grandiloquent prose bored readers who wanted a straightforward account.
cloze: The {{grandiloquent}} lawyer filled his speech with inflated phrases and Latin quotations that confused the jury.
mnemonic: GRAND + eLOQUENT: speech that is too grand.

definition: impressively large in scale, often pretentiously so
examples: The king drew up grandiose plans for a palace bigger than any in Europe.
Her grandiose promises of overnight wealth made the investors suspicious.
cloze: Critics mocked the {{grandiose}} scheme as an absurdly expensive monument to the mayor's vanity.
mnemonic: GRAND + dioSE: way too grand.

definition: uncalled for; done without good reason
examples: The film was criticized for its gratuitous violence, which added nothing to the story.
Her gratuitous insult left the whole room in stunned silence.
cloze: The critic's {{gratuitous}} attack on the author's family had nothing to do with the book under review.
mnemonic: GRATIS means free; gratuitous things are free extras no one needs.

definition: fond of company; sociable
examples: The gregarious host greeted every guest and soon had the whole room laughing.
Wolves are gregarious animals that live and hunt in packs.
cloze: Unlike her shy sister, she was {{gregarious}} and thrived at large parties, quickly making new friends.
mnemonic: GREG-arious: GREG the guy who loves a GREAT crowd (grex = flock).

definition: to behave in a servile, humble way to win favor
examples: He groveled before his boss, begging to keep a job he had badly failed at.
I refuse to grovel to anyone for a reward I earned honestly.
cloze: Courtiers would {{grovel}} before the tyrant, bowing low and flattering him in hope of survival.
mnemonic: To GROVEL is to crawl on the GROund like a worm.

definition: to laugh loudly and boisterously
examples: The crowd began to guffaw when the actor slipped on the banana peel.
He could not help but guffaw at the ridiculous costume.
cloze: Despite the solemn setting, the old man began to {{guffaw}} so loudly that heads turned.
mnemonic: GUFF-AW! The sound itself is a big laugh.

definition: a rule or principle that directs behavior or action
examples: The university issued new guidelines for citing online sources.
Health agencies published guidelines to reduce the risk of heart disease.
cloze: Researchers must follow strict ethical {{guidelines}} when working with human participants.
mnemonic: GUIDE + LINE: a line that guides.

definition: clever deceit or cunning
examples: The con man used guile, not force, to cheat his victims.
With guile and patience, the fox lured the chickens away from their coop.
cloze: Her political success owed more to {{guile}} than to any genuine principle or policy.
mnemonic: GUILE sounds like GUILTy trick: sly deception.

definition: free of deceit; innocent and honest
examples: The guileless child told the officer exactly where the cookies were hidden.
Her guileless smile made it impossible to suspect her of any trickery.
cloze: Because he was so {{guileless}}, he never imagined that his business partner was cheating him.
mnemonic: GUILE + LESS: without trickery.

definition: easily deceived or persuaded to believe things
examples: Gullible tourists often fall for scams run by street vendors.
He was so gullible that he believed his brother's claim that the moon was made of cheese.
cloze: Too {{gullible}} to question the stranger's story, she handed over her savings within minutes.
mnemonic: GULL (a fool) + ible: easy to fool, or swallowed like a GULLet.

definition: initiative and resourcefulness; practical courage
examples: She had the gumption to start her own business with nothing but a loan and a plan.
It takes gumption to speak up when everyone else in the room is silent.
cloze: With little money but plenty of {{gumption}}, the brothers built the shop from scratch.
mnemonic: GUMption: you chew GUM and get things done with grit.

definition: lacking originality because of overuse; trite
examples: The hackneyed plot had been used in a hundred earlier films.
He winced at the hackneyed phrase 'time heals all wounds.'
cloze: The speech was full of {{hackneyed}} expressions, such as 'think outside the box,' that no one noticed anymore.
mnemonic: HACKNEY horses were rented for hire so were overused and worn out.

definition: excessively flattering about a person; treating someone as a saint
examples: The hagiographic biography portrayed the founder as flawless and ignored his many failures.
Critics found the documentary hagiographic, with no hint of the leader's cruelty.
cloze: Instead of a balanced portrait, the memoir was {{hagiographic}}, presenting the author's mentor as a saint.
mnemonic: HAGIO = holy; a HAGIOgraphy is a life of a saint, so overly glowing.

definition: to greet or acclaim enthusiastically; to praise publicly
examples: Critics hailed the novel as a masterpiece of modern fiction.
Crowds hailed the returning hero as the savior of the city.
cloze: The press was quick to {{hail}} the young scientist as a visionary after her breakthrough.
mnemonic: Hail Caesar! A cheer in his honor.

definition: calm, peaceful, and happy, often looking back to the past
examples: She remembered the halcyon days of her childhood summers by the lake.
The country enjoyed a halcyon decade of peace and prosperity.
cloze: He often longed for the {{halcyon}} years before the war, when life was tranquil and carefree.
mnemonic: The legendary halcyon bird calmed the seas to nest.

definition: to hinder or impede the movement or progress of
examples: Heavy snow hampered rescue efforts and delayed the arrival of supplies.
Poor lighting hampered the surgeon's ability to see the wound clearly.
cloze: Outdated equipment will continue to {{hamper}} the lab's research unless it is replaced.
mnemonic: A picnic HAMPER is heavy and slows your walking.

definition: made unable to act effectively; crippled
examples: The mayor was hamstrung by a council that rejected every proposal.
The team was hamstrung by an injured star and a tiny budget.
cloze: The agency, {{hamstrung}} by budget cuts, could no longer inspect the factories.
mnemonic: Cut the HAMSTRING tendon and you cannot run.

definition: lacking order or planning; random
examples: The books were stacked in a haphazard heap on the floor, with no order or pattern at all.
His haphazard approach to studying, with no schedule or notes, led to poor grades that term.
cloze: The {{haphazard}} filing system made it nearly impossible to find any document when needed.
mnemonic: HAP (chance) + HAZARD: left to chance.

definition: unlucky; deserving pity
examples: The hapless traveler lost his wallet, passport, and luggage in a single day.
Rescuers reached the hapless sailors after three nights adrift at sea.
cloze: The {{hapless}} clerk was blamed for the error even though he had followed his instructions exactly.
mnemonic: HAP means luck; hapLESS is without luck.

definition: to lecture someone aggressively and at length
examples: The coach would harangue his players for an hour after every defeat.
Protesters gathered to harangue the minister as she left the building.
cloze: She was tired of the neighbor who would {{harangue}} anyone passing his gate about local politics.
mnemonic: HARANGUE sounds like HANG-gang: a gang yelling at you.

definition: a sign or forerunner of something to come
examples: The first robin of the year is often seen as a harbinger of the coming spring.
Economists saw the factory closures as a harbinger of a wider economic downturn.
cloze: Dark clouds on the horizon were a {{harbinger}} of the storm that would hit by evening.
mnemonic: HARBINGER: a person at the HARBOR announcing a ship is coming.

definition: strained and worn out by constant demands or harassment
examples: The harried waiter dashed between tables, juggling a dozen orders at once.
A harried parent, she answered emails while making breakfast and finding lost shoes.
cloze: The {{harried}} clerk had no time for lunch because of the constant stream of angry customers.
mnemonic: HARRIED = HARassed and worRIED.

definition: arrogantly superior and disdainful
examples: The haughty clerk looked down on customers who could not afford the shop's goods.
With a haughty toss of her head, she ignored the greeting.
cloze: His {{haughty}} manner, always looking down on others, made him few friends at the school.
mnemonic: HAUGHTY sounds like HIGH: nose held high.

definition: arrogant haughtiness in manner
examples: The headwaiter greeted us with such hauteur that we felt unworthy of the restaurant.
She spoke with the cool hauteur of someone who had never been refused.
cloze: Her {{hauteur}} made her colleagues feel that she regarded them as lesser beings.
mnemonic: HAUTE (high) + eur: looking down from on HIGH.

definition: to bully or harass with loud, intimidating talk
examples: The coach hectored the players until some of them quit.
Do not hector your employees; they respond better to encouragement.
cloze: The older boys would {{hector}} the new students on the bus every morning.
mnemonic: HECTOR the blustering bully, from Homer's tale.

definition: to avoid committing oneself; to protect against loss
examples: The spokesman hedged when asked whether the company would close the factory.
Investors hedge against inflation by buying gold and other assets.
cloze: Rather than give a plain answer, the minister chose to {{hedge}} and offer vague promises.
mnemonic: A HEDGE is a boundary to hide behind.

definition: a person who pursues pleasure as the chief aim in life
examples: The hedonist spent his fortune on feasts, travel, and parties.
Critics called him a hedonist, concerned only with his own comfort.
cloze: Unlike his ascetic brother, the {{hedonist}} indulged every appetite and avoided all discomfort.
mnemonic: HEDONIST: HE DOes ONly what's pleasant.

definition: dominance of one group or state over others
examples: The empire exerted hegemony over the neighboring tribes for centuries.
Rival powers formed alliances to challenge the hegemony of the largest nation.
cloze: Economic {{hegemony}} allowed the country to set trade rules that smaller nations had to follow.
mnemonic: HEGEMONY: HE G(ot) MONEY and the control.

definition: for this reason; as a consequence
examples: The soil is poor; hence the region produces little grain.
Metals expand when heated, hence bridges include gaps to allow movement.
cloze: The ice sheet reflects sunlight; {{hence}} its loss would speed up warming.
mnemonic: HENCE = from HERE comes the result.

definition: one who holds beliefs contrary to accepted doctrine
examples: Centuries ago, a heretic who challenged church teaching could be put on trial.
In the physics community, he was almost a heretic for doubting the accepted model.
cloze: The scientist was treated as a {{heretic}} for rejecting the field's cherished theory.
mnemonic: HERETIC: picks (haeresis = choice) his own beliefs.

definition: holding views that oppose established beliefs
examples: The scientist's heretical theory challenged centuries of accepted astronomy and angered the university's leaders.
Such ideas were considered heretical by the strict church leaders.
cloze: The {{heretical}} suggestion that the earth moved around the sun once earned scholars severe punishment.
mnemonic: HERETIC is the person with the HERETICal idea.

definition: sealed airtight; isolated from outside influence
examples: The scientists stored the delicate sample in a hermetic container so that no air could reach it.
He lived a hermetic life, cut off from friends, family, and all news of the world.
cloze: The jar had a {{hermetic}} seal, so no air or moisture could ever reach the food inside.
mnemonic: HERMit sealed in his cave: HERMETIC.

definition: made up of different or varied parts
examples: The city's population is heterogeneous, with people from dozens of countries.
A heterogeneous mix of rock, sand, and clay filled the valley.
cloze: Because the class was {{heterogeneous}}, with students of very different ages and abilities, the teacher varied her methods.
mnemonic: HETERO = different; compare HOMO = same.

definition: the period of greatest success or popularity
examples: In its heyday, the mill employed thousands of workers and fed the whole town.
The singer, long past her heyday, still drew devoted fans.
cloze: The grand hotel recalled the {{heyday}} of rail travel, when travelers filled its ballroom.
mnemonic: Hey, day! The best days.

definition: to draw special attention to something
examples: The report highlights the need for more funding in rural schools.
The documentary highlights the effects of deforestation on local wildlife.
cloze: The lecturer used a graph to {{highlight}} the sharp rise in global temperatures.
mnemonic: HIGHLIGHT with a bright marker: make it light up.

definition: to make progress difficult or slow
examples: Thick fog hindered the search for the missing ship.
Lack of funding hindered the development of the new vaccine.
cloze: Poor roads {{hinder}} trade between mountain villages and the coastal markets.
mnemonic: HINDER = stay BEHIND, hold back.

definition: overly dramatic or theatrical in behavior
examples: His histrionic sobbing over a minor scratch embarrassed his friends.
The actress's histrionic gestures were too exaggerated for the small stage.
cloze: Embarrassed by her {{histrionic}} outburst, the family tried to calm her and change the subject.
mnemonic: HISTRIONIC: HIS TRIO of dramatic fits, like an actor.

definition: very old; gray or white with age
examples: The hoary oak had stood at the crossroads since long before the town existed.
He told the same hoary joke at every dinner, and everyone groaned.
cloze: The {{hoary}} professor, white-bearded and slow, had taught at the college for fifty years.
mnemonic: HOARy frost covers things in white: hair white with age.

definition: to walk with difficulty; to hinder or restrict movement or progress
examples: The injured runner hobbled across the finish line on a twisted ankle.
Excessive regulation can hobble small businesses and keep them from growing.
cloze: Strict budget limits threatened to {{hobble}} the research team just as it neared a breakthrough.
mnemonic: HOBBLE rhymes with WOBBLE - a wobbly, limping walk.

definition: a confused mixture of unlike things
examples: The attic was a hodgepodge of broken lamps, old books, and dusty toys.
His essay was a hodgepodge of half-formed ideas with no central argument.
cloze: The menu, a {{hodgepodge}} of cuisines from five continents, left diners confused.
mnemonic: HODGE-PODGE: a stew where everything is tossed in.

definition: of the same kind; uniform throughout
examples: The village was homogeneous, with nearly everyone sharing the same language, religion, and traditional customs.
Stir the paint thoroughly until the whole mixture looks homogeneous and no streaks of color remain.
cloze: The culture of the small island was highly {{homogeneous}}, with almost no variation in customs or dress.
mnemonic: HOMO = same; HOMOgenized milk is the same throughout.

definition: to sharpen or perfect over time
examples: He spent years honing his skills as a violinist before he finally performed in public.
The chef used a steel rod to hone the edge of his knife.
cloze: Through endless practice, the debater began to {{hone}} her arguments until they were nearly flawless.
mnemonic: A HONE is a whetstone; HONE your skills like a blade.

definition: to fool or con someone
examples: The con artist hoodwinked the retirees into investing in a worthless scheme.
Do not let the flashy advertisement hoodwink you into overpaying.
cloze: The swindler tried to {{hoodwink}} the buyers with a fake certificate of authenticity.
mnemonic: Pull a HOOD over the eyes and WINK, so they cannot see the truth.

definition: strongly urging or encouraging
examples: The coach gave a hortatory speech before the final match.
Her hortatory tone made the audience feel they had to act at once.
cloze: The pastor's {{hortatory}} sermon urged the congregation to give generously to the poor.
mnemonic: HORT sounds like exHORT.

definition: to pursue or harass relentlessly
examples: Reporters hounded the actress for days after the scandal broke.
Creditors hounded him with calls until he finally paid the bill.
cloze: The press continued to {{hound}} the retired politician, camping outside his home at every hour.
mnemonic: A HOUND is a hunting dog that tracks you down.

definition: excessive pride or self-confidence
examples: The general's hubris led him to ignore his advisers and march into a trap.
In Greek tragedy, hubris often leads to the hero's downfall.
cloze: The CEO's {{hubris}} blinded him to the risks of his reckless acquisitions, and the company collapsed.
mnemonic: HUBRIS: HUGE BRisk ego that crashes.

definition: lacking excitement or variety; dull and routine
examples: She longed to escape her humdrum life of commuting and filing reports.
The humdrum routine of the factory left workers feeling bored and restless.
cloze: After the adventure of travel, the {{humdrum}} routine of office work felt almost unbearable.
mnemonic: HUM-DRUM: a droning, boring beat that never changes.

definition: deliberate and obvious exaggeration for effect
examples: Saying that you have told someone a million times is hyperbole.
The ad's hyperbole, claiming it was the best pizza in the universe, amused many.
cloze: His claim that the exam lasted 'forever' was clearly {{hyperbole}}; it had taken only two hours.
mnemonic: HYPER + bole: speech that goes hyper.

definition: pretending to hold virtues or beliefs one does not actually have
examples: The politician's hypocrisy was clear when he denounced corruption while accepting bribes.
She could not stand the hypocrisy of preaching honesty and cheating on taxes.
cloze: Critics accused the leader of {{hypocrisy}} for lecturing others on thrift while buying luxury jets.
mnemonic: HYPO-CRISY: a CRISis of honesty beneath a mask.

definition: a proposed explanation that can be tested by investigation
examples: The biologist's hypothesis was that warmer water would speed up algae growth.
Experiments failed to support the original hypothesis about the origin of the fossils.
cloze: Before running the trial, the team wrote a clear {{hypothesis}} that the data could confirm or reject.
mnemonic: HYPO (under) + THESIS: an idea placed under test.

definition: someone who challenges or attacks traditional beliefs and institutions
examples: The iconoclast delighted in challenging every tradition of the art world.
As a young iconoclast, she dismissed the academy's rules and invented her own style.
cloze: A true {{iconoclast}}, he mocked the sacred customs that everyone else treated with reverence.
mnemonic: ICON + CLAST (breaker): breaks icons.

definition: attacking cherished beliefs or traditions
examples: The iconoclastic painter rejected every convention of the academy.
His iconoclastic essays outraged the literary establishment.
cloze: The {{iconoclastic}} scientist dismissed the prevailing theory and was ridiculed for it.
mnemonic: ICON + CLAST (break): smasher of idols.

definition: exactly the same in every detail
examples: Identical twins share nearly the same genetic code.
The two paintings looked identical until experts examined the brushwork under a microscope.
cloze: The lab produced {{identical}} samples so that each group could be tested under the same conditions.
mnemonic: IDENTICAL = ID card copies: no difference.

definition: a system of ideas that forms the basis of a political theory
examples: The party's ideology emphasized equality and shared ownership, and every policy it adopted reflected those beliefs.
He rejected the rigid ideology of both extremes and preferred to judge each issue on its own merits.
cloze: The group's {{ideology}} shaped every policy it adopted, from taxation to education.
mnemonic: IDEA + LOGY: a system of ideas.

definition: a peculiar habit or trait characteristic of one person
examples: His one idiosyncrasy was wearing mismatched socks on every important day.
Every writer has idiosyncrasies, such as writing only at dawn with a pencil.
cloze: Her {{idiosyncrasy}} of eating dessert before dinner amused her whole family.
mnemonic: IDIO = own/personal: your own odd mix.

definition: peculiar to one individual; quirky
examples: His idiosyncratic habit of wearing two watches puzzled his coworkers.
The chef's idiosyncratic recipes combine ingredients no one else would try.
cloze: The professor's {{idiosyncratic}} teaching method, involving songs and puppets, baffled new students.
mnemonic: IDIO = own: one's OWN odd way.

definition: dishonorable; of low moral character
examples: He met an ignoble end, abandoned by the friends he had betrayed.
The senator's ignoble scheme to profit from the disaster shocked his supporters.
cloze: It was an {{ignoble}} act to take credit for a colleague's discovery.
mnemonic: IG-NOBLE: not noble.

definition: deserving or bringing public shame
examples: The general suffered an ignominious defeat in the battle and was dismissed in disgrace the next morning.
His ignominious exit from politics followed revelations of fraud, and he never held public office again.
cloze: After an {{ignominious}} end to his career, he lived quietly and never spoke about the scandal.
mnemonic: IG + NOMEN (name): loss of name.

definition: forbidden by law or custom
examples: Police broke up an illicit trade in stolen goods that had been operating in the port for years.
They had an illicit meeting that no one was supposed to know about.
cloze: The smugglers profited from the {{illicit}} sale of rare birds across the border.
mnemonic: IL + LICIT (licit = legal): not legal.

definition: to make clear by examples or pictures
examples: The professor used a diagram to illustrate how glaciers carve valleys.
Her paintings illustrate daily life in a medieval village.
cloze: This case study will {{illustrate}} the challenges of managing a fishery sustainably.
mnemonic: ILLUSTRATE: LUSTER lights up the idea.

definition: distinguished, famous, and admired for achievements
examples: The university boasts many illustrious graduates, including two Nobel laureates.
She came from an illustrious family of statesmen and scholars.
cloze: The hall displayed portraits of the college's most {{illustrious}} alumni.
mnemonic: ILLUSTRIOUS: lustrous, shining with glory.

definition: to drink; to absorb ideas or knowledge
examples: The guests imbibed freely at the wedding reception.
Young children imbibe language simply by listening to their parents.
cloze: Students will {{imbibe}} the school's values simply by living among its traditions.
mnemonic: IM-BIBE: a BIB catches the drink you take in.

definition: a confusing and embarrassing situation or entanglement
examples: The tax imbroglio dragged on for years, baffling even the lawyers.
A diplomatic imbroglio erupted when the two ambassadors gave conflicting statements.
cloze: The scandal turned into an international {{imbroglio}} that no one seemed able to untangle.
mnemonic: Italian for 'tangle': an in-BROIL-io.

definition: perfectly clean or without flaw
examples: The maid left the hotel room immaculate, without a speck of dust anywhere on the furniture.
She wore an immaculate white dress, and not a single stain or wrinkle could be seen on it.
cloze: The chef kept his kitchen {{immaculate}}, wiping every surface after each service.
mnemonic: IM + MACULA (spot): no spots.

definition: unimportant or irrelevant to the matter at hand
examples: Whether the defendant likes sports is immaterial to the question of his guilt.
The color of the car is immaterial; all I need is a reliable one.
cloze: Your age is {{immaterial}} to this job; only your skills and experience matter.
mnemonic: IM-MATERIAL: has no matter, so it doesn't matter.

definition: extremely large or great
examples: Immense glaciers once covered much of northern Europe.
The invention of the telescope was of immense importance to astronomy.
cloze: The construction of the canal required an {{immense}} amount of labor and money.
mnemonic: IM + MENSE (measure): beyond measure.

definition: to confine within walls; to imprison
examples: The tyrant immured his rivals in a remote tower for decades.
She felt immured in the quiet village, longing for the bustle of the city.
cloze: The scholar would {{immure}} himself in the library for weeks to finish his book.
mnemonic: IM-MURE: put inside the MUR (wall).

definition: unchanging over time; unable to be changed
examples: The scientist believed the basic laws of physics were immutable and would never change over time.
She held immutable principles that no argument, however clever, could ever persuade her to alter.
cloze: The old king insisted that his decrees were {{immutable}}, never to be altered by any later ruler.
mnemonic: IM + MUTABLE: cannot mutate.

definition: a strong effect on something
examples: The impact of tourism on the island's coral reefs has been severe.
Advances in printing had a lasting impact on education and politics.
cloze: Economists studied the {{impact}} of the new tariff on small businesses.
mnemonic: IM-PACT: a PACKed punch.

definition: treating all sides equally; unbiased
examples: A judge must remain impartial and not favor either side.
The committee sought an impartial expert to settle the argument.
cloze: As an {{impartial}} observer with no stake in the outcome, she described the dispute fairly.
mnemonic: IM + PARTIAL: takes no part or side.

definition: not showing emotion
examples: The judge remained impassive as the verdict was read, showing neither relief nor anger to the crowd.
Her impassive face gave no clue to what she was thinking.
cloze: He listened with an {{impassive}} expression, revealing neither anger nor sympathy.
mnemonic: IM + PASSION: without passion shown.

definition: flawless; without fault
examples: Her manners were impeccable, and everyone praised her poise.
The chef's impeccable reputation brought diners from across the country.
cloze: He gave an {{impeccable}} performance, without a single missed note.
mnemonic: IM-PECC-: cannot sin (peccare), so perfect.

definition: having little or no money
examples: The impecunious student lived mostly on bread and tea because he could not afford anything better.
An impecunious poet, he often borrowed from friends to pay the rent.
cloze: Although born to a rich family, he became {{impecunious}} after squandering his inheritance.
mnemonic: IM + PECUNIA (money): no money.

definition: to hinder or obstruct progress
examples: Fallen trees across the road impeded the rescue crews, who had to clear a path by hand.
Poor roads and high taxes impede trade between the two regions and keep prices high for farmers.
cloze: Heavy snow can {{impede}} traffic and delay deliveries to remote villages by several days.
mnemonic: IM + PED (foot): put a trap on the foot.

definition: about to happen; looming
examples: Dark clouds on the horizon warned the sailors of the impending storm.
Workers were anxious about the impending layoffs announced on Monday.
cloze: With the {{impending}} deadline only hours away, the team worked through the night.
mnemonic: Pending over your head: hanging above you.

definition: arrogantly domineering and commanding
examples: The imperious queen demanded that everyone bow whenever she entered.
His imperious tone made clear that questions would not be tolerated.
cloze: The director's {{imperious}} manner annoyed the cast, who resented being ordered about like servants.
mnemonic: IMPERIOUS: like an EMPEROR giving orders.

definition: not allowing liquids or gases to pass through
examples: The raincoat is made of an impermeable fabric that keeps out even heavy rain.
Clay soil is nearly impermeable, so water pools on its surface after storms.
cloze: The tank's {{impermeable}} lining prevents chemicals from seeping into the surrounding ground.
mnemonic: IM-PERMEABLE: can't permeate, nothing gets through.

definition: rude and disrespectful; improperly bold
examples: The impertinent child told the guest that her hat looked silly.
It was impertinent of him to ask his boss about her salary.
cloze: The principal sent the {{impertinent}} student out of class for mocking the teacher.
mnemonic: IMPERTINENT: not PERTINENT in his manners - out of line (also: irrelevant).

definition: unable to be upset or excited; calm
examples: She remained imperturbable even as the angry audience booed and jeered throughout her entire speech.
The imperturbable pilot calmly landed the plane through the storm while the passengers gripped their seats.
cloze: With {{imperturbable}} calm, the surgeon continued the operation despite the alarm sounding behind him.
mnemonic: IM + PERTURB: cannot be disturbed.

definition: not allowing passage; not affected by something
examples: The raincoat was impervious to water, even in the heaviest storm.
She remained impervious to criticism and pursued her own plan regardless.
cloze: Seemingly {{impervious}} to flattery, the judge responded only to evidence and sound argument.
mnemonic: IM + PERVIOUS: no PATH through (per via).

definition: acting quickly without thought; rash
examples: The impetuous young man quit his job in a fit of anger.
Her impetuous decision to buy the house without inspecting it caused problems.
cloze: An {{impetuous}} remark in the meeting cost him the support of two senior colleagues.
mnemonic: IMPETUOUS: an IMP who acts on impulse.

definition: unable to be appeased or pacified
examples: The implacable enemy rejected every offer of peace and demanded complete surrender from the town.
Her implacable anger had not softened in thirty years, despite many apologies from her sister.
cloze: The two rivals remained {{implacable}}, refusing to shake hands even after years of mediation.
mnemonic: IM + PLACABLE (placate): cannot be placated.

definition: not seeming reasonable or likely to be true
examples: The detective dismissed the implausible story as a poor attempt to cover the theft.
Critics found the movie's twist implausible, since it contradicted everything shown earlier.
cloze: His excuse was so {{implausible}} that no one believed it for a moment.
mnemonic: IM (not) + PLAUSIBLE: you wouldn't applaud it.

definition: to put a plan or system into effect
examples: The government plans to implement stricter pollution controls next year.
Schools that implemented the new curriculum reported higher test scores.
cloze: The committee voted to {{implement}} the recycling program across the entire campus.
mnemonic: IMPLEMENT a tool: you use tools to get things done.

definition: to show or suggest that someone is involved in a crime or wrongdoing
examples: The leaked email implicated several senior officials in the cover-up.
He refused to implicate his friend, even under pressure from police.
cloze: The testimony of the informant was enough to {{implicate}} the businessman in the fraud scheme.
mnemonic: IM-PLICATE: fold (plic) someone INTO the crime.

definition: a possible effect or conclusion that is suggested but not stated
examples: The study has important implications for how cities manage water.
The professor explained the economic implications of falling birth rates.
cloze: One {{implication}} of the discovery is that the species may be older than scientists believed.
mnemonic: IMPLY gives an IMPLICATION: hinted, not said.

definition: impossible to measure, estimate, or fully work out
examples: The long-term effects of the policy remain imponderable, since so many factors are unknown.
She faced imponderable questions about whether the risk was worth taking.
cloze: Whether the experiment will succeed depends on {{imponderable}} factors that no one can calculate.
mnemonic: Cannot be PONDERed or weighed: IM-PONDER-able.

definition: pleaded with or pressed persistently for something
examples: Beggars importuned the tourists outside the station until the guards drove them off.
The senator was importuned by lobbyists day after day to change his vote.
cloze: The child {{importuned}} his parents for a puppy until they finally gave in.
mnemonic: Keep 'importing' the same request again and again until they give in.

definition: to force something to be accepted or followed
examples: The council imposed a ban on cars in the historic district.
Colonial powers often imposed their languages on the people they ruled.
cloze: Governments may {{impose}} taxes on sugary drinks to reduce consumption.
mnemonic: IMPOSE: you POSE a rule ON people.

definition: impossible to capture or break into; unassailable
examples: The castle on the cliff was considered impregnable by every invading army.
The champion's defense seemed impregnable, and no opponent scored against it all season.
cloze: The bank's vault was supposedly {{impregnable}}, yet thieves still found a way in.
mnemonic: IM-PREGN-able: cannot be entered or taken.

definition: done without preparation; spontaneous
examples: She gave an impromptu speech when the microphone was handed to her.
The friends held an impromptu picnic when the weather turned warm.
cloze: The musician's {{impromptu}} performance in the park drew a large crowd of surprised listeners.
mnemonic: IN PROMPT time: no prep.

definition: not providing for the future; careless with money
examples: His improvident spending left the family with nothing when the factory closed.
The improvident farmer ate his seed grain and had nothing to plant in spring.
cloze: An {{improvident}} saver, she spent each paycheck within days and never planned ahead.
mnemonic: IM-PROVIDE-nt: doesn't provide for later.
