definition: unwise; showing poor judgment and lack of caution
examples: It was imprudent to invest all your savings in a single risky venture.
The imprudent hiker ignored the storm warning and set off up the ridge.
cloze: Making such a large purchase without checking your finances was {{imprudent}}.
mnemonic: IM-PRUDENT: not prudent.

definition: rudely disrespectful and bold
examples: The impudent boy stuck out his tongue at the teacher.
Her impudent reply to the general shocked everyone present.
cloze: The waiter's {{impudent}} answer to the customer cost him his job.
mnemonic: IM-PUDENT: no PUDor (shame) at all.

definition: to challenge the truth or honesty of a statement
examples: The lawyer tried to impugn the witness's testimony by exposing past lies.
It is unfair to impugn a person's motives without evidence.
cloze: Critics were quick to {{impugn}} the study's findings, claiming that the data had been manipulated.
mnemonic: IM-PUGN: PUGNacious attack on someone's word.

definition: to attribute a fault or quality to someone, often unfairly
examples: It is unfair to impute selfish motives to her generous gift.
The prosecutor imputed the failure to the director's negligence.
cloze: Do not {{impute}} malice to what was really an honest mistake.
mnemonic: IM-PUTE: PUT the blame ON someone.

definition: not done on purpose; unintentional
examples: His inadvertent remark during the party revealed the surprise that his friends had planned for weeks.
An inadvertent click of the mouse deleted the whole file, and three days of work disappeared.
cloze: The {{inadvertent}} error, caused by a slip of the finger, cost the company thousands of dollars.
mnemonic: IN + ADVERT (turn toward): did not turn attention.

definition: silly; lacking sense or substance
examples: His inane remarks about the weather filled the empty minutes but contributed nothing to the discussion.
The show's inane humor depended entirely on people falling over, and the audience grew bored quickly.
cloze: The meeting was dominated by {{inane}} chatter, and no useful decision was reached.
mnemonic: INANE sounds like IN-SANE: silly, senseless.

definition: silliness; a foolish or meaningless remark
examples: He grew tired of the inanity of the show's dialogue.
Her speech was full of inanities that offered no real ideas.
cloze: The committee wasted hours on the {{inanity}} of a debate over office paint colors.
mnemonic: IN-ANE-ity: totally insane and empty.

definition: unable to express oneself clearly in words
examples: Overcome with grief, he was inarticulate and could only nod.
The inarticulate candidate stumbled through simple questions.
cloze: She was {{inarticulate}} with rage and could only sputter in reply.
mnemonic: Not ARTICULATE: words cannot join up clearly.

definition: to make extremely angry
examples: The new tax incensed citizens, who gathered outside city hall to protest.
His careless remarks incensed his colleagues and ended the meeting early.
cloze: The unfair ruling was sure to {{incense}} fans who had traveled across the country.
mnemonic: Incense burns and so do you: set aflame with anger (stress on -cense).

definition: something that motivates a person to act
examples: Tax credits give homeowners an incentive to install solar panels.
Scholarships serve as a powerful incentive for students to maintain high grades.
cloze: Farmers had little {{incentive}} to adopt the new method because it cost more and paid less.
mnemonic: IN-CENT-ive: a few CENTs motivate action.

definition: continuing without pause
examples: The incessant noise of traffic outside kept her awake for the whole night.
Their incessant quarreling exhausted everyone in the house, and the neighbors could hear it through the walls.
cloze: The {{incessant}} rain lasted for a week, flooding roads and fields without a single break.
mnemonic: IN + CESS (cease): never ceases.

definition: just begun and not fully formed
examples: He had only an inchoate idea of what the novel would be about when he began.
The inchoate movement lacked leaders, funding, and clear goals, so few people took it seriously yet.
cloze: His plans were still {{inchoate}}, little more than scattered notes and a few vague hopes.
mnemonic: IN-CHOATE sounds like CHAOTIC beginning: raw and shapeless.

definition: intelligently analytical and clear and direct
examples: The critic's incisive review pointed out the film's central weakness.
Her incisive questions revealed flaws in the plan at once.
cloze: With {{incisive}} reasoning, the lawyer cut through the confusion and exposed the heart of the dispute.
mnemonic: INCISive: INCISion, cuts right to the point.

definition: unpleasantly cold, stormy, or harsh, of weather
examples: The game was postponed because of inclement weather and a flooded field.
Travelers were stranded for hours by the inclement conditions on the mountain pass.
cloze: Because of the {{inclement}} weather, the ceremony was held indoors.
mnemonic: IN-CLEMENT: lacking CLEMENCY, the weather shows no mercy.

definition: out of place; not fitting with surroundings
examples: A neon sign looked incongruous on the ancient stone cottage.
His cheerful mood seemed incongruous at such a solemn event.
cloze: The modern glass tower looked {{incongruous}} among the centuries-old houses of the village square.
mnemonic: IN + CONGRUENT: does not match.

definition: impossible to deny or dispute
examples: DNA gave the investigators incontrovertible proof of the suspect's presence at the scene.
The evidence was incontrovertible, and the defense had no reply.
cloze: Her results were so {{incontrovertible}} that even skeptical colleagues had to accept them.
mnemonic: IN-CONTROVERT-ible: you can't CONTRA-dict it, can't argue back.

definition: to include something as part of a whole
examples: Modern architects incorporate natural light into building designs.
The new edition incorporates recent research on climate change.
cloze: The author chose to {{incorporate}} local legends into her history of the town.
mnemonic: IN + CORPUS (body): put into the body.

definition: unable to be reformed or corrected
examples: The incorrigible rascal broke the rule again within minutes of being warned.
She was an incorrigible optimist who found hope in every setback.
cloze: The boy was an {{incorrigible}} prankster, ignoring every punishment his parents devised.
mnemonic: IN + CORRECT + ible: cannot be corrected.

definition: necessary as a duty or obligation; also currently holding an office
examples: It is incumbent upon every citizen to vote.
The incumbent senator won reelection easily, as voters stayed with the familiar name.
cloze: As the senior partner, it was {{incumbent}} on her to explain the firm's decision to the staff.
mnemonic: INCUMBENT: the one who has CUMmed to rest ON the seat now - and must serve.

definition: not in good taste; improper or unseemly
examples: His indecorous laughter at the funeral shocked all the other mourners present.
Wearing sneakers to the formal dinner was seen as indecorous by the older guests.
cloze: The senator's {{indecorous}} outburst in the chamber earned him a formal reprimand.
mnemonic: IN-DECOROUS: lacks DECOR and manners.

definition: to show or point out something
examples: Tree rings indicate how much rainfall the area received each year.
Survey results indicate that most students prefer online classes.
cloze: Rising levels of carbon dioxide {{indicate}} that human activity is altering the atmosphere.
mnemonic: INDICATE: INDEX finger points.

definition: to formally charge with a crime
examples: A grand jury indicted the executive on charges of fraud.
The prosecutor will indict the suspects once she has gathered enough evidence.
cloze: The jury voted to {{indict}} the former official on corruption charges.
mnemonic: INDICT sounds like 'indite' – pronounced in-DITE, you write up charges.

definition: lack of interest, concern, or sympathy
examples: Her indifference to the suffering around her shocked the volunteers.
The crowd greeted the speech with total indifference and began to leave.
cloze: His {{indifference}} to the outcome of the match made the coach angry, since the team needed passion.
mnemonic: IN-DIFFERENCE: no difference to him which way it goes.

definition: originating naturally in a particular place; native
examples: Kangaroos are indigenous to Australia, whereas rabbits were brought there by European settlers long ago.
The museum honors the traditions of the indigenous peoples of the region.
cloze: Several plants {{indigenous}} to the island are found nowhere else on earth.
mnemonic: INDI-GENous: born (gen) IN the place.

definition: poor; needy
examples: The charity provided free meals to indigent families who could not afford to feed their children.
Lawyers provide free services to indigent defendants who cannot pay.
cloze: Many {{indigent}} residents of the city rely on shelters and food banks to survive winter.
mnemonic: INDI-GENT: a GENT in need.

definition: angry because of perceived unfair treatment or insult
examples: The indignant customer demanded a refund after being accused of shoplifting.
She was indignant that her honest report had been called a fabrication.
cloze: The mayor was {{indignant}} at the suggestion that he had accepted a bribe.
mnemonic: INDIGN- sounds like 'in dignity': angry that your dignity was hurt.

definition: habitually lazy; avoiding work
examples: The indolent clerk spent most of the day staring out of the window.
Her indolent brother slept until noon every day and never helped around the house.
cloze: Too {{indolent}} to look for a job, he lay on the sofa all week and let his family support him.
mnemonic: INDOLENT: IN DOLE (idle) - lying around.

definition: diligent and hardworking
examples: The industrious student studied every night until midnight.
Ants are famed as industrious creatures, always gathering food.
cloze: Our {{industrious}} neighbor spent every weekend repairing the old barn.
mnemonic: INDUSTRY - busy as a factory.

definition: too great to be expressed in words
examples: They felt an ineffable joy as the sun rose over the mountain.
The beauty of the cathedral was ineffable; no photograph could capture it.
cloze: She felt an {{ineffable}} sorrow that no words could describe when the old house was finally sold.
mnemonic: IN + EFFABLE (effare = speak): cannot be spoken.

definition: impossible to avoid or escape; inevitable
examples: Death is the ineluctable fate of all living things.
The company's ineluctable decline began when its main product became obsolete.
cloze: Faced with the {{ineluctable}} approach of the storm, the villagers boarded up their windows and fled.
mnemonic: IN-ELUCT-able: can't wrestle out (luctari, to struggle) of it.

definition: clumsy; lacking skill or competence
examples: The inept waiter spilled soup on three different customers during a single busy evening.
An inept manager can ruin a promising company in a matter of months by making poor decisions.
cloze: His {{inept}} handling of the negotiations cost the firm its biggest client.
mnemonic: IN + EPT (apt): not apt.

definition: lack of fairness or justice; an unfair situation
examples: Advocates demanded an end to the inequity in school funding between rich and poor districts.
He protested the inequity of a system that rewarded privilege rather than effort.
cloze: The report highlighted a glaring {{inequity}} in how the law treated rich and poor defendants.
mnemonic: IN + EQUITY: not equal, not fair.

definition: lacking the ability or will to move or act
examples: The patient lay inert on the bed, too weak to speak.
Helium is an inert gas that does not react with other elements.
cloze: The {{inert}} bureaucracy ignored the crisis and did nothing for weeks.
mnemonic: IN + ERT (art, skill): no activity.

definition: certain to happen and impossible to avoid
examples: Some historians argue that war was inevitable after the treaty collapsed.
As glaciers melt, rising sea levels seem inevitable for coastal towns.
cloze: Given the rapid growth of the population, shortages of fresh water were {{inevitable}}.
mnemonic: IN-EVIT-able: cannot EVADE it.

definition: in a way that cannot be avoided
examples: Technologies inevitably become cheaper as production increases.
Populations inevitably decline when their habitat disappears.
cloze: Languages {{inevitably}} change as societies come into contact with one another.
mnemonic: INEVITABLY: sure as the tide.

definition: unstoppable; relentless and impossible to prevent
examples: The inexorable rise of the sea level threatens many coastal towns.
Time's inexorable march meant that the old castle would eventually crumble.
cloze: The {{inexorable}} advance of the glacier slowly swallowed the village over the course of a century.
mnemonic: IN + EXORABLE (exorare=to move by prayer): cannot be moved by pleas.

definition: unfortunate; poorly chosen or ill-suited
examples: His infelicitous joke at the funeral left the mourners shocked and silent.
The infelicitous phrasing of the contract caused confusion for years.
cloze: An {{infelicitous}} remark in the interview later cost the candidate dearly.
mnemonic: IN + FELIX (happy): not happy or apt.

definition: to reach a conclusion from evidence and reasoning
examples: Geologists can infer the age of a rock layer from the fossils it contains.
From the tone of the letter, historians infer that the author was deeply worried.
cloze: Readers must {{infer}} the narrator's feelings because the novel never states them directly.
mnemonic: INFER = IN-FERring: carry meaning in from clues.

definition: easily set on fire (same as flammable)
examples: Gasoline is highly inflammable and must be stored away from heat.
Workers wore protective gear around the inflammable chemicals in the warehouse.
cloze: Warning labels on the drum read {{inflammable}}, so no one lit a match nearby.
mnemonic: INFLAME: it can inflame, so it is NOT the opposite of flammable.

definition: clever, original, and inventive
examples: The engineer devised an ingenious way to bring water to the village.
Her ingenious plan solved the problem with almost no money.
cloze: The {{ingenious}} gadget could peel, slice, and core an apple in a single motion.
mnemonic: INGENIOUS has GENIUS inside.

definition: cleverness and inventiveness in solving problems
examples: The engineers solved the leak with an ingenuity that surprised their supervisors.
Using only string and scrap wood, the children showed remarkable ingenuity in building a boat.
cloze: Survival on the island demanded {{ingenuity}}, since the castaways had almost no tools.
mnemonic: INGENUITY has 'genius' inside: genius-level inventing.

definition: innocent and trusting; without guile
examples: The ingenuous child cheerfully told the stranger her full name and exactly where she lived.
His ingenuous smile suggested he had no idea of the scandal around him.
cloze: Too {{ingenuous}} to suspect treachery, the young officer trusted every word the merchant said.
mnemonic: INGENUOUS (innocent) is not INGENIOUS (clever).

definition: to win favor by deliberate effort
examples: He tried to ingratiate himself with the boss by laughing at every joke.
The newcomer sought to ingratiate herself with the neighbors by baking cakes.
cloze: Hoping to {{ingratiate}} himself with the director, the actor brought coffee for the entire crew.
mnemonic: IN + GRATE (pleasing, like grateful): get into someone's good graces.

definition: existing as a natural, permanent part of something
examples: Risk is inherent in any scientific exploration of unknown territory.
The inherent flexibility of bamboo makes it ideal for building in earthquake zones.
cloze: Uncertainty is an {{inherent}} feature of long-term climate forecasting.
mnemonic: IN + HERE: it sticks inside, always HERE.

definition: to hold back or slow down a process
examples: Cold temperatures inhibit the growth of many bacteria.
Fear of failure can inhibit creativity in the classroom.
cloze: Certain chemicals in the soil {{inhibit}} the germination of seeds.
mnemonic: IN-HIBIT: put IN a HABIT-blocker.

definition: harmful or hostile
examples: Smoking is inimical to good health, and doctors have warned patients about its dangers for decades.
The regime was inimical to free speech, so it jailed the critics who dared to publish their opinions.
cloze: Policies {{inimical}} to small business drove many family shops out of the town.
mnemonic: INIMICAL contains ENEMY (inimicus).

definition: so unique that it cannot be imitated
examples: The singer's inimitable voice made her instantly recognizable.
He had an inimitable style that no imitator could capture.
cloze: Chaplin's {{inimitable}} comic timing has never been matched.
mnemonic: IN-IMITABLE: cannot be IMITATED.

definition: happening at the beginning
examples: The initial results of the survey surprised the researchers.
Scientists made an initial estimate of the damage before further tests.
cloze: The {{initial}} stage of the project involved collecting soil samples from twelve sites.
mnemonic: INITIAL = first letter of a name.

definition: a slight hint or vague notion
examples: She had no inkling that her friends were planning a surprise party.
He had an inkling that the deal would fall through but said nothing.
cloze: The detective had an {{inkling}} that the butler was lying, though nothing proved it yet.
mnemonic: An INKLING is a drop of INK - a tiny trace.

definition: inborn; existing from birth
examples: She had an innate talent for music and could play any tune by ear without lessons.
Humans appear to have an innate ability to learn language, even without formal lessons from adults.
cloze: The puppy showed an {{innate}} fear of water that no amount of training could remove.
mnemonic: IN + NATE (born): born in.

definition: not harmful or offensive
examples: The innocuous remark was never meant to hurt anyone, yet it caused a long argument.
The garden snake was innocuous, with no venom at all, so the children played near it without fear.
cloze: An {{innocuous}} comment about the weather somehow offended her, though it was meant kindly.
mnemonic: IN + NOC (harm): no harm.

definition: to introduce new ideas, methods, or products
examples: Companies must innovate constantly to stay ahead of competitors.
Ancient engineers innovated ways to move heavy stones using ramps and levers.
cloze: Universities encourage students to {{innovate}} by funding experimental projects.
mnemonic: IN + NOVA (new): bring in something new.

definition: impossible to understand or interpret; mysterious
examples: His inscrutable expression gave no hint of what he was thinking.
The ancient inscription remained inscrutable to scholars for centuries.
cloze: The judge's {{inscrutable}} face revealed nothing about which way the verdict would go.
mnemonic: IN + SCRUTinize: you can't scrutinize your way into it.

definition: spreading harmfully in a subtle, stealthy way
examples: The disease is insidious, causing no obvious symptoms until it has already spread through the body.
The insidious influence of propaganda slowly changed public opinion without most citizens ever noticing the shift.
cloze: The {{insidious}} rumor spread quietly through the town, doing damage before anyone could challenge it.
mnemonic: INSIDious: sits INSIDE and harms secretly (like a sneaky SIDE-kick).

definition: a deep understanding of a situation
examples: Fossils give scientists insight into how ancient animals lived.
The interviews offered valuable insight into how immigrants adapt to a new culture.
cloze: The experiment provided new {{insight}} into how the brain stores memories.
mnemonic: IN + SIGHT: seeing inside.

definition: lacking flavor, interest, or spirit
examples: The soup was so insipid that no amount of salt could save it.
Critics found the novel insipid, lacking any memorable characters or ideas.
cloze: Everyone found the speaker's {{insipid}} lecture dull, since it contained neither humor nor original thought.
mnemonic: IN + SIPID (sapid = tasty): no taste.

definition: rudely disrespectful
examples: The insolent student rolled his eyes and flatly refused to answer the teacher's question in front of the class.
The servant's insolent tone angered the master, who had never before been spoken to so rudely.
cloze: Fired for his {{insolent}} behavior toward customers, the waiter was told he was no longer welcome.
mnemonic: IN + SOLENT sounds like SOLDIER talking back; bold, disrespectful.

definition: unable to pay debts; bankrupt
examples: The insolvent company closed its doors, owing millions to suppliers.
After years of mismanagement, the firm was declared insolvent by the court.
cloze: Unable to pay its creditors, the {{insolvent}} airline filed for bankruptcy.
mnemonic: IN + SOLVENT: cannot dissolve (solve) debts.

definition: a carefree lack of concern
examples: She faced the audition with insouciance, as if the outcome mattered very little to her.
His insouciance about deadlines infuriated his anxious and overworked manager every single week.
cloze: With casual {{insouciance}}, the young heir wasted his fortune on yachts and parties.
mnemonic: IN + SOUCI (care): no care at all.

definition: a particular example or case of something
examples: In one instance, a single storm destroyed the entire fishing fleet.
Plants offer many instances of cooperation, such as roots sharing nutrients with fungi.
cloze: For {{instance}}, the Nile flooded each year and enriched the farmland along its banks.
mnemonic: INSTANCE: a thing that STANDs as an example.

definition: unbearable; too annoying or arrogant to tolerate
examples: His insufferable bragging made the dinner party hard to endure.
The heat in the crowded train car was nearly insufferable.
cloze: She found her boss {{insufferable}}, always boasting and never listening to anyone.
mnemonic: IN-SUFFER-able: you can't SUFFER through it.

definition: not enough
examples: Insufficient rainfall led to crop failure in the region.
The evidence was insufficient to convict the accused.
cloze: The lab had {{insufficient}} funding to complete the second phase of the project.
mnemonic: IN + SUFFICIENT: not enough.

definition: ignorant of or uninterested in other cultures; isolated
examples: The insular village distrusted all outsiders and rarely welcomed visitors from other towns or countries.
His insular outlook came from never having left his small hometown or met anyone from abroad.
cloze: Residents of the {{insular}} community rarely traveled and showed little interest in the wider world.
mnemonic: INSULAR = ISLAND: cut off by water.

definition: to combine parts into a unified whole
examples: Modern universities try to integrate technology into every course.
Immigrants often integrate into a new society by learning its language and customs.
cloze: The architect hoped to {{integrate}} the new library with the existing historic buildings.
mnemonic: INTEGER = whole: INTEGRATE makes a whole.

definition: to act in a way that affects each other
examples: Predators and prey interact in complex food webs.
Students interact with professors more often in small seminars.
cloze: Certain chemicals {{interact}} to produce the vivid colors in autumn leaves.
mnemonic: INTER (between) + ACT: act between.

definition: stopping and starting at intervals; not continuous
examples: Intermittent rain throughout the afternoon forced the picnic indoors several times.
He suffered intermittent pain that came and went without warning.
cloze: The radio signal was {{intermittent}}, fading in and out as the truck climbed the hills.
mnemonic: INTER + MITT: sending in bursts between pauses.

definition: destructive to both sides in a conflict; or occurring within a group
examples: The internecine struggle within the party weakened it more than any outside rival could.
The two rival clans fought an internecine war that left both of them in ruins.
cloze: The {{internecine}} feuding among the heirs drained the family's fortune and left them all poorer.
mnemonic: INTER + NECare (to kill): kill each other.

definition: to explain the meaning of something
examples: Archaeologists interpret ancient wall paintings as records of religious ceremonies.
Different critics interpret the poem's final line in very different ways.
cloze: It is difficult to {{interpret}} the data without knowing how the survey was conducted.
mnemonic: INTER-PRET: a go-between who explains meaning.

definition: to hint or suggest indirectly (pronounced with a long a)
examples: She intimated that she might resign, but she did not say so outright.
The letter intimated that the company was in financial trouble.
cloze: The senator did not state his plans but merely {{intimate}}d that he might run again.
mnemonic: The verb INTIMATE (-ate) hints; the adjective (-it) means close.

definition: a subtle hint or sign of something
examples: She gave no intimation that she planned to resign the next day.
There was an intimation of trouble in the quiet way he closed the door.
cloze: With only a faint {{intimation}} of the coming storm, the villagers failed to prepare in time.
mnemonic: INTIMate whisper: a quiet hint.

definition: refusing to change one's views or compromise
examples: The intransigent union leader rejected every offer the company made.
Both sides were intransigent, and the talks collapsed after only an hour.
cloze: His {{intransigent}} stance, refusing every compromise, made it impossible to reach any agreement.
mnemonic: IN + TRANS + IGENT: won't TRANSit (move) to another view.

definition: fearless and enduring
examples: The intrepid explorer crossed the entire desert alone and on foot, despite warnings from the locals.
Intrepid journalists reported from the war zone despite great danger.
cloze: Only the most {{intrepid}} climbers dared to attempt the north face in winter.
mnemonic: IN + TREPID (trembling): not trembling.

definition: belonging naturally to the essential nature of something
examples: Many artists believe that creative work has intrinsic value apart from its price.
Intrinsic motivation, such as curiosity, often produces deeper learning than rewards.
cloze: The gem's {{intrinsic}} beauty has nothing to do with the fortune it would fetch at auction.
mnemonic: INTRINSIC = INside, TRuly its own.

definition: to overwhelm with a flood of things
examples: Fans inundated the singer with thousands of letters after her concert, and she could not answer them all.
Heavy rains threatened to inundate the low-lying villages along the river, so families moved to higher ground.
cloze: The small office was {{inundated}} with applications after the job was posted.
mnemonic: IN-UNDA (wave): a wave comes in.

definition: to accustom to something unpleasant, making one tolerant
examples: Years in the emergency room had inured her to the sight of blood.
Soldiers are gradually inured to hardship through long, harsh training.
cloze: Living beside the highway, the residents became {{inure}}d to the constant roar of traffic.
mnemonic: INURE sounds like 'in your' routine: used to it.

definition: harsh, abusive language
examples: The politician hurled invective at his rivals during the debate.
The editorial was full of invective but short on evidence.
cloze: The crowd greeted the traitor with a torrent of {{invective}}.
mnemonic: IN-VECTIVE sounds like 'invective = INjure with words'.

definition: to examine something carefully to find facts
examples: Geologists investigated the cause of the sudden landslide.
Historians investigate old letters to understand daily life in earlier centuries.
cloze: A team of biologists will {{investigate}} why the bee population has declined so sharply.
mnemonic: IN + VEST + IGATE: follow the TRACKS (vestigium).

definition: firmly established by long habit
examples: He was an inveterate gambler who could not walk past a casino without going inside.
Her inveterate optimism survived every setback, and she always expected tomorrow to be better than today.
cloze: An {{inveterate}} liar, he had deceived friends and family for so many years that no one trusted him.
mnemonic: IN + VETERAN: a veteran at a habit.

definition: likely to cause resentment because unfair or discriminatory
examples: Judging students by their family name creates an invidious distinction.
The manager faced the invidious task of picking one friend over another for the promotion.
cloze: It would be {{invidious}} to praise one child's talent and ignore the others.
mnemonic: INVIDIA = envy: a comparison that breeds envy.

definition: too sacred or important to be broken or violated
examples: Many nations treat the right to a fair trial as inviolable.
The treaty declared the border inviolable, binding both countries for a century.
cloze: To the monks, the vow of silence was {{inviolable}} and never to be broken.
mnemonic: IN-VIOLATE-able: you cannot VIOLATE it.

definition: free from violation, injury, or desecration; untouched
examples: The ancient grove remained inviolate, protected from loggers for centuries.
The treaty declared the border inviolate, forbidding any crossing by force.
cloze: The library kept the rare manuscript {{inviolate}}, sealed in a vault where nobody could touch it.
mnemonic: IN-VIOLATE: cannot be VIOLATEd.

definition: complicated and hard to follow
examples: The plot of the novel is so involved that readers need a chart.
She gave a long and involved explanation that left everyone confused.
cloze: The tax code is far too {{involved}} for most ordinary citizens to understand.
mnemonic: INVOLVED: tangled in knots, you can't unwind it.

definition: easily angered; hot-tempered
examples: The irascible old man shouted angrily at any child who dared to walk across his lawn.
Her irascible nature made even simple conversations tense, and colleagues avoided disagreeing with her in meetings.
cloze: The {{irascible}} chef erupted into a rage whenever an order was returned or a plate was delayed.
mnemonic: IRE (anger) + ascible: easily full of ire.

definition: to irritate or annoy
examples: It irks me when people talk during a film.
His constant tardiness irked his manager.
cloze: Little things like a dripping faucet can really {{irk}} my father.
mnemonic: IRK sounds like 'jerk' - a jerk irks you.

definition: so clearly true it cannot be disproved
examples: The fingerprints provided irrefutable proof of the burglar's presence.
Her argument was irrefutable, leaving the skeptics with nothing to say.
cloze: The scientist offered {{irrefutable}} evidence that even the harshest critics could not dispute.
mnemonic: IR + REFUTE + able: cannot be refuted.

definition: hesitant; uncertain how to act
examples: The irresolute leader kept changing his mind about the plan.
She stood irresolute at the door, unable to decide whether to enter.
cloze: Too {{irresolute}} to commit to a decision, he let the offer expire while he debated for days.
mnemonic: IR + RESOLUTE: not resolved.

definition: impossible to undo or take back
examples: Once the papers are signed by both parties, the decision is irrevocable and cannot be undone.
He made an irrevocable promise to protect the village, whatever the cost.
cloze: The court issued an {{irrevocable}} order that no later ruling could reverse.
mnemonic: IR + REVOKE + able: cannot revoke.

definition: to separate something from others so it stands alone
examples: Chemists isolated the active compound from the leaves of the plant.
Patients with the infection were isolated to prevent the disease from spreading.
cloze: The researchers tried to {{isolate}} a single variable so they could measure its effect.
mnemonic: ISOLATE = ISLAND: alone, cut off.

definition: moving from place to place, often for work
examples: The itinerant preacher moved from village to village, never staying in one place for more than a week.
Itinerant workers followed the harvest from farm to farm, living wherever there was work to be done.
cloze: An {{itinerant}} musician by trade, he never stayed in one town for longer than a week.
mnemonic: ITINERARY = route; ITINERANT follows a route.

definition: specialized words of a profession that outsiders find hard to understand
examples: The lawyer's legal jargon left the jury confused about what the contract actually meant.
Tech companies often hide very simple ideas behind confusing jargon that outsiders cannot decode.
cloze: The report was full of medical {{jargon}}, so the patients could barely follow it.
mnemonic: JARring gobbledygook for outsiders.

definition: affected by bitterness, envy, or prejudice (usually jaundiced)
examples: He viewed the proposal with a jaundiced eye, expecting another empty promise.
Years of betrayal gave her a jaundiced view of politicians.
cloze: The critic's {{jaundice}}d opinion of modern art made him dismiss every gallery he entered.
mnemonic: Jaundice turns skin yellow and sour, like a yellow-tinted worldview.

definition: bitter, cynical, or prejudiced, especially from disappointing experience
examples: After years of broken promises, he viewed every new political pledge with a jaundiced eye.
Her jaundiced opinion of critics came from reading too many unfair reviews of her work.
cloze: The veteran reporter's {{jaundiced}} view of politicians made him doubt even their most sincere speeches.
mnemonic: Jaundice turns skin yellow; a 'yellow' outlook sees everything sourly.

definition: naive and simplistic; also dull and uninteresting
examples: The essay's jejune analysis ignored every complication that serious scholars had raised.
Audiences found the sequel jejune, a thin retread of the original's clever ideas.
cloze: Her {{jejune}} argument, lacking depth and evidence, failed to impress the experienced panel of judges.
mnemonic: Sounds like 'juvenile' — childish and shallow.

definition: to throw overboard or discard something unneeded or burdensome
examples: The crew had to jettison cargo to keep the sinking boat afloat.
After the merger, the company decided to jettison several unprofitable product lines.
cloze: To lighten the overloaded balloon, the pilot chose to {{jettison}} the sandbags and rise above the storm.
mnemonic: JET-tison: a jet dumps fuel to lighten its load.

definition: extreme, aggressive patriotism, especially favoring warlike foreign policy
examples: The newspaper's jingoism pushed readers to demand war over a minor border dispute.
Critics condemned the senator's jingoism as reckless flag-waving that ignored the cost of conflict.
cloze: The rally's {{jingoism}} alarmed diplomats, who feared the crowd's belligerent nationalism would provoke a war.
mnemonic: JINGO sounds like 'by jingo!' — a loud patriot itching for a fight.

definition: an extreme nationalist who favors aggressive foreign policy
examples: The jingoist demanded war against the neighboring country.
Newspapers owned by jingoists whipped up war fever.
cloze: The retired colonel, a loud {{jingoist}}, called for invading at the slightest provocation.
mnemonic: JINGO - 'by jingo!' - chest-thumping patriot.

definition: fond of joking; humorous and playful
examples: The jocular host kept the whole dinner table laughing with his silly stories.
Despite the tense meeting, her jocular tone made everyone relax and smile.
cloze: Normally serious, the professor was in a {{jocular}} mood and teased students with puns throughout the lecture.
mnemonic: JOKEr — a jocular person jokes.

definition: cheerful and friendly
examples: The jovial innkeeper greeted every guest with a laugh and a free drink.
Her jovial mood lifted the spirits of everyone gathered in the cold waiting room.
cloze: The old man's {{jovial}} manner made children flock to his porch each evening.
mnemonic: JOVIAL comes from Jove (Jupiter), the happy king of gods.

definition: expressing great joy and triumph
examples: Jubilant fans poured into the streets after their team won the championship.
She was jubilant when the letter confirmed her admission to the university.
cloze: The {{jubilant}} crowd cheered and sang for hours as the war's end was announced.
mnemonic: JUBILANT: a JUBILEE party - everyone is overjoyed.

definition: showing good judgment and sound sense
examples: Her judicious use of limited funds kept the small charity running through the recession.
A judicious editor trims only what weakens the story and leaves the rest alone.
cloze: The manager made a {{judicious}} decision, weighing every risk carefully before approving the expensive purchase.
mnemonic: JUDGE-icious: a good judge shows good judgment.

definition: an overwhelming, unstoppable force
examples: The advertising juggernaut crushed its small competitors within a year.
The political juggernaut rolled through every primary, defeating all rivals.
cloze: No opponent could stop the {{juggernaut}} of the rising tech giant.
mnemonic: From a huge Hindu temple cart (Jagannath) that crushed everything.

definition: a small group that rules a country after seizing power
examples: The military junta suspended the constitution and banned all political parties.
After the coup, a junta of generals governed the country for nearly a decade.
cloze: Citizens feared the {{junta}}, which jailed critics and censored the newspapers.
mnemonic: JUNTA sounds like 'hunter': a few hunters who seized the state.

definition: to show or prove that something is reasonable
examples: Scientists must justify their conclusions with reliable evidence.
The high cost of the telescope was justified by the discoveries it made.
cloze: The author tried to {{justify}} her decision to omit the final chapter.
mnemonic: JUST (fair) + IFY: make it fair.

definition: to place side by side to compare or contrast
examples: The museum chose to juxtapose ancient pottery with modern ceramics to show how styles evolved.
The film juxtaposes scenes of lavish parties with images of poverty outside the gates.
cloze: The artist likes to {{juxtapose}} bright, cheerful colors with grim subject matter for a jarring effect.
mnemonic: JUXTA means 'next to' — put things next to each other.

definition: to behave in an excessively submissive or servile way
examples: Employees were expected to kowtow to the new manager, praising every idea he had.
She refused to kowtow to the powerful donors, even if it cost her the job.
cloze: The weak ruler would {{kowtow}} to any foreign power that threatened him.
mnemonic: Chinese 'kou tou': to touch your head to the ground.

definition: praise and honor received for an achievement
examples: The entire team received kudos from the director for finishing the project ahead of schedule.
She earned kudos from critics for her bold and thoughtful first novel.
cloze: The chef received {{kudos}} from diners and reviewers alike for the restaurant's inventive new menu.
mnemonic: KUDOS sounds like 'good-os' — good things said about you.

definition: requiring much effort and time; tedious
examples: Translating the ancient text was a laborious task that took the scholar five years.
The laborious climb up the steep hill left everyone exhausted.
cloze: Copying every record by hand was a {{laborious}} process that consumed the clerks' entire week.
mnemonic: LABORious: full of LABOR.

definition: complicated and confusing like a maze
examples: Tourists quickly got lost in the narrow, labyrinthine alleys of the ancient walled city.
The labyrinthine tax code baffled even experienced accountants who had studied it for years.
cloze: Applicants struggled through the {{labyrinthine}} bureaucracy, passing from office to office without any answers.
mnemonic: Labyrinth: the Minotaur's maze in Crete.

definition: to tear or cut roughly; to wound deeply, physically or emotionally
examples: Thorns lacerated his arms as he pushed through the bramble.
The critic's cruel review lacerated the young author's confidence.
cloze: Broken glass can {{lacerate}} bare feet, so the children were warned to wear shoes on the beach.
mnemonic: LACERATE sounds like LACE-rate: tearing the skin to ribbons like lace.

definition: tearful; given to weeping or causing tears
examples: The lachrymose widow wept openly through the entire funeral.
The lachrymose melodrama left half the audience reaching for tissues.
cloze: His {{lachrymose}} farewell speech brought tears to the eyes of nearly everyone in the room.
mnemonic: LACHRYMose sounds like 'lack-ry-MOSE': lacking dry eyes; Latin lacrima, tear.

definition: using very few words; terse
examples: The laconic cowboy answered every question with a single word or a shrug.
Her laconic reply, just 'No', ended the debate faster than any speech could.
cloze: Known for his {{laconic}} style, the general replied to the long accusation with a single curt sentence.
mnemonic: Laconia (Sparta): Spartans were famous for brief, blunt speech.

definition: to criticize harshly and severely
examples: Reviewers lambasted the film as a tedious, poorly acted mess.
The coach lambasted his players for their lazy performance in the first half.
cloze: The editorial board will {{lambast}} the mayor for ignoring the city's crumbling infrastructure.
mnemonic: LAMB-BLAST: a lamb getting blasted with criticism.

definition: to criticize harshly
examples: Reviewers lambasted the new film as a bloated, incoherent mess that wasted both money and talent.
The coach lambasted his players in the locker room after the humiliating defeat.
cloze: Newspapers continued to {{lambaste}} the mayor for ignoring the flooding crisis in poorer districts.
mnemonic: LAMB-BASTE: imagine basting (beating) a poor lamb with words.

definition: to mock or ridicule publicly, usually through satire
examples: The comedy show lampooned the president's awkward speeches in sketches that aired week after week.
Cartoonists have long lampooned politicians by exaggerating their features and mocking their habits in print.
cloze: The magazine would {{lampoon}} anyone in power with sharp satirical sketches and cartoons.
mnemonic: LAMPoon: shine a LAMP on foolishness and tease it.

definition: lacking energy; slow and relaxed, often pleasantly
examples: On the hot afternoon, the languid cat stretched out and refused to move.
She gave a languid wave from the hammock, too relaxed to say hello.
cloze: The {{languid}} pace of the island, where nobody hurried, soothed the stressed tourists.
mnemonic: LANGUish — to languish is to droop without energy.

definition: to lose vitality; to remain neglected or suffering
examples: Many bills languish in committee for years without ever coming to a vote.
The prisoner languished in his cell, growing weaker with each passing month.
cloze: Without funding, the promising research project will {{languish}} in obscurity.
mnemonic: LANGUISH: limp, 'languid' like a wilting flower.

definition: generous giving of money or gifts; the gifts themselves
examples: The university depended on the largess of wealthy alumni to fund its new library.
The king distributed largess to the poor on his coronation day.
cloze: Thanks to the donor's {{largess}}, the struggling school finally received new computers and books.
mnemonic: LARGE-ss: a large gift.

definition: showing lustful, indecent desire
examples: The film was criticized for its lascivious scenes.
He cast a lascivious glance at the passing woman.
cloze: The king's court was notorious for {{lascivious}} parties and scandal.
mnemonic: LASCIVious sounds like 'lass-civilized-not'.

definition: a state of physical or mental weariness; lack of energy
examples: A deep lassitude settled over the town during the long, humid summer afternoons.
After the marathon, he felt a heavy lassitude and could barely climb the stairs.
cloze: The sudden {{lassitude}} that overcame the patient was a warning sign that the illness was returning.
mnemonic: LASS-itude: LASt of your energy is gone.

definition: present but hidden or not yet active
examples: The virus can remain latent in the body for years before symptoms appear.
Her latent talent for music emerged only when she picked up a guitar at thirty.
cloze: Teachers sought to uncover the {{latent}} abilities of students who had never been given a chance to shine.
mnemonic: LATENT sounds like 'late' — shows up late, hiding till then.

definition: to praise highly
examples: Critics lauded the young pianist for her flawless and emotional performance.
The mayor lauded the volunteers whose tireless work saved the town's library.
cloze: The committee chose to {{laud}} the scientist publicly for her groundbreaking discovery.
mnemonic: LAUD sounds like 'loud' — praise out LOUD.

definition: deserving praise, even if not fully successful
examples: Her laudable effort to feed the homeless earned the town's respect.
The team's goal was laudable, even though the project ultimately fell short.
cloze: Cutting waste to protect the environment is a {{laudable}} aim that most people would applaud.
mnemonic: LAUD + ABLE: able to be praised.

definition: extravagant, given or spent in great quantity
examples: The billionaire threw a lavish party with fireworks, live orchestras, and gourmet food.
They showered the new baby with lavish gifts far beyond what was needed.
cloze: Despite the firm's losses, the executives continued their {{lavish}} lifestyle of private jets and luxury hotels.
mnemonic: LAVish — LAVa flowing freely, a flood of excess.

definition: not strict, careful, or severe
examples: Lax airport security allowed a dangerous item to slip unnoticed through the checkpoint last month.
Her lax approach to deadlines frustrated the entire team and delayed the whole project.
cloze: Because the landlord was {{lax}} about enforcing the rules, tenants regularly ignored them.
mnemonic: LAX sounds like 'relax' — too relaxed about rules.

definition: wary and suspicious, especially because of past experience
examples: After being cheated once, she was leery of strangers offering bargains.
Investors remained leery of the company after the accounting scandal.
cloze: The cat was {{leery}} of the new dog and kept a careful distance.
mnemonic: LEERY: leering eyes watching you suspiciously.

definition: allowed by law or reasonable and valid
examples: The rebels did not recognize the legitimate government of the province.
Historians raised legitimate questions about the reliability of the chronicle.
cloze: Only a {{legitimate}} claim to the land would be accepted by the court.
mnemonic: LEGIT: LEGal and fair.

definition: sluggish, lacking energy or enthusiasm
examples: The heat left the whole class feeling lethargic and unable to concentrate.
After the huge meal, he felt lethargic and wanted only to nap on the couch.
cloze: The patient was pale and {{lethargic}}, barely able to raise his head from the pillow.
mnemonic: LETHE, river of forgetfulness: so sleepy you forget to move.

definition: humor or lack of seriousness, especially at an inappropriate time
examples: A moment of levity relieved the tension in the long, grim negotiation.
The judge scolded the lawyer for treating the serious charges with levity.
cloze: His joke brought a brief note of {{levity}} to an otherwise solemn funeral service.
mnemonic: LEVIty = LIGHT (like 'elevate'); opposite of GRAVITY.

definition: morally unrestrained, especially in sexual matters
examples: The novel scandalized readers with its portrayal of a licentious aristocracy.
Puritan leaders condemned the theater as a school of licentious behavior.
cloze: The poet's {{licentious}} lifestyle, filled with wild parties and affairs, shocked polite society.
mnemonic: LICENSE to do anything — a licentious person has no limits.

definition: in the same way; also
examples: Frogs breathe partly through their skin; salamanders likewise absorb oxygen this way.
The first group received a lecture; the second group was likewise given printed notes.
cloze: Some birds migrate thousands of miles each year, and many butterflies {{likewise}} travel great distances.
mnemonic: LIKE + WISE: in a like manner.

definition: perfectly clear and transparent
examples: The limpid water of the lake let us see the stones far below.
Her limpid prose made even complex ideas easy to follow.
cloze: The author's {{limpid}} style makes the book accessible to ordinary readers.
mnemonic: LIMPID rhymes with 'limp-id': water so clear it lies flat and still.

definition: to treat as a celebrity; to give great attention and praise to
examples: The press lionized the astronauts and invited them to every important event.
After the victory, the city lionized its young captain as a national hero.
cloze: Society tends to {{lionize}} athletes while giving little recognition to teachers and nurses.
mnemonic: Treat someone like a LION — king of beasts.

definition: lacking energy or interest
examples: The listless students stared out the window, uninterested in the lesson.
After weeks of illness, she felt listless and showed no appetite or enthusiasm.
cloze: The team gave a {{listless}} performance, moving slowly and showing no sign of ambition.
mnemonic: Without a LIST of goals, you're LISTLESS.

definition: a long, tedious list or series; a repetitive recital
examples: He recited a litany of complaints, from cold coffee to slow elevators.
The report offered a litany of failures, each worse than the last.
cloze: She listened as the tenant unleashed a {{litany}} of grievances about the building.
mnemonic: LITANY is a church prayer recited in a long list.

definition: reluctant, unwilling
examples: She was loath to leave her hometown, where all her friends lived.
Experts are loath to predict the outcome while evidence remains so limited.
cloze: The senator was {{loath}} to criticize his party's leader, fearing the consequences.
mnemonic: LOATHe means hate; loath (no e) = hating to do something.

definition: to find the position of something
examples: Archaeologists used radar to locate the buried foundations of the temple.
The company decided to locate its new factory near the river.
cloze: Sonar helps scientists {{locate}} shipwrecks on the ocean floor.
mnemonic: LOCATE = LOCATION: find the place.

definition: very talkative
examples: The loquacious taxi driver chatted about politics, weather, and football for the entire ride.
Shy at first, she became loquacious once the topic turned to her favorite novels.
cloze: Our {{loquacious}} neighbor can turn a quick hello into an hour-long conversation.
mnemonic: LOQU- means speak: a LOQUacious person LOQs (talks) a lot.

definition: clear and easy to understand; also rational and clear-minded
examples: The teacher's lucid explanation made the difficult theorem suddenly easy to follow.
Though very ill, the old man remained lucid and recalled every detail of the event.
cloze: The author's prose is so {{lucid}} that even complex economic ideas become simple to grasp.
mnemonic: LUCId contains LUX/light: light makes things clear.

definition: producing a great deal of profit
examples: He left teaching for a lucrative career in investment banking.
The company signed a lucrative contract that doubled its annual revenue.
cloze: Selling rare coins turned out to be a surprisingly {{lucrative}} hobby that earned him a fortune.
mnemonic: LUCRe sounds like LUCRative: filthy lucre means money.

definition: looking or sounding sad and dismal, often exaggeratedly
examples: The lugubrious violin music made the already gloomy funeral feel even heavier.
He wore a lugubrious expression all week, as though the whole world had let him down.
cloze: The dog's {{lugubrious}} howl echoed through the empty house, a mournful sound that chilled everyone.
mnemonic: LUGUBrious: a LUG-ging, BRIO-less (lifeless) mood.

definition: to soothe or calm, often into a false sense of security
examples: Soft music and the gentle rocking of the cradle lulled the baby to sleep within minutes.
Years of peace lulled the city into believing that an attack could never happen.
cloze: The con artist's friendly manner was meant to {{lull}} victims into trusting him with their savings.
mnemonic: A LULLaby lulls you to sleep.

definition: giving off light; bright; also brilliantly clear
examples: The luminous moon lit the path through the dark forest.
Critics praised the luminous prose of the memoir, so clear it seemed to glow.
cloze: The deep-sea fish had a {{luminous}} lure that glowed in the lightless water to attract prey.
mnemonic: LUMINary, ILLUMINate: all about light.

definition: shocking, sensational; or glaringly vivid in color
examples: Tabloids filled their front pages with lurid details of the scandal.
The sunset turned the sky a lurid orange that seemed almost unnatural.
cloze: The author was criticized for the {{lurid}} descriptions of violence that seemed designed only to shock readers.
mnemonic: LURID — 'lure' of horrid details that lure readers.

definition: grim and disturbing, because of an association with death
examples: The film's macabre opening scene took place in a moonlit graveyard.
He had a macabre fascination with skeletons and old burial customs.
cloze: The old house, with its coffin-shaped doors, had a {{macabre}} charm that thrilled the visitors.
mnemonic: MACABRE sounds like 'Mac, a bear' dancing in a graveyard (Danse Macabre).

definition: to plot or scheme, especially to harm someone
examples: The vizier machinated against the king, secretly hoping to seize the throne.
Rivals machinated behind the scenes to have the director removed.
cloze: Members of the court would {{machinate}} night and day, each scheming to win the king's favor.
mnemonic: MACHINATE: build a MACHINE of schemes.

definition: authoritative and commanding; also, domineering
examples: The professor delivered the lecture in a magisterial tone that discouraged questions.
Her magisterial biography of Lincoln is considered the definitive work on the subject.
cloze: With a {{magisterial}} wave of his hand, the headmaster silenced the entire hall.
mnemonic: MAGISTER = master: speaks like a master.

definition: generous and forgiving, especially toward a rival or someone less powerful
examples: The magnanimous winner praised her opponent and offered to help him train.
He was magnanimous in victory, refusing to gloat over the defeated team.
cloze: Instead of seeking revenge, the king was {{magnanimous}} and pardoned the rebels who had surrendered.
mnemonic: MAGNA (great) + ANIMUS (soul): a great soul.

definition: a wealthy and influential person, especially in business
examples: The shipping magnate owned dozens of tankers and a famous football club.
As a media magnate, he controlled newspapers, radio stations, and television channels across the country.
cloze: The steel {{magnate}} used his vast fortune to shape the nation's politics for decades.
mnemonic: MAGNate: has MAGNitude of wealth.

definition: to keep something in good condition or continue it
examples: Volunteers maintain the trails so hikers can cross the mountains safely.
Mammals maintain a constant body temperature regardless of the weather outside.
cloze: The museum must {{maintain}} a stable temperature to protect its fragile manuscripts.
mnemonic: MAIN-TAIN: hold with the MAIN hand.

definition: clumsy or awkward; lacking skill or tact
examples: The maladroit waiter dropped a tray of glasses in front of the guests.
His maladroit handling of the delicate negotiation left both sides offended.
cloze: Her {{maladroit}} remark about the host's cooking embarrassed everyone at the table.
mnemonic: MAL (bad) + ADROIT (skilled): badly skilled.

definition: a disease or ailment; a deep-seated problem
examples: A mysterious malady kept her in bed for months.
Corruption is the chronic malady of the whole administration.
cloze: Doctors could not identify the strange {{malady}} afflicting the village cattle.
mnemonic: MAL = bad; MALady is a bad condition.

definition: the comic misuse of a word by confusing it with a similar-sounding one
examples: Saying 'a nice arrangement of epitaphs' instead of 'epithets' is a classic malapropism.
The character's malapropisms, like 'pineapple of politeness,' made the audience laugh.
cloze: His speech was full of {{malapropism}}s, including calling a fireman a 'fire extinguisher.'
mnemonic: Mrs. MALAPROP, a character who garbled words (mal a propos = badly placed).

definition: having or showing a wish to do evil
examples: The villain gave the hero a malevolent smile before locking the door.
She felt a malevolent presence watching her from the dark corner.
cloze: The {{malevolent}} rumor was spread by a rival who wanted nothing but to ruin the senator's reputation.
mnemonic: MAL (bad) + VOLENT (wishing): wishing bad.

definition: wrongdoing, especially by a public official
examples: The mayor was charged with malfeasance after taking bribes.
An audit exposed malfeasance in the pension fund.
cloze: The board accused the treasurer of {{malfeasance}} for hiding the losses.
mnemonic: MAL (bad) + FEASANCE (doing): bad deeds.

definition: to speak harmful untruths about; slander
examples: Rivals tried to malign her reputation by spreading false rumors about her past work.
He felt unjustly maligned by newspapers that portrayed him as a crook.
cloze: Politicians frequently {{malign}} their opponents with accusations that have no basis in fact.
mnemonic: MAL (bad) + sign — speaking bad.

definition: a person who pretends to be ill to avoid work
examples: The doctor suspected the soldier was a malingerer faking a sore back.
No manager enjoys dealing with a malingerer who calls in sick every Monday.
cloze: The supervisor, convinced he was a {{malingerer}}, demanded a note from the doctor.
mnemonic: MAL (bad) + linger: lingering sick on purpose.

definition: easily shaped or influenced
examples: Gold is highly malleable and can be hammered into extremely thin sheets.
Young children's malleable minds absorb languages far more easily than adults'.
cloze: The politician's opinions proved {{malleable}}, changing whichever way the powerful donors pushed them.
mnemonic: MALLET: you can hammer it into shape.

definition: having a bad smell
examples: A malodorous cloud rose from the garbage dump in the heat of summer.
He opened the window to let out the malodorous fumes from the chemistry lab.
cloze: The {{malodorous}} swamp made hikers hurry along the trail with their noses covered.
mnemonic: MAL (bad) + odor.

definition: the edge or border; an amount of difference
examples: The candidate won by a narrow margin of only two votes.
Monks wrote notes in the margins of the ancient manuscript.
cloze: Small businesses often have a very low profit {{margin}} in their first few years.
mnemonic: MARGIN: the MARGIN of a page is the edge.

definition: relating to war or the military
examples: The festival included a display of martial arts and a parade of soldiers.
The country was placed under martial law after the riots shut down the city.
cloze: The general's {{martial}} bearing, with straight back and sharp gaze, impressed every recruit.
mnemonic: MARTial comes from MARS, the Roman god of war.

definition: a strict disciplinarian who insists on exact obedience
examples: The new sergeant was a martinet who punished even a single wrinkle in a uniform.
Students feared the martinet principal, who enforced every petty rule without exception.
cloze: The captain, a {{martinet}}, inspected the barracks daily and punished any dust he found.
mnemonic: Named after General MARTINET, who drilled French soldiers harshly.

definition: fully grown or developed
examples: Mature trees in the old forest can reach heights of seventy meters.
The economy of the region became mature once heavy industry was established.
cloze: Salmon return to the river where they hatched once they become {{mature}}.
mnemonic: MATURE: MATure by the time you are grown.

definition: tearfully and foolishly sentimental
examples: After three drinks he became maudlin, weeping over old memories of his schooldays.
Critics dismissed the film as a maudlin melodrama designed to force tears.
cloze: The speaker's {{maudlin}} tribute, full of exaggerated sobbing, embarrassed the guests more than it moved them.
mnemonic: Mary MAGDALENE is often painted weeping — 'maudlin' evolved from her name.

definition: to talk or move in a rambling, aimless way
examples: The old man maundered on about his youth while the guests grew restless.
She maundered through the garden, lost in thought, without any destination.
cloze: The speaker began to {{maunder}}, and soon even his most loyal listeners were glancing at the clock.
mnemonic: MAUNDER: sounds like WANDER - a wandering talk.

definition: an independent person who refuses to follow the group or conform
examples: The maverick scientist ignored the consensus and pursued her own unpopular theory.
A political maverick, he often voted against his own party.
cloze: As a {{maverick}} in the fashion world, she rejected trends and designed clothes in her own odd style.
mnemonic: Named for Samuel Maverick, whose cattle roamed unbranded.

definition: sentimental in a feeble or sickly way
examples: The mawkish love song was so sugary and sentimental that it made even romantic listeners cringe.
Critics dismissed the novel's ending as mawkish and manipulative, a shameless attempt to draw tears.
cloze: The greeting card's {{mawkish}} verse was so syrupy that it made her laugh instead of cry.
mnemonic: MAWKish: a MAWful sticky-sweet taste.

definition: a short saying expressing a general truth or rule of conduct
examples: "Honesty is the best policy" was the maxim by which she lived.
The teacher wrote a maxim on the board each morning for the class to discuss.
cloze: Her favorite {{maxim}} was "Measure twice, cut once," and she applied it to everything.
mnemonic: MAXIM: a MAXIMum amount of wisdom in the MINImum words.

definition: to wander aimlessly; or to follow a winding course
examples: The river meanders through the valley before reaching the sea.
On Sundays they would meander through the market without any plan.
cloze: The speaker tended to {{meander}} from topic to topic, never really reaching his main point.
mnemonic: Maeander River in Turkey famously winds back and forth.

definition: a system of parts or a process that produces an effect
examples: The study describes the mechanism by which plants absorb water.
Scientists discovered a defense mechanism that allows the frog to survive freezing.
cloze: The clock's {{mechanism}} consists of hundreds of tiny gears working together.
mnemonic: MECHANISM: MECHANical works.

definition: deep, lingering sadness without obvious cause
examples: A deep melancholy settled over him as autumn turned the leaves brown.
The violin's mournful tune filled the room with melancholy.
cloze: A sense of {{melancholy}} hung over the empty house after the family moved away.
mnemonic: MELAN = black, CHOLY = bile: 'black bile' of medieval gloom.

definition: a confused, chaotic fight or struggle among many people
examples: A melee broke out in the stands after the final whistle.
The photographer was knocked to the ground in the melee outside the courthouse.
cloze: Police rushed into the {{melee}} to pull the angry supporters apart.
mnemonic: MELEE sounds like 'May-lay': May lay about with fists in a brawl.

definition: sweet and smooth sounding, pleasant to hear
examples: The announcer's mellifluous voice made even the weather report soothing.
Birds filled the garden with mellifluous song at dawn.
cloze: Her {{mellifluous}} singing voice flowed over the audience like warm honey.
mnemonic: MELLI (honey) + FLU (flow): honey flowing from the throat.

definition: lying; dishonest
examples: The mendacious witness was exposed when his story contradicted the video evidence.
Voters grew tired of the mendacious claims in the candidate's advertisements.
cloze: The {{mendacious}} salesman made false promises about the car's history to close the deal.
mnemonic: MEN-DACIOUS: 'men deceive us.'

definition: untruthfulness; the habit of lying
examples: The senator's mendacity became clear when reporters compared his statements with the records.
Nothing destroys trust faster than a leader's mendacity.
cloze: Voters grew weary of the candidate's {{mendacity}} and demanded honest answers.
mnemonic: MENDACITY: 'men' who deceive; Latin mendax = liar.

definition: a beggar, especially a member of a religious order living on alms
examples: The mendicant sat outside the temple gate, holding out a worn wooden bowl.
Wandering mendicants relied entirely on the generosity of villagers for food.
cloze: A {{mendicant}} in tattered robes asked the travelers for bread and a place to sleep.
mnemonic: MENDICANT: 'mend' my hunger, please.

definition: motivated chiefly by money
examples: Critics accused the agent of mercenary motives rather than genuine concern for his clients.
The mercenary soldier fought for whichever army paid the most.
cloze: Her {{mercenary}} attitude was obvious: she would only help if the pay was high enough.
mnemonic: MERCenary — MERCantile: all about money.

definition: subject to sudden, unpredictable changes of mood
examples: Her mercurial temper meant staff never knew whether she would praise or scold them.
The mercurial star was adored one week and booed the next.
cloze: The {{mercurial}} dictator would be charming at breakfast and furiously cruel by lunch.
mnemonic: Mercury (quicksilver) moves fast and changes shape.

definition: to hold someone spellbound; to hypnotize
examples: The magician mesmerized the children with his tricks.
The dancer's graceful movements mesmerized the audience.
cloze: The flickering flames seemed to {{mesmerize}} the camper, who stared for hours.
mnemonic: Named for Franz MESMER, the hypnotist.

definition: extremely rapid, like a meteor
examples: The singer's meteoric rise brought her fame within months.
His meteoric career ended as quickly as it began.
cloze: The start-up's {{meteoric}} growth made its founder a millionaire in a year.
mnemonic: METEOR streaks across the sky: fast and bright.

definition: showing great attention to detail; very careful
examples: The meticulous accountant checked every figure twice before signing the report.
Her meticulous notes allowed the team to reconstruct the experiment exactly.
cloze: A {{meticulous}} restorer spent months repairing the painting, correcting every tiny crack with patience.
mnemonic: METICulous: a METIC-ulous person measures every detail like a meter.

definition: courageous and spirited
examples: The mettlesome young colt refused to be broken by any rider.
A mettlesome reporter, she pursued the story despite the threats.
cloze: The {{mettlesome}} young sailors faced the storm with spirit and daring.
mnemonic: METTLE = courage: a mettlesome person has mettle.

definition: to move from one region or habitat to another
examples: Monarch butterflies migrate thousands of kilometers to warmer forests each autumn.
Many rural workers migrated to cities during the industrial revolution.
cloze: Several species of whales {{migrate}} to tropical waters to breed during winter.
mnemonic: MIGRATE: MIGhty trip, GRATE-ful to arrive.

definition: a person who hates or distrusts other people
examples: The misanthrope lived alone on a mountain, avoiding all human contact.
Molière's famous play portrays a misanthrope disgusted by the hypocrisy of society.
cloze: A confirmed {{misanthrope}}, he declined every invitation and complained about the stupidity of humanity.
mnemonic: MIS (hate) + ANTHROPOS (man); opposite of PHILANTHROPE.

definition: to credit something to the wrong person or source
examples: Many people misattribute that famous quotation to Einstein, though he never said it.
The museum had misattributed the painting to a famous master for over a century.
cloze: It is easy to {{misattribute}} old proverbs to authors who never wrote them.
mnemonic: MIS + ATTRIBUTE: giving credit to the wrong person.

definition: to interpret wrongly
examples: She misconstrued his silence as anger when he was merely tired.
Do not misconstrue my criticism as a personal attack.
cloze: Readers may {{misconstrue}} the satire and take it for a sincere endorsement.
mnemonic: MIS + CONSTRUE: construe (interpret) wrongly.

definition: a person who behaves badly or breaks the law
examples: The police finally caught the miscreant who had been vandalizing the park.
Teachers sent the young miscreant to the principal for tormenting younger students.
cloze: The village rejoiced when the notorious {{miscreant}} was finally put behind bars.
mnemonic: MIS + creed: one with a wrong creed.

definition: a person who hoards money and spends as little as possible
examples: The miser counted his coins nightly and refused to buy himself a warm coat.
Known as a miser, he never tipped and reused his tea bags for a week.
cloze: The village {{miser}} lived in a freezing house rather than pay for firewood.
mnemonic: MISERable life: the miser makes himself miserable to save money.

definition: a wrong or inaccurate name or term
examples: Calling the small hill a mountain is a misnomer, since it is barely two hundred feet high.
'Peanut' is a misnomer because the peanut is actually a legume rather than a nut.
cloze: It is a {{misnomer}} to call the whale a fish, because whales are mammals.
mnemonic: MIS (wrong) + NOM (name): wrong name.

definition: a person who hates or distrusts women
examples: The senator was called a misogynist after his remarks about female voters.
Critics labelled the novel's narrator a misogynist who scorned every woman he met.
cloze: Her colleagues quietly avoided the {{misogynist}} manager, who openly mocked women's abilities.
mnemonic: MISO (hate) + GYN (woman): hater of women.

definition: to make less severe or harmful
examples: Planting trees can mitigate the effects of urban heat during summer.
The judge reduced the sentence because of mitigating circumstances in the defendant's past.
cloze: Engineers added extra drainage to {{mitigate}} the risk of flooding after heavy rains.
mnemonic: MITigate sounds like 'mitt': a mitt softens a blow.

definition: a small amount of something
examples: He showed not even a modicum of remorse for what he had done.
With a modicum of effort, you could have passed the test.
cloze: The scheme succeeded only because the victims had a {{modicum}} of trust and little time to verify it.
mnemonic: MODEst amount — a MODicum is a small measure.

definition: to change something slightly, usually to improve it
examples: Engineers modified the bridge design after the first tests revealed weaknesses.
Farmers have modified crops over centuries through selective breeding.
cloze: The author had to {{modify}} several chapters to satisfy the editor's concerns.
mnemonic: MODIFY = MODe-ify: change the mode.

definition: to soothe the anger of; to appease
examples: The airline offered free tickets to mollify the angry passengers.
Nothing she said could mollify her furious boss after the missed deadline.
cloze: The manager tried to {{mollify}} the irate customer with a refund and a sincere apology.
mnemonic: MOLLify: make MOLLusk-soft; soften anger.

definition: to pamper or overprotect
examples: Parents who mollycoddle their children may prevent them from learning independence.
The coach refused to mollycoddle the players and made them run extra laps.
cloze: Critics say that the school tends to {{mollycoddle}} students instead of preparing them for real challenges.
mnemonic: A MOLLY (girl) COD-dled like a delicate egg.

definition: importance or consequence (as in 'of great moment')
examples: The treaty was a decision of great moment for the entire region.
Nothing of moment occurred during the quiet council meeting.
cloze: It was a matter of great {{moment}}, and the entire cabinet gathered to discuss its consequences.
mnemonic: MOMENTous events carry great MOMENT.

definition: no longer relevant or of practical significance; open to debate
examples: The question became moot once the company closed its doors for good.
Whether the law should pass is moot, since the vote has already taken place.
cloze: With the contract already canceled, the dispute over its terms is now {{moot}}.
mnemonic: MOOT (as in moot court): a practice debate with no real stakes.

definition: sharply biting or caustic, especially in humor or style
examples: The columnist's mordant wit left politicians squirming in their seats.
He had a mordant sense of humor that frightened new acquaintances.
cloze: The comedian's {{mordant}} remarks about the mayor stung, but the audience laughed all the same.
mnemonic: MORDANT: Latin 'to bite' - a MORDant joke bites like mordida.

definition: on the point of death; stagnant and lacking vitality
examples: The moribund industry employed only a fraction of the workers it once had.
Doctors feared the moribund patient would not last the night.
cloze: Once the pride of the town, the {{moribund}} mill now stood nearly silent and falling apart.
mnemonic: MORI = death (mortal): near death.

definition: gloomy, sullen, and withdrawn
examples: He sat morose and silent at the party, refusing to join any conversation.
The long winter left the villagers feeling morose and irritable.
cloze: After losing his job, he became {{morose}}, staying in his room and speaking to nobody.
mnemonic: MOROSE sounds like 'more sore' — more sad and grumpy.

definition: to change gradually into something different
examples: The small startup morphed into a global corporation.
In the film, the character's face morphs into a wolf.
cloze: Through years of compromise, the movement began to {{morph}} into the very thing it opposed.
mnemonic: MORPH from metaMORPHosis: change of shape.

definition: to defraud or swindle; to extract money by fine or trickery
examples: The con artist mulcted elderly residents of their life savings.
The city mulcted drivers with excessive fines for minor parking violations.
cloze: The corrupt official tried to {{mulct}} the farmers by demanding unnecessary fees.
mnemonic: MULCT sounds like 'milk it': drain people of their money.

definition: having many varied parts or kinds
examples: The city's multifarious culture includes cuisines and customs from every continent.
A manager must handle the multifarious demands of staff, clients, and budgets.
cloze: The curator's {{multifarious}} collection ranged from ancient coins to modern robots.
mnemonic: MULTI (many) + 'variety' — many varieties.

definition: ordinary, dull, everyday
examples: After the excitement of travel, she returned to the mundane routine of office life.
He wrote about mundane events, like making breakfast, with surprising beauty.
cloze: Despite her glamorous image, her daily life was filled with {{mundane}} chores such as laundry and shopping.
mnemonic: MUNDANE comes from 'mundus' (world): worldly, everyday.

definition: extremely generous, especially with money or gifts
examples: The munificent donor gave millions to build the new hospital wing.
Guests were overwhelmed by the munificent hospitality of their hosts.
cloze: Thanks to the {{munificent}} gift of a local philanthropist, the library was able to double its collection.
mnemonic: MUNI (gifts) + FICENT (make): one who makes gifts.

definition: liable to change
examples: Public opinion is mutable and can shift dramatically within a single week.
Early scientists believed the species were fixed, but later evidence showed they are mutable.
cloze: Fashion is a {{mutable}} thing, constantly shifting from one season to the next.
mnemonic: MUTate: able to mutate.

definition: softened or toned down in sound, color or intensity
examples: The room was decorated in muted greens and grays that felt calming.
Their muted response to the news suggested they were disappointed.
cloze: The crowd gave a {{muted}} cheer, subdued by the long and tiring day.
mnemonic: Press the MUTE button: quieter.

definition: lacking foresight; shortsighted
examples: The myopic policy solved this year's budget problem but created an even bigger one later.
Critics called the executive myopic for ignoring the long-term consequences of his cost cutting.
cloze: A {{myopic}} focus on quarterly profits ruined the company's chance of future growth.
mnemonic: Myopia = nearsightedness; the mind also sees only what is near.

definition: countless; extremely numerous
examples: The night sky displayed myriad stars far from any city lights.
Immigrants face myriad challenges, from language barriers to unfamiliar customs.
cloze: The ocean hosts a {{myriad}} of creatures, from tiny plankton to enormous whales.
mnemonic: MYRIAD = ten thousand in Greek; too many to count.

definition: the lowest or worst point of something
examples: The company hit its nadir when profits collapsed and half the staff were laid off.
For the team, the humiliating defeat was the nadir of the season.
cloze: His career reached its {{nadir}} when he lost his job, his home, and his savings in a single year.
mnemonic: NADIR sounds like 'down'; opposite of ZENITH.

definition: just coming into existence; beginning to develop
examples: The nascent democracy faced many challenges in building its institutions.
Investors were wary of the nascent technology, which was still unproven.
cloze: The {{nascent}} movement began as a small group of students but soon grew across the country.
mnemonic: NASCENT ~ NATAL: just born.

definition: vague, unclear, lacking definite form
examples: The manager gave only a nebulous plan, leaving the staff confused about what to do.
His nebulous ideas about the future never turned into a real strategy.
cloze: The contract's {{nebulous}} wording left both sides unsure of what was actually required.
mnemonic: A NEBULA is a hazy cloud.

definition: wicked or criminal
examples: Detectives uncovered the villain's nefarious plot to steal the city's gold reserves.
The company's nefarious practices included bribing officials and hiding toxic waste.
cloze: The {{nefarious}} scheme to defraud pensioners was uncovered by an investigative journalist.
mnemonic: NE (not) + FAS (right): not right.

definition: so small or unimportant that it can be ignored
examples: The difference in cost between the two models was negligible.
The risk of side effects is negligible, according to the trial's results.
cloze: A {{negligible}} amount of rainfall fell during the whole summer, barely wetting the dust.
mnemonic: You can NEGLect it: too small to care about.

definition: a beginner; a person new to a subject or activity
examples: The neophyte skier fell repeatedly on her first day on the slopes.
As a neophyte in politics, he had much to learn about compromise.
cloze: Experts patiently guide each {{neophyte}} who joins the club and has never held a camera before.
mnemonic: NEO (new) + PHYTE (plant): a new plant.

definition: irritating, troublesome, vexing
examples: The nettlesome problem delayed the project for weeks.
He dealt with the nettlesome details of the contract himself.
cloze: The senator avoided the {{nettlesome}} question about her donors.
mnemonic: NETTLE stings you; a nettlesome issue stings too.

definition: not supporting either side; having no strong features
examples: Switzerland stayed neutral during both world wars.
Scientists should remain neutral when presenting data to the public.
cloze: The mediator took a {{neutral}} position and did not favor either party in the dispute.
mnemonic: NEUTRAL: NEITHER side.

definition: extremely unpleasant, especially smelly or harmful
examples: A noisome stench drifted up from the unwashed hold of the old ship.
The marsh gave off noisome vapors that made travelers sick.
cloze: Residents complained of the {{noisome}} fumes from the factory chimneys.
mnemonic: Noisome is not noisy: it's NOXious and nasty.

definition: calm and casually unconcerned
examples: He remained nonchalant while everyone else panicked about the approaching storm.
She gave a nonchalant shrug, as though winning the prize meant nothing.
cloze: Despite the high stakes, the pilot was {{nonchalant}} about the turbulence and kept sipping his coffee.
