mnemonic: NON + CHALANT (be warm): not warmed up about it.

definition: an unimportant person or thing
examples: Before the election, he was a political nonentity whom few voters could even name.
Ignored by the bosses, she felt like a nonentity in the large corporation.
cloze: The new clerk was treated as a {{nonentity}}, ignored by managers and rarely invited to meetings.
mnemonic: NON + ENTITY: not a being of importance.

definition: so surprised and confused that one is unsure how to react
examples: The sudden question left the speaker nonplussed, unable to say a word.
She was nonplussed by the stranger's odd gift and simply stared.
cloze: The candidate was {{nonplussed}} by the unexpected accusation and stood speechless at the podium.
mnemonic: NON + PLUS: no more (moves) to make.

definition: a standard or pattern regarded as typical
examples: Arranged marriage was the norm in many traditional societies.
Students who break academic norms can face serious penalties.
cloze: Rapid technological change has become the {{norm}} in modern industry.
mnemonic: NORM = NORMal.

definition: a questionable remedy or pet solution claimed to cure problems
examples: Politicians offered simple nostrums for the complex economic crisis, none of which actually worked.
He sold a bottle of colored water as a miracle nostrum for baldness.
cloze: The doctor refused to prescribe the so-called {{nostrum}}, a useless tonic marketed as a cure-all.
mnemonic: NOSTRUM = 'our' in Latin: 'our own secret' remedy.

definition: worthy of attention because of importance
examples: Darwin made notable observations during his voyage to the Galapagos Islands.
The region is notable for its ancient cave paintings.
cloze: One {{notable}} exception to the pattern is the platypus, which lays eggs.
mnemonic: NOTE-able: worth taking NOTE of.

definition: a belief, idea, or understanding of something
examples: The notion that the Earth was flat was rejected by ancient Greek scholars.
Students often hold the mistaken notion that memorizing is the same as understanding.
cloze: Early philosophers developed the {{notion}} that everything in nature is made of tiny particles.
mnemonic: NOTION: a NOTE in your mind.

definition: famous for something bad
examples: The notorious bandit had already escaped from three prisons and was wanted in several states.
The restaurant is notorious for its rude waiters, long delays, and consistently terrible service.
cloze: The street was {{notorious}} for pickpockets, so tourists were warned to avoid it at night.
mnemonic: NOTable for the wrong thing: NOTorious.

definition: a person new to a field or activity
examples: A novice at chess, she lost her first ten games.
The novice chef followed the recipe step by step, afraid to improvise.
cloze: Even a {{novice}} could use the simple software without any training.
mnemonic: NOVICE contains NOVel/NEW.

definition: harmful, poisonous, or very unpleasant
examples: Factories released noxious fumes that made it hard for nearby residents to breathe.
A noxious smell drifted from the neglected pond and made everyone nearby cover their faces.
cloze: Workers were required to wear masks to avoid breathing the {{noxious}} gases released by the chemicals.
mnemonic: NOX = harm; NOXious = NOT OK for you.

definition: a subtle difference in meaning, expression, or tone
examples: A good translator captures every nuance of the original poem.
The debate lacked nuance, reducing a complex issue to slogans.
cloze: Only a native speaker could grasp the subtle {{nuance}} that separated the two similar words.
mnemonic: NU-ance = a tiny NEW shade (nuage = cloud in French).

definition: to make legally invalid; to cancel out
examples: The court's ruling nullified the contract because one party had been misled.
One careless decision can nullify months of careful work by the entire design team.
cloze: The new evidence could {{nullify}} the verdict and force the court to hold a fresh trial.
mnemonic: NULL means zero; nullify = make zero.

definition: stubbornly refusing to change one's opinion or course
examples: The obdurate negotiator refused every compromise, no matter how reasonable.
Despite pleas from his family, the old man remained obdurate and would not sell the farm.
cloze: The {{obdurate}} dictator ignored all appeals from world leaders and refused to step down.
mnemonic: OB-DURATE: DURable like a hard rock; won't bend.

definition: deferential respect; a gesture of submission such as bowing
examples: The courtiers made deep obeisance to the queen as she entered the hall.
The tribe paid obeisance to the chief by kneeling before him.
cloze: Visitors were expected to show {{obeisance}} to the emperor by bowing low in his presence.
mnemonic: OBEY-sance: you obey and bow.

definition: to make unclear or hard to understand
examples: The company used technical jargon to obfuscate the true cost of the plan.
Lawyers often obfuscate the issue with legal language rather than clarify it.
cloze: Instead of answering honestly, the official tried to {{obfuscate}} the facts with confusing statistics.
mnemonic: OB (over) + FUSC (dark): cover with darkness.

definition: based on facts rather than personal feelings
examples: A good historian tries to give an objective account of events.
Scientists use objective measurements to avoid bias in their experiments.
cloze: The judge made an {{objective}} decision based solely on the evidence.
mnemonic: OBJECT-ive: look at the OBJECT, not your feelings.

definition: to scold or rebuke harshly
examples: The captain objurgated the crew for their carelessness during the storm.
She objurgated her assistant for losing the contract, shouting for several minutes.
cloze: The coach would {{objurgate}} any player who ignored the game plan.
mnemonic: OB-JURGATE: JARring words thrown at someone.

definition: willing to help; accommodating
examples: The obliging clerk carried our bags to the car without being asked.
An obliging neighbor fed our cat every day whenever we traveled abroad.
cloze: She was an {{obliging}} host, always ready to make room for one more guest.
mnemonic: You feel OBLIGEd to help: the obliging person gladly does.

definition: indirect or evasive; slanting
examples: He made only an oblique reference to the scandal, never naming anyone.
The oblique rays of the evening sun cast long shadows across the lawn.
cloze: Instead of answering directly, she gave an {{oblique}} hint that left the audience guessing.
mnemonic: OBLIQUE: sounds like 'a slick slant' - not straight.

definition: unaware of or not concerned about what is happening around one
examples: Wearing headphones, he was oblivious to the loud siren behind him.
She was oblivious to the stares as she hummed down the hallway.
cloze: The tourist, {{oblivious}} to the danger, wandered happily into the path of the oncoming cyclist.
mnemonic: OBLIVion — you forget everything around you.

definition: strong public condemnation; disgrace resulting from it
examples: The traitor died in obloquy, hated by the country he betrayed.
She endured years of obloquy from the press after the failed expedition.
cloze: The disgraced official lived out his days in {{obloquy}}, shunned by former friends and colleagues.
mnemonic: OB + LOQU (speak): speak against.

definition: not well known; hard to understand
examples: The little-known poet was obscure during her life, and only gained fame after her death.
The instructions were so obscure that no one could assemble the shelf.
cloze: Few people have heard of the author, a rather {{obscure}} figure in nineteenth-century literature.
mnemonic: OBSCURE: covered (ob) in dark (scur).

definition: excessively eager to please or obey; fawning
examples: The obsequious assistant laughed at every one of his boss's feeble jokes.
Waiters hovered around the celebrity in an obsequious manner, bowing and flattering.
cloze: The senator was surrounded by {{obsequious}} aides who agreed with everything he said.
mnemonic: OBSEQUIOUS ~ 'OB-SEQUel': follows behind you like a sequel.

definition: no longer used; out of date
examples: Typewriters quickly became obsolete once affordable personal computers arrived in most homes and offices.
The old software is obsolete and no longer receives updates.
cloze: Technology moves so quickly that last year's phone may already be {{obsolete}} today.
mnemonic: OBSOLETE: has 'slipped' out (soleo) of use.

definition: stubbornly refusing to change one's mind
examples: The obstinate child refused to eat anything except pasta, no matter what his parents offered.
Her obstinate refusal to listen to advice led to repeated mistakes.
cloze: The {{obstinate}} mule would not move, no matter how hard the farmer pulled the rope.
mnemonic: OBSTINATE — 'obstacle' in the path of your plans.

definition: noisy and difficult to control
examples: The obstreperous crowd shouted down every speaker at the meeting.
Teachers struggled to calm the obstreperous class after the fire drill.
cloze: The {{obstreperous}} toddler screamed and kicked, refusing to put on his coat.
mnemonic: OBSTRUCT + stripe-rowdy: a rowdy crowd obstructing order.

definition: to get or acquire something
examples: Researchers obtained soil samples from deep beneath the Antarctic ice.
Students must obtain permission from the library before borrowing rare books.
cloze: Biologists were able to {{obtain}} DNA from fossilized bones that were thousands of years old.
mnemonic: OB-TAIN: TAIN-t your hand holding it: you got it.

definition: slow to understand; insensitive or dull
examples: He was too obtuse to notice the hints that she wanted him to leave.
Her obtuse reply showed she had missed the point of the joke.
cloze: Are you being deliberately {{obtuse}}, or do you truly not see why the plan failed?
mnemonic: OBTUSE angle is blunt, not sharp; blunt mind.

definition: to remove a need or difficulty; to make unnecessary
examples: The new software obviates the need for employees to enter all the data manually.
Careful planning can obviate many problems before they arise and save the team considerable time.
cloze: A well-designed bridge would {{obviate}} the long detour that commuters now take each morning.
mnemonic: OBVIATE: get OUT of the VIA (way) — the obstacle is removed.

definition: to happen or take place
examples: Earthquakes occur most often along the edges of tectonic plates.
Mutations occur naturally in all living organisms.
cloze: Many accidents {{occur}} when drivers are tired and cannot focus on the road.
mnemonic: OCCUR: a thing that RUNS (curr) up to you.

definition: extremely unpleasant; deserving hatred
examples: The odious landlord raised rents on the poorest tenants every month.
Betraying a lifelong friend for money is an odious act that few people ever forgive.
cloze: Most people found the dictator's cruelty {{odious}} and called for the world to condemn him.
mnemonic: ODIous sounds like ODIOUS - you hate it, an ODD, ODOR.

definition: annoyingly eager to give orders or interfere
examples: The officious clerk insisted on checking every form three times, annoying the customers.
An officious neighbor kept offering unwanted advice about my garden.
cloze: Visitors found the {{officious}} guard irritating as he ordered them around over trivial rules.
mnemonic: OFFICIOUS: acts like he runs the OFFICE.

definition: to balance or cancel out the effect of something
examples: Higher exports offset the decline in domestic sales.
Planting trees can offset some of the carbon released by factories.
cloze: The company tried to {{offset}} rising costs by raising its prices slightly.
mnemonic: OFF + SET: set off against the loss.

definition: suggesting that something bad will happen
examples: Dark ominous clouds gathered above the picnic, warning of a coming storm.
The ominous silence from the enemy camp worried the soldiers.
cloze: An {{ominous}} rumble from the volcano told the villagers it was time to flee.
mnemonic: OMEN-ous: an omen of trouble.

definition: burdensome; requiring great effort
examples: The onerous task of auditing every account took the team months.
Small businesses complained about the onerous regulations that cost time and money.
cloze: Caring for three young children on her own was an {{onerous}} responsibility that left her exhausted.
mnemonic: ONERous contains ONUS: a burden.

definition: continuing to happen; still in progress
examples: Researchers have an ongoing study of the glacier's rate of melting.
The ongoing drought has damaged farms throughout the valley.
cloze: There is an {{ongoing}} debate among historians about the causes of the empire's decline.
mnemonic: ON + GOING: still going on.

definition: not transparent; hard to understand
examples: The window was made of opaque glass, so no one could see inside.
The scientist's opaque writing made the findings difficult for ordinary readers to follow.
cloze: Critics complained about the government's {{opaque}} decision-making, which hid its reasoning from the public.
mnemonic: OPAQUE ~ 'opacity': you can't see through it.

definition: harsh public criticism or disgrace
examples: The scandal brought public opprobrium upon the senator and his family.
Her decision to betray the team was met with widespread opprobrium.
cloze: The company faced international {{opprobrium}} after reports of its unsafe factories emerged.
mnemonic: O-PROB-rium: PROBlem for your reputation.

definition: great wealth and luxury
examples: The opulence of the palace, with its gold ceilings, astonished the visitors.
He grew up amid opulence but chose a simple life.
cloze: Guests marveled at the {{opulence}} of the ballroom, with its crystal chandeliers and marble floors.
mnemonic: OPULENCE: OPUlent = the OPen PUrse that overflows with wealth.

definition: ostentatiously rich and luxurious
examples: The opulent palace had golden staircases and crystal chandeliers in every hall.
Their opulent lifestyle included yachts, private chefs, and a dozen vacation homes.
cloze: Guests were stunned by the {{opulent}} ballroom, with its gilded ceilings and priceless tapestries.
mnemonic: OPULENT ~ 'opulence' ~ OPEN wallet.

definition: elaborately decorated
examples: The cathedral's ornate ceiling was covered in gold leaf and carved angels.
She wrote in an ornate style, full of long sentences and flowery phrases.
cloze: The king sat on an {{ornate}} throne decorated with jewels, carvings, and golden vines.
mnemonic: ORNAment — ORNATE means full of ornaments.

definition: bad-tempered and stubborn
examples: The ornery old farmer scowled at everyone who walked across his field.
The ornery mule refused to carry any load that morning.
cloze: Grandpa grows {{ornery}} whenever anyone tries to rearrange his tools or reorganize his shed.
mnemonic: ORNERY sounds like 'ordinary' gone sour.

definition: conforming to established or traditional beliefs
examples: The doctor rejected orthodox treatments in favor of experimental ones.
Her orthodox views on education matched the school's long-standing traditions.
cloze: The professor's ideas were hardly {{orthodox}}, often shocking colleagues who clung to the established theories.
mnemonic: ORTHO (right) + DOX (opinion): right opinion.

definition: to swing back and forth; to waver between choices
examples: The pendulum oscillated steadily back and forth, ticking away each second inside the old clock.
Voters oscillate between the two parties, never staying loyal for long.
cloze: The manager continued to {{oscillate}} between expansion and cost-cutting, unable to make a decision.
mnemonic: OSCILLATE ~ OSCILLoscope waves going up and down.

definition: to become rigid, set in habits, or hardened like bone
examples: Without fresh ideas, the bureaucracy began to ossify into a rigid, slow machine.
Her opinions had ossified over the years, and she refused to consider new evidence.
cloze: Tradition can {{ossify}} an institution until it can no longer adapt to changing times.
mnemonic: OSS = bone (like 'osseous'): turn to bone.

definition: appearing to be true, but not necessarily real
examples: The ostensible reason for the trip was business, though they spent the week at the beach.
His ostensible friendliness hid a deep desire to see his rival fail.
cloze: The {{ostensible}} purpose of the meeting was to share news, but the real goal was to remove the director.
mnemonic: OSTENSIBLE ~ ostentatious: 'on show', only for show.

definition: showy, designed to impress or attract attention
examples: Their ostentatious mansion, with golden gates and marble lions, annoyed the neighbors.
He avoided ostentatious displays of his wealth and drove an ordinary car.
cloze: The tycoon's {{ostentatious}} parties, complete with ice sculptures and diamond favors, were meant to impress.
mnemonic: OSTENT = show; ostentatious people put on a show.

definition: to exclude someone from a group by general consent
examples: Villagers ostracized the family after the scandal and refused to speak to them.
Teenagers who dress differently are sometimes ostracized by their classmates.
cloze: The club chose to {{ostracize}} the cheater, banning him from every game and gathering.
mnemonic: Ancient Greeks voted to banish with OSTRAKA (pottery shards).

definition: the result of an action or process
examples: The outcome of the election surprised even the experts.
Educators measure learning outcomes to see whether the program works.
cloze: The final {{outcome}} of the experiment depends on the temperature of the water.
mnemonic: OUT + COME: what comes out.

definition: to extend over and cover part of something
examples: The ranges of the two bird species overlap in the central valley.
The courses overlap, so students who take both will see some topics twice.
cloze: The roles of the two departments {{overlap}}, which causes confusion about who is responsible.
mnemonic: OVER + LAP: lay over each other.

definition: done or shown openly; not hidden
examples: There was no overt hostility between the rivals, though tension filled the room.
The party's overt support for the policy surprised no one.
cloze: His {{overt}} contempt for the rules was obvious to everyone, and he made no attempt to hide it.
mnemonic: OVERT ~ 'over' the table, in the open.

definition: arrogantly overconfident; excessive
examples: His overweening pride finally led to his downfall.
The overweening manager insisted he alone deserved credit.
cloze: Her {{overweening}} ambition blinded her to the risks of the plan.
mnemonic: OVER + WEENING (thinking): thinking too highly of oneself.

definition: to quiet or calm a troubled person
examples: The mother tried to pacify the crying baby by humming a gentle song and rocking the cradle.
Officials sought to pacify the angry protesters by promising a full investigation into the incident.
cloze: Only a sincere apology could {{pacify}} her furious client.
mnemonic: PACIFY: PACIFIC ocean = peaceful.

definition: pleasant to taste; acceptable
examples: The soup was bland but palatable after a long hike.
The council softened the bill to make it more palatable to voters.
cloze: The chef added herbs to make the bitter greens more {{palatable}} to the children.
mnemonic: PALATE: it's pleasing to the palate.

definition: to talk idly or at length, often in a flattering way
examples: The two old friends palavered on the porch until the sun went down.
He palavered with the officials for hours but accomplished nothing.
cloze: Instead of working, the men would {{palaver}} at the fence about nothing in particular.
mnemonic: PALAVER sounds like 'pal-a-lot-of-talk'.

definition: a manuscript erased and reused, with traces of earlier writing; any layered record
examples: Scholars used ultraviolet light to read the original text on the palimpsest.
The old city is a palimpsest, with each era visible beneath the next.
cloze: Under the new paint, the wall was a {{palimpsest}} of earlier murals still faintly visible.
mnemonic: PALIM (again) + PSEST (scraped): scraped again and rewritten.

definition: to ease the severity of something without curing it
examples: Painkillers can palliate the symptoms, but they do not cure the disease.
The government tried to palliate public anger with small temporary measures.
cloze: The nurse used warm compresses to {{palliate}} the pain until the doctor arrived.
mnemonic: PALLIATE: a PAL helps you feel better.

definition: a supposed remedy that cures all problems
examples: No single policy is a panacea for the nation's economic troubles.
Some patients view the new drug as a panacea, though it treats only one condition.
cloze: Technology is often presented as a {{panacea}}, but it cannot solve every social problem.
mnemonic: PAN (all) + ACEA (cure): cures all.

definition: flamboyant style and confident dash
examples: The singer performed with panache, sweeping onto the stage in a bright cape.
She handled the crisis with such panache that no one noticed her nerves.
cloze: He carried off the daring outfit with {{panache}}, turning every head in the room.
mnemonic: A white PLUME on a hat: PANACHE originally meant a feather plume.

definition: a speech or writing of high praise
examples: The obituary was a panegyric that listed every virtue of the late statesman.
His retirement dinner turned into an extended panegyric of his decades of service.
cloze: The biography read less like history than a {{panegyric}}, celebrating its hero without any criticism.
mnemonic: PAN (all) + AGORA (gathering): speech to all, praising.

definition: a typical model or pattern that shapes how a field thinks
examples: Darwin's theory of evolution became the dominant paradigm for understanding the diversity of living things.
The discovery forced physicists to abandon the old paradigm and build an entirely new framework.
cloze: Copernicus's work triggered a {{paradigm}} shift that changed how astronomers pictured the universe.
mnemonic: PARA + DIGM: a pair of dimes set the standard model.

definition: appearing self-contradictory yet possibly true
examples: It is paradoxical that people sometimes feel lonelier in crowded cities than alone.
The paradoxical result puzzled the researchers, since more fertilizer reduced the yield.
cloze: It seems {{paradoxical}} that the more he studied, the less certain he felt about the answers.
mnemonic: PARA + DOX: beyond belief, a PARADOX.

definition: a person or thing regarded as a perfect example of a quality
examples: She was a paragon of diligence, never missing a deadline in twenty years.
The village held up the retired teacher as a paragon of integrity and kindness.
cloze: The new chancellor was hailed as a {{paragon}} of fairness, admired even by her rivals.
mnemonic: A PAIR of GONE flaws: nothing wrong — a perfect model.

definition: a limit or measurable factor that defines a system
examples: Scientists set the parameters of the experiment before collecting any data.
Temperature is a key parameter in determining the rate of the reaction.
cloze: The study operated within strict {{parameter}} to ensure the results could be compared.
mnemonic: PARA (beside) + METER: measure beside the rules.

definition: a person rejected and shunned by society
examples: After the scandal, he became a pariah in the city's business community.
The whistleblower was treated like a pariah by her former colleagues.
cloze: The regime's isolation turned the country into an international {{pariah}}, cut off from most trade.
mnemonic: PARIAH: sounds like 'Pariah = pah, a rejected one'.

definition: narrow in outlook; limited to a small area or local concerns
examples: His parochial views kept him from understanding customs outside his tiny village.
The magazine was criticized for its parochial focus on local affairs.
cloze: Her {{parochial}} outlook made it difficult for her to appreciate other cultures.
mnemonic: PAROCHIAL: like a PARISH, small and local.

definition: extremely unwilling to spend money; stingy
examples: The parsimonious landlord refused to repair the heater even in the coldest winter.
Her parsimonious habits meant she reused tea bags and wrapping paper for years.
cloze: Despite his vast fortune, the {{parsimonious}} old man haggled over every penny of the bill.
mnemonic: PARSI-MONEY-ous: he pars down every bit of money he spends.

definition: strongly supporting one side, often blindly and without balance
examples: The partisan crowd booed every decision the referee made against the home team.
Debate in the legislature grew so partisan that no compromise seemed possible.
cloze: The commission's report was criticized as {{partisan}} because it ignored all evidence favoring the opposition.
mnemonic: PARTISAN takes a PART — only one part, one side.

definition: a person who has newly gained wealth or status but lacks the accepted manners
examples: The old aristocracy sneered at the parvenu who bought the mansion on the hill.
The parvenu tried to impress his neighbors by flaunting his new fortune.
cloze: Despite his riches, he remained a {{parvenu}} to the established families of the town.
mnemonic: PARVENU: has just 'arrived' (venu) in high society.

definition: relating to peaceful country life; idealizing rural scenes
examples: The painting showed a pastoral scene of shepherds resting beneath shady trees.
They retreated from the city to enjoy the pastoral calm of the countryside.
cloze: The poet filled his verses with {{pastoral}} images of meadows, sheep, and quiet brooks.
mnemonic: PASTOR as shepherd: tending flocks in the country.

definition: completely clear and obvious
examples: It was patent to everyone that the witness was lying.
His patent insincerity annoyed the audience.
cloze: The company's {{patent}} disregard for safety led to a government inquiry.
mnemonic: A PATENT is open for all to see; things patent are in plain view.

definition: to treat in a condescending way; also to be a regular customer of
examples: He patronized the new intern, explaining simple tasks in a slow, superior voice.
Don't patronize me; I understand the problem as well as you do.
cloze: The doctor's habit of {{patronize}}ing his patients made many of them seek a second opinion.
mnemonic: PATRON-ize: acting like a superior patron over inferiors.

definition: a small or insufficient amount of something
examples: The paucity of rainfall left the reservoirs nearly empty by August.
Critics noted a paucity of original ideas in the otherwise polished film.
cloze: A {{paucity}} of reliable data made it impossible to draw firm conclusions from the study.
mnemonic: PAUCITY sounds like 'poor city' — poor in supplies.

definition: relating to money
examples: The charity had no pecuniary interest in the deal, only a desire to help.
Pecuniary difficulties forced the family to sell their old home.
cloze: The officer was fined for using his position for {{pecuniary}} gain.
mnemonic: Pecus = cattle in Latin: early wealth was in cows.

definition: overly concerned with minor rules and displays of learning
examples: The pedantic editor corrected every comma but missed the article's larger flaws.
His pedantic lectures on grammar bored students who simply wanted to communicate clearly.
cloze: She grew tired of her {{pedantic}} colleague, who interrupted meetings to correct trivial errors in pronunciation.
mnemonic: PEDANT = 'ped' like pedal: he pedals on tiny details endlessly.

definition: lacking inspiration; dull
examples: The film's pedestrian script offered no surprises, and the audience could predict every scene in advance.
His pedestrian prose bored readers who had hoped for something original, lively, or at least memorable.
cloze: The meal was {{pedestrian}}, neither bad nor memorable.
mnemonic: PEDESTRIAN: walking on foot — slow plodding.

definition: irritable and easily annoyed, often about trivial matters
examples: The peevish child complained about everything on the menu.
She grew peevish when her nap was interrupted.
cloze: Tired and hungry, the travelers became {{peevish}} and snapped at one another.
mnemonic: PEEVISH: a PEEVE-ish grumble.

definition: expressing contempt or disapproval
examples: 'Bookworm' can be used as a pejorative term for a studious person.
The critic's pejorative remarks about the film drew protest.
cloze: Calling someone a 'slacker' is a {{pejorative}} label that implies laziness.
mnemonic: PEJOR = worse, like 'pejorative makes it worse'.

definition: transparently clear, in appearance or in style
examples: The pellucid mountain stream allowed us to see every pebble on the bottom.
Her pellucid prose made even the most complex economic theory easy to follow.
cloze: The lawyer's {{pellucid}} explanation left the jury with no doubt about the sequence of events.
mnemonic: PELLUCID contains LUCID, meaning clear.

definition: a strong and continuing liking or inclination for something
examples: He has a penchant for old jazz records and spends weekends searching used shops.
The young chef's penchant for bold spices made her dishes unforgettable.
cloze: Her {{penchant}} for risky investments eventually cost the family most of its savings.
mnemonic: PENCHANT: a PEN CHANT — she loves to chant while writing with a pen.

definition: feeling sorrow for having done wrong
examples: The penitent thief returned the stolen jewels to their owner and tearfully asked for forgiveness.
He stood penitent before the judge, hoping that his sincere remorse would earn him a lighter sentence.
cloze: The {{penitent}} sinner knelt and begged for forgiveness.
mnemonic: PENITENT: PENANCE — you do penance when sorry.

definition: extremely poor; or very stingy
examples: The penurious student lived on bread and tea for most of the winter.
He was penurious even in his later wealth, refusing to turn on the lights.
cloze: After the factory closed, the once-thriving town became {{penurious}}, with families struggling to buy food.
mnemonic: PENURY sounds like 'pen-you-ry': you have only a pen, no money.

definition: to become aware of something through the senses or mind
examples: Bees perceive ultraviolet light that humans cannot see.
Many consumers perceive handmade goods as higher in quality.
cloze: Infants can {{perceive}} differences between sounds long before they can speak.
mnemonic: PER + CEIVE: take in through the senses.

definition: having keen insight and understanding
examples: The percipient teacher noticed that the quiet boy was struggling with his eyesight.
A percipient observer, she saw tension in the room long before anyone spoke.
cloze: The {{percipient}} critic grasped the novel's hidden meaning on a single reading.
mnemonic: PERCIPIENT: you PERCEIVE things quickly.

definition: insisting on immediate obedience; brooking no refusal
examples: The captain issued a peremptory order, and the crew obeyed at once.
Her peremptory tone made clear that discussion was over.
cloze: With a {{peremptory}} wave of his hand, the manager dismissed the committee and ended the debate.
mnemonic: PEREMPTORY: kills (emere) all objection; 'per-empt-ory' = it's final.

definition: lasting for a very long time; constantly recurring
examples: Traffic jams are a perennial problem in the capital, appearing every single morning and evening without fail.
The garden's perennial flowers return each spring without any need for the owner to replant them.
cloze: Flooding is a {{perennial}} concern for villages along the river, which recur nearly every spring.
mnemonic: PER + ANNUAL: through the years.

definition: deceitful and untrustworthy; disloyal
examples: The perfidious general secretly sold the army's plans to the enemy.
She felt betrayed by her perfidious friend, who had spread rumors behind her back.
cloze: History remembers him as a {{perfidious}} ally who broke every treaty the moment it became inconvenient.
mnemonic: PERFIDIOUS: 'per-FIDO-us' — a dog (Fido) that is NOT faithful.

definition: deliberate betrayal of trust
examples: History remembers the general mainly for his perfidy, since he sold secrets to the enemy during the war.
The peace treaty collapsed because of the perfidy of its signers, who had never intended to honor it.
cloze: The spy's {{perfidy}} cost many soldiers their lives.
mnemonic: PERFIDY: no FIDELITY.

definition: done quickly as a routine, without real care or effort
examples: He gave the report only a perfunctory glance before signing it.
The clerk's perfunctory apology did little to calm the angry customer.
cloze: The inspector's {{perfunctory}} check missed the cracks that later caused the bridge to close.
mnemonic: PERFUNCTORY: 'per-FUNCTION' — just going through the function.

definition: traveling from place to place; wandering
examples: The peripatetic salesman spent most of the year on the road.
Her peripatetic childhood included homes in six different countries.
cloze: As a {{peripatetic}} scholar, he taught in a different city every semester.
mnemonic: PERI (around) + PATH: walking around, like Aristotle strolling as he taught.

definition: of secondary importance; located at the edge
examples: The mayor's role in the project was merely peripheral, and he attended almost none of the meetings.
Peripheral vision lets you notice movement at the very edge of your field of sight.
cloze: These details are {{peripheral}} to the main argument and can safely be left out.
mnemonic: PERIPHERAL: PERIMETER — the outer edge.

definition: causing harm in a gradual, subtle way
examples: Rumors can have a pernicious effect on a team's morale over time.
Scientists warned of the pernicious influence of pollutants that build up slowly in the soil.
cloze: The {{pernicious}} spread of misinformation slowly eroded the public's trust in the health system.
mnemonic: PERNICIOUS: sounds like 'pernicious = perish-ious' — it makes things perish.

definition: to cause to continue indefinitely
examples: Stereotypes in the media perpetuate false ideas about certain groups for generations.
The family business was perpetuated by each new generation, which kept the old traditions alive.
cloze: Repeating the old rumors will only {{perpetuate}} the misunderstanding between the two towns.
mnemonic: PERPETUAL motion: keep it going.

definition: to confuse someone completely
examples: The strange noise coming from the engine continued to perplex even the most experienced engineers in the shop.
Her sudden silence at the meeting perplexed everyone at the table, since she normally had plenty to say.
cloze: The complicated instructions continued to {{perplex}} even the most experienced users.
mnemonic: PERPLEX: PER + PLEX (tangled): tangled thoughts.

definition: a benefit or privilege that comes with a job, beyond the pay
examples: A company car was one of the perquisites of the senior position.
Free lunches and gym access were the perquisites that drew many applicants.
cloze: Among the {{perquisites}} offered to executives were a private jet and a driver.
mnemonic: The short form is PERK: PER-QUISITE a perk of the job.

definition: to continue firmly despite difficulty
examples: Symptoms of the disease persisted for several weeks.
Some ancient customs persist in remote villages even today.
cloze: If the drought continues to {{persist}}, farmers will be forced to abandon the land.
mnemonic: PERSIST = PERSevere + exIST.

definition: a particular way of viewing things
examples: Historians offer a new perspective on the causes of the war.
Studying abroad gave her a broader perspective on world cultures.
cloze: From a biological {{perspective}}, the behavior helps the species survive.
mnemonic: PER + SPECT: look through to see.

definition: having keen insight; mentally sharp in understanding
examples: The perspicacious detective noticed the single detail everyone else had overlooked.
A perspicacious investor, she sensed the market's collapse months before it happened.
cloze: Her {{perspicacious}} reading of the negotiations helped her predict the rival's next move.
mnemonic: PERSPICACIOUS: you can see (spic = look) right through things.

definition: directly relevant to the matter at hand
examples: The lawyer asked only pertinent questions, steering clear of anything off topic.
She collected all the pertinent documents before the meeting began.
cloze: Please leave out details that are not {{pertinent}}; the essay should address only the question asked.
mnemonic: PERTINENT: it PERTAINS to the issue.

definition: to make anxious or unsettled; to disturb
examples: The strange noise outside perturbed her and she checked the locks twice.
Nothing could perturb the calm captain, even in the worst storm.
cloze: News of the layoffs did {{perturb}} the staff, who feared for their jobs.
mnemonic: PER (thoroughly) + turb (turbulence): stirred up inside.

definition: to read or examine carefully and thoroughly
examples: She perused the contract line by line before signing it.
The detective perused the files for any hint of the missing clue.
cloze: Before the meeting, I will {{peruse}} the report to catch any errors.
mnemonic: PER (through) + USE: use your eyes all the way through.

definition: spreading widely through every part of something
examples: A pervasive smell of smoke filled the entire building after the fire.
Social media has become a pervasive part of teenage life.
cloze: The {{pervasive}} sense of fear in the city kept people off the streets after dark.
mnemonic: PERVASIVE: it PERVADES — goes everywhere, like a pervading smell.

definition: childishly sulky or bad-tempered
examples: The petulant child threw his toys when told to go to bed.
Her petulant reply showed that she was still angry about losing.
cloze: The star's {{petulant}} refusal to leave his dressing room delayed the show for an hour.
mnemonic: PETULANT: like a PET that is spoiled and whines.

definition: dreamlike, fantastic, with a shifting series of strange images
examples: The film's phantasmagorical scenes blurred the line between dream and waking life.
He described a phantasmagorical carnival of glowing lanterns and shifting shadows.
cloze: The painter's {{phantasmagorical}} landscapes seemed to melt and swirl like a feverish dream.
mnemonic: PHANTOM + MAGICAL: ghostly shows that shift.

definition: an observable fact or event, especially a remarkable one
examples: The northern lights are a natural phenomenon caused by charged solar particles.
Urbanization is a global phenomenon that has reshaped modern society.
cloze: Scientists are still trying to explain the strange {{phenomenon}} of ball lightning.
mnemonic: PHENOMENON: PHEN-omenal event you can see.

definition: hostile or indifferent to art, culture, and learning
examples: His philistine attitude kept him from ever visiting a museum.
The philistine mayor cut funding for the symphony.
cloze: Many artists complained that the {{philistine}} public cared only for money and entertainment.
mnemonic: The ancient Philistines were seen as rough and uncultured.

definition: calm and not easily excited or upset
examples: The phlegmatic pilot kept his voice steady even as the engine sputtered.
Her phlegmatic temperament made her an ideal negotiator in tense situations.
cloze: Unlike his excitable brother, he remained {{phlegmatic}} when the results arrived, simply nodding and returning to work.
mnemonic: PHLEGM makes you sluggish — a phlegmatic person is slow to react.

definition: petty; of little value
examples: He wasted time arguing over picayune details of the contract.
The manager criticized the picayune complaints that distracted the team from real problems.
cloze: Don't waste your breath on such {{picayune}} matters when the big issues remain unresolved.
mnemonic: A 'pick-a-yoon' small coin: tiny worth.

definition: to attack or ridicule publicly
examples: The press pilloried the minister for his lavish spending during the crisis.
She was pilloried online after her careless remark went viral.
cloze: Newspapers continued to {{pillory}} the mayor over the failed construction project.
mnemonic: A PILLORY was a wooden frame where criminals were publicly shamed.

definition: to long for painfully; to waste away from grief
examples: She pined for her homeland during the long exile.
The dog pined at the gate until its owner returned.
cloze: Soldiers far from home often {{pine}} for the comforts of their families.
mnemonic: PINE like a lonely tree wasting away, longing.

definition: the highest point of achievement or success
examples: Winning the Nobel Prize was the pinnacle of her scientific career.
The climbers reached the pinnacle of the mountain at dawn.
cloze: For most actors, an Oscar is the {{pinnacle}} of professional success.
mnemonic: PIN on top of the cone: the very tip.

definition: pleasantly sharp or spicy; stimulating
examples: The piquant sauce brought a pleasant heat to the plain rice.
Her piquant wit kept the dinner conversation lively and slightly provocative.
cloze: A {{piquant}} blend of chili and lime gave the soup its bright flavor.
mnemonic: PIQUANT and PIQUE: it pricks your tongue.

definition: to arouse curiosity or interest
examples: The mysterious letter without a return address piqued her curiosity, and she opened it at once.
The documentary piqued many students' interest in astronomy, and several later joined the school's science club.
cloze: The strange symbol on the door was enough to {{pique}} the visitors' curiosity.
mnemonic: PIQUE: a PEEK at a pique of curiosity.

definition: the essential part or core meaning of something
examples: The pith of her speech was simple: invest in children, and the future follows.
He summarized the pith of the argument in one short paragraph.
cloze: Cut away the digressions and focus on the {{pith}} of the argument, which is its central claim.
mnemonic: PITH is the white inner core of an orange peel - the heart of it.

definition: concise and forcefully meaningful in expression
examples: His pithy remarks summed up the entire debate in a single sentence.
Proverbs are pithy sayings that carry a lot of wisdom in few words.
cloze: The editor praised the writer's {{pithy}} style, in which every sentence carried real weight.
mnemonic: PITHY: the PITH is the core of an orange — the essence.

definition: a very small amount of money, especially an inadequate wage
examples: The workers were paid a pittance for twelve hours of hard labor.
She sold the antique for a mere pittance, never realizing its true worth.
cloze: The charity received only a {{pittance}} from the government, far too little to fund the program.
mnemonic: A PITTANCE is a PITIful amount.

definition: of crucial importance because other things depend on it
examples: The pivotal moment of the game came in the final minute, when the goalkeeper saved a penalty.
She played a pivotal role in the negotiations, bringing both sides together after weeks of deadlock.
cloze: The court's ruling proved {{pivotal}} to the outcome of the election.
mnemonic: PIVOTAL: a PIVOT — the point that everything turns on.

definition: to calm someone's anger by giving in or making concessions
examples: The manager offered a refund to placate the furious customer.
Nothing the mayor said could placate the crowd demanding his resignation.
cloze: The company tried to {{placate}} angry shareholders by promising higher dividends next year.
mnemonic: PLACATE sounds like 'PLACID' — make someone placid.

definition: calm and peaceful; not easily upset
examples: The placid lake reflected the mountains without a ripple.
He had a placid temperament and rarely raised his voice.
cloze: The cow's {{placid}} nature meant that even loud noises could not disturb her.
mnemonic: PLACID like PLACATE: pacified, calm.

definition: a dull, overused remark presented as if it were fresh
examples: The speech was full of platitudes about hard work and never giving up.
Offering a platitude like 'everything happens for a reason' comforted no one.
cloze: Rather than offering real solutions, the senator hid behind a {{platitude}} about the importance of family values.
mnemonic: PLATITUDE: a flat PLATE of attitude — flat, dull words.

definition: seeming reasonable and believable
examples: The detective found his alibi plausible but could not verify it with any witnesses.
It is plausible that prices will rise again next year, given the current shortage of supplies.
cloze: Her {{plausible}} excuse for being late convinced the teacher.
mnemonic: PLAUSIBLE: APPLAUSE-ible: worth applause because it makes sense.

definition: an excessive or very large amount of something
examples: The menu offered a plethora of choices, which left every one of us unable to decide.
A plethora of evidence pointed to the defendant's guilt, and the jury convicted him quickly.
cloze: Shoppers faced a {{plethora}} of brands, each claiming to be the healthiest choice.
mnemonic: PLETHORA: 'plenty-ora' — plenty!

definition: slow-moving, laborious, and lacking spark
examples: The plodding pace of the film bored most of the audience.
His plodding prose made even exciting events seem tedious to read.
cloze: Although {{plodding}}, the clerk's steady work ensured that no detail was ever missed.
mnemonic: A PLODDING person PLODS: heavy steps in mud.

definition: a clever maneuver to gain an advantage
examples: His fake limp was a ploy to avoid the exam.
The sale was a ploy to attract customers to the shop.
cloze: The candidate's tears were a calculated {{ploy}} to win sympathy from voters.
mnemonic: A PLOY is a play: a trick in the game.

definition: brave and spirited in the face of difficulty
examples: The plucky underdog team held its much stronger rivals to a draw.
A plucky young girl, she faced the bullies without flinching.
cloze: The {{plucky}} little boat pushed bravely through the heavy waves toward shore.
mnemonic: PLUCK: to pull up your courage like pulling a feather.

definition: evoking a keen sense of sadness or sympathy
examples: The film's poignant ending, in which the old friends said goodbye, left many viewers in tears.
He gave a poignant speech about the childhood friends he had lost over the years.
cloze: The soldier's last letter home was a {{poignant}} reminder of the war's human cost.
mnemonic: POIGNANT: sounds like 'point' — it pierces the heart.

definition: a strong written or spoken attack on a belief or policy
examples: The columnist's polemic against the new tax outraged many readers.
Her book is less a balanced study than a fierce polemic against industrial farming.
cloze: The pamphlet was a bitter {{polemic}} aimed at everyone who had supported the war.
mnemonic: POLEMIC: sounds like 'poll-EMIC' — arguing about politics, not a calm poll.

definition: slow and clumsy because of great weight; dull and labored
examples: The ponderous elephant lumbered slowly and heavily across the dusty clearing toward the watering hole.
His ponderous prose made the annual report a long and tiresome chore to read.
cloze: The professor's {{ponderous}} lecture, heavy with jargon, put half the class to sleep.
mnemonic: PONDEROUS: pound-erous — heavy as a pound.

definition: to speak in a pompous, dogmatic way
examples: He loved to pontificate about politics at family dinners, ignoring everyone who tried to disagree with him.
The critic pontificated for an hour on what real art should be and who could be called an artist.
cloze: Rather than listen, the professor would {{pontificate}} to students on every subject.
mnemonic: PONTIFF (pope) pontificates — speaks as an authority.

definition: a sign that something important or bad is about to happen
examples: Dark clouds on the horizon were a portent of the coming storm.
Many saw the sudden loss of power as a portent of worse trouble.
cloze: The falling bird numbers were a {{portent}} of ecological trouble to come.
mnemonic: PORTENT: a PORT-ent — a ship in port warns of a storm.

definition: ominously significant, foreshadowing; also pompously solemn
examples: The portentous dark clouds gathered, warning of the storm to come.
Her portentous tone suggested that something dreadful was about to be announced.
cloze: The sky took on a {{portentous}} yellow hue before the tornado struck.
mnemonic: PORTENT = omen; a portentous event is an omen.

definition: to put forward as a basis for argument; to assume as true
examples: Scientists posit that a vast ocean lies beneath the moon's icy crust.
The author posits that most failures come from poor communication.
cloze: Let us {{posit}} that the market will grow, and then calculate the likely profit.
mnemonic: POSITion: you set an idea in position.

definition: possible but not yet realized
examples: Researchers warned of the potential dangers of the new chemical.
The company sees great potential customers among university students.
cloze: Geologists identified several {{potential}} sites for the new mine.
mnemonic: POTENTIAL: POTent in the future.

definition: an informal conference or meeting
examples: The coaches held a powwow near the bench to discuss strategy.
After a quick powwow, the neighbors decided to repair the fence together.
cloze: Before the vote, the senators held a brief {{powwow}} in the hallway.
mnemonic: POW! WOW! A quick talk-shop session.

definition: dealing with problems in a practical rather than idealistic way
examples: Her pragmatic approach focused on what would actually work rather than what sounded noble.
The pragmatic mayor chose a cheaper repair over an ambitious but unaffordable rebuild.
cloze: Rather than chase an ideal solution, the {{pragmatic}} committee settled on a plan it could actually afford.
mnemonic: PRAGMATIC: 'pragma' means deed in Greek — focus on deeds that work.

definition: to talk foolishly or at length about trivial things
examples: The children prattled happily about toys and cartoons through the entire long car ride to the coast.
He prattled on about the weather for an hour, never noticing that nobody was listening.
cloze: Guests continued to {{prattle}} about celebrity gossip all evening.
mnemonic: PRATTLE: sounds like 'rattle' of talking.

definition: dangerously unstable or uncertain
examples: The climber's precarious position on the narrow ledge made everyone nervous.
With sales falling, the small firm's financial situation became increasingly precarious.
cloze: He lived a {{precarious}} existence, never sure whether he could pay next month's rent.
mnemonic: PRECARIOUS: sounds like 'pre-carry-us' — about to drop us.

definition: to come before something in time or order
examples: A series of small tremors often precedes a major earthquake.
In most textbooks, a summary precedes the detailed chapters.
cloze: The invention of the written alphabet had to {{precede}} the development of widespread literacy.
mnemonic: PRE (before) + CEDE (go): go before.

definition: an earlier event or ruling that serves as a guide
examples: The court's decision set a precedent that later judges would follow for decades.
There was no precedent for such a fast recovery in the history of the disease.
cloze: Lawyers cited a famous {{precedent}} to argue that the rule should be upheld.
mnemonic: PRE-CEDENT: it CEDES, or goes before, to guide later cases.

definition: done suddenly and without careful thought
examples: Selling the house so quickly was a precipitate decision that he would later come to regret.
The government's precipitate withdrawal from the region left the local population in chaos and confusion.
cloze: Critics accused the president of a {{precipitate}} decision that was made before the facts were known.
mnemonic: PRECIPITATE: rain 'precipitates' from the sky suddenly — falls headlong.

definition: dangerously steep; sudden and sharp
examples: The hikers edged along a precipitous cliff with no guardrail.
Stock prices took a precipitous drop after the surprise announcement.
cloze: The {{precipitous}} slope made the descent dangerous even for experienced climbers.
mnemonic: PRECIPITOUS: the PRECIPICE, a cliff edge falling away.

definition: to make something impossible; to prevent in advance
examples: A knee injury precluded him from playing in the final.
The contract's wording precludes either party from ending the deal early.
cloze: Her tight schedule will {{preclude}} any chance of a vacation before the end of the year.
mnemonic: PRE + CLUDE (close): close the door before it opens.

definition: showing unusually early development in skill or maturity
examples: The precocious child was reading novels at four years old.
A precocious musician, she performed with the orchestra at eleven.
cloze: The {{precocious}} young chess player defeated several grandmasters before she turned ten.
mnemonic: PRE-COCIOUS: cooked (coq) before time - ripe too early.

definition: a person or thing that comes before and leads to another
examples: The telegraph was an early precursor of the modern telephone, paving the way for later inventions.
Economic uncertainty is often a precursor to political unrest, as history has shown many times.
cloze: The small experiment proved to be a {{precursor}} to a major scientific breakthrough.
mnemonic: PRE + CURSOR: the one that runs before.

definition: to say what will happen in the future
examples: Meteorologists use satellite data to predict the path of hurricanes.
Economists struggled to predict the collapse of the housing market.
cloze: Scientists cannot yet {{predict}} exactly when a volcano will erupt.
mnemonic: PRE (before) + DICT (say): say before.

definition: a strong preference or special liking for something
examples: He has a predilection for spicy food that surprises his guests.
Her predilection for mystery novels filled the shelves of her small apartment.
cloze: The director's {{predilection}} for dark, moody settings is evident in all his films.
mnemonic: PRE-DIL-ection: you 'pre-elect' what you like.

definition: most common or most powerful among several
examples: Wheat was the predominant crop in the region throughout the nineteenth century.
The predominant view among economists changed after the financial crisis.
cloze: In this ecosystem, grasses are the {{predominant}} form of plant life.
mnemonic: PRE-DOMINANT: DOMINANT already.

definition: to prevent by acting first; to take the place of
examples: The company preempted a strike by raising wages before the union could ask.
The breaking news preempted the regular television schedule for the night.
cloze: The mayor moved to {{preempt}} criticism by publishing the budget before reporters could demand it.
mnemonic: PRE + EMPT (buy): buy it first, before others.

definition: done in advance to prevent something or gain an advantage
examples: The government took preemptive measures to stop the virus from spreading.
A preemptive strike was launched before the enemy could finish preparing.
cloze: The company filed a {{preemptive}} lawsuit to block its rival from entering the market.
mnemonic: PRE + EMPT(buy): buy first, act before others.

definition: coming before the main part; preparatory
examples: Preliminary results suggest that the new drug may reduce inflammation.
The committee held a preliminary meeting to set the agenda for the conference.
cloze: A {{preliminary}} survey of the site revealed traces of an ancient settlement.
mnemonic: PRE + LIMIT: before the limit (the main part).

definition: knowledge of events before they happen; foresight
examples: His prescience about the housing crash made him a fortune.
The novelist's prescience was remarkable, since she described the internet decades before it arrived.
cloze: Her {{prescience}} saved the firm, as she predicted the downturn long before others noticed.
mnemonic: PRE + SCIENCE: knowing before.

definition: having knowledge of events before they happen
examples: His prescient warning about the housing bubble was ignored until too late.
The novelist's prescient vision of mobile phones astonished later readers.
cloze: Her {{prescient}} forecast of the crisis came true almost exactly as she had described it.
mnemonic: PRE + SCI (know): knowing before.

definition: a feeling that something, usually bad, will happen
examples: She had a presentiment of disaster before the plane took off.
A strange presentiment kept him from boarding the ship.
cloze: The old sailor felt a dark {{presentiment}} as the sky grew strangely still.
mnemonic: PRE + SENT(feel): feeling ahead of time.

definition: having high status and honor
examples: She won a prestigious international award for her research on climate and ocean currents.
He attended a prestigious university in London, which later helped him secure his dream job.
cloze: The {{prestigious}} firm hired only the very best graduates.
mnemonic: PRESTIGIOUS: PRESTIGE.

definition: arrogant overconfidence, or something taken for granted as true
examples: It was sheer presumption for the newcomer to rearrange the senior staff's offices.
The law rests on the presumption that a defendant is innocent until proven guilty.
cloze: His {{presumption}} in speaking for the whole committee annoyed the other members.
mnemonic: PRE-SUME: you assume before you know.

definition: overstepping bounds with arrogant boldness
examples: It was presumptuous of the intern to correct the director.
The presumptuous guest rearranged the host's furniture.
cloze: It seems {{presumptuous}} to assume you will win before the race begins.
mnemonic: PRE-SUME: assuming too much beforehand.

definition: trying to impress by pretending to be more important or cultured than one is
examples: The pretentious diner kept dropping French phrases to show off his sophistication.
Reviewers found the film pretentious, mistaking vague mumbling for deep wisdom.
cloze: His {{pretentious}} use of obscure words annoyed readers more than it impressed them.
mnemonic: PRETEND-tious: he pretends to be more than he is.

definition: a false reason given to hide the true purpose
examples: He left the party early on the pretext of a headache.
The invasion was launched under the pretext of protecting local citizens.
cloze: She used a {{pretext}} of checking the files to eavesdrop on their meeting.
mnemonic: PRE + TEXT: a story written before the real reason.

definition: to win out; to be widespread or in force
examples: In the end, reason will prevail over fear and prejudice.
Customs that prevail in one region may seem strange in another.
cloze: Despite the early losses, the underdog team managed to {{prevail}} in the final match.
mnemonic: PRE + VAIL (strong): the strong one wins.

definition: to speak evasively in order to avoid telling the truth
examples: The witness began to prevaricate when asked where he had been that night.
Rather than give a straight answer, the minister chose to prevaricate.
cloze: When pressed about the missing funds, the treasurer would {{prevaricate}} and change the subject.
mnemonic: PREVARICATE: 'pre-VARY-cate' — he varies his story.

definition: the condition of being most important or ranked first
examples: The primacy of the individual is a core idea in the nation's constitution.
Scholars debated the primacy of reason over emotion in decision making.
cloze: The company's {{primacy}} in the market was unchallenged for decades.
mnemonic: PRIMe or PRIMary: first.

definition: most important; first in order
examples: Agriculture was the primary source of income for the early settlers.
Historians prefer primary sources, such as diaries, to later summaries.
cloze: The {{primary}} cause of the decline was overfishing, though pollution also played a role.
mnemonic: PRIMARY = PRIME: first and best.

definition: a basic rule or law that explains how something works
examples: The principle of natural selection explains how species adapt over time.
Engineers apply the same physical principles when designing both bridges and airplanes.
cloze: The experiment demonstrated the {{principle}} that every action has an equal and opposite reaction.
mnemonic: PRINCIPLE: PRINCIPAL rule, spelled with LE for LEgal rule.

definition: existing or occurring earlier
examples: Applicants need prior experience in laboratory research.
Prior to the invention of printing, books were copied by hand.
cloze: Students are expected to have {{prior}} knowledge of algebra before taking this course.
mnemonic: PRIOR = PRIORity earlier in time.

definition: in its original, unspoiled condition; perfectly clean
examples: The pristine beach had never seen a single footprint, a bottle, or a scrap of litter.
Despite being fifty years old, the vintage car was still in pristine condition.
cloze: Hikers marveled at the {{pristine}} lake, untouched by pollution or development.
mnemonic: PRISTINE: 'pristine' is the first state, like the 'primitive' one.

definition: complete honesty and strong moral principles
examples: The judge was admired for his probity and refusal to accept any favors.
Public officials must act with probity when handling taxpayer money.
cloze: The auditor's reputation for {{probity}} made both sides trust her findings.
mnemonic: PROBITY: you can PROBE him and find no flaw.

definition: spending money wastefully and recklessly
examples: The prodigal heir squandered his entire inheritance on parties and gambling within just two years.
Critics condemned the government's prodigal spending on projects that nobody had asked for or needed.
cloze: The {{prodigal}} son wasted his fortune on luxuries and returned home penniless.
mnemonic: PRODIGAL: 'pro-di-gal' — he pro-digs his money away.

definition: remarkably great in size, power, or degree
examples: The young pianist showed prodigious talent at the age of seven, astonishing every teacher she met.
Building the great pyramids required a prodigious amount of labor, planning, and stone.
cloze: He had a {{prodigious}} appetite, finishing three full meals without apparent effort.
mnemonic: PRODIGIOUS: a PRODIGY has an enormous ability.

definition: recklessly extravagant or immoral
examples: The profligate duke spent his fortune on parties and gambling.
Critics attacked the city's profligate spending, which left it deeply in debt.
cloze: His {{profligate}} lifestyle drained the family estate within a single generation.
mnemonic: PROFLIGATE: 'pro-FLIGHT-gate' — money flies out the gate.

definition: abundant; given or flowing freely
examples: The nurse tried to stop the profuse bleeding from the wound.
She offered profuse apologies for being late, repeating them several times.
cloze: The garden was a riot of {{profuse}} blossoms, spilling over every wall and fence.
mnemonic: PRO-FUSE: pours forth like a fuse burning wildly.

definition: an abundant, lavish quantity
examples: Wildflowers bloomed in profusion across the meadow after the spring rains.
The profusion of choices on the menu left him unable to decide.
cloze: A {{profusion}} of poppies covered the hillside, so thick that the green was hardly visible.
mnemonic: PROFUSION: pour forth, like FUSE and flow in huge amounts.

definition: a prediction or forecast of future events
examples: The economist's gloomy prognostication of a deep recession proved remarkably accurate.
Astrologers built careers on prognostication, though few of their forecasts came true.
cloze: Despite their confident {{prognostication}}, the analysts failed to anticipate the sudden collapse.
mnemonic: PRO-GNOSTICATION: knowing ahead, like a gnostic prophet.

definition: to forbid something by law or rule
examples: Many countries prohibit hunting of endangered animals.
The university rules prohibit students from copying material without citing the source.
cloze: Federal regulations {{prohibit}} the dumping of toxic waste into rivers.
mnemonic: PRO-HIBIT: HIBIT sounds like HABIT you may not keep.

definition: to increase rapidly in number
examples: Fast-food restaurants have proliferated along the highway in recent years.
Rumors began to proliferate as soon as the factory announced its closure.
cloze: Online scams {{proliferate}} during the holiday season, preying on people hurrying to shop.
mnemonic: PRO + LIFE + rate: life produces offspring rapidly.

definition: producing a great deal; very productive
examples: The prolific author wrote over sixty novels, dozens of short stories, and countless essays in her lifetime.
Rabbits are prolific breeders, and a small group can double in number within a few months.
cloze: A {{prolific}} composer, he completed dozens of symphonies before he turned forty.
mnemonic: PROLIFIC: PRO-LIFE-ic: lots of life produced.

definition: using too many words; tediously lengthy
examples: The prolix speaker bored the audience for two full hours with details that no one had asked for.
Her prolix report could easily have been cut in half without losing a single important point.
cloze: The contract was {{prolix}}, filled with repetitive and unnecessary clauses.
mnemonic: PROLIX: a LONG pro-lix.

definition: wordiness; tediously long speech or writing
examples: The prolixity of the report made it nearly impossible to find the main recommendation.
His prolixity at meetings caused colleagues to dread his turn to speak.
cloze: The editor cut the chapter by half, citing the author's {{prolixity}} as the main weakness.
mnemonic: PRO-LIX: a long LIQUID flow of words.

definition: to announce or spread an idea or law publicly
examples: The government promulgated the new tax law across the country.
Missionaries promulgated their beliefs in every village they visited.
cloze: The king will {{promulgate}} the decree at dawn, announcing it from every public square.
mnemonic: PRO + mulg: push a law forward publicly, like a town crier.

definition: a natural tendency to behave in a particular way
examples: He has a propensity to exaggerate when telling stories about his travels.
Some dog breeds have a propensity for barking at strangers.
cloze: Her {{propensity}} for procrastination meant that assignments were always finished at the last minute.
mnemonic: PROPENSITY: 'prop-ensity' — props you up to lean toward something.

definition: to win over or appease someone who is angry
examples: The villagers offered gifts to propitiate the angry gods and end the drought.
He tried to propitiate his furious boss with a heartfelt apology and a bouquet.
cloze: She sent flowers to {{propitiate}} her neighbor after the noisy party.
mnemonic: PROPITIATE = pro-pit-y: seeking pity to calm anger.

definition: giving or indicating a good chance of success; favorable
examples: The clear sky and gentle wind made it a propitious day for sailing.
Investors saw the falling interest rates as a propitious sign for the economy.
cloze: The team waited for a {{propitious}} moment to launch the product, when competitors were distracted.
mnemonic: PROPITIOUS: 'propi-' sounds like 'proper' — the proper time.

definition: a person who argues in favor of a cause or idea
examples: She was a leading proponent of renewable energy.
Proponents of the bill said it would create thousands of jobs.
cloze: A vocal {{proponent}} of reform, he spoke at rallies across the state.
mnemonic: PRO + opponent: opposite of opponent.

definition: a part considered in relation to the whole
examples: A large proportion of the planet's fresh water is locked in ice.
The proportion of students studying abroad has doubled in a decade.
cloze: Only a small {{proportion}} of the species survived the mass extinction.
mnemonic: PRO-PORTION: a PORTION of the whole.

definition: dull and ordinary; lacking imagination or poetry
examples: The poet's prosaic description of the sunset disappointed his readers.
Her prosaic job as a filing clerk offered little excitement.
cloze: After the grand opening, the rest of the evening felt {{prosaic}} and uninspired.
mnemonic: PROSAIC = PROSE, not poetry — plain.

definition: to forbid officially; to prohibit
examples: The new law proscribes the sale of tobacco to anyone under the age of eighteen.
Many religions proscribe the eating of certain foods during their most sacred periods of the year.
cloze: The council moved to {{proscribe}} the use of plastic bags within city limits.
mnemonic: PRO-SCRIBE: you write a ban down: no scribing allowed.

definition: to try to convert others to a belief or cause
examples: Missionaries proselytized across the region for decades.
He proselytized for vegetarianism at every dinner party.
cloze: The group began to {{proselytize}} among the villagers, urging them to adopt the new faith.
mnemonic: PROSELYTE = a convert; proselytize means 'make converts'.

definition: able to change shape or character easily
examples: The actor's protean talent allowed him to play a villain one year and a saint the next.
The protean landscape shifted its colors and shapes constantly with the changing of the seasons.
cloze: Her {{protean}} personality let her adapt to any social setting with ease.
mnemonic: PROTEUS, the Greek sea god who changed his shape.

definition: wise in planning for the future; thrifty
examples: A provident farmer, she stored grain for the lean winter months.
The provident couple saved part of every paycheck for emergencies.
cloze: His {{provident}} habit of saving each month rescued him when the factory closed.
mnemonic: PRO + VIDE (see): see ahead and provide.

definition: unsophisticated; narrow in outlook, or relating to a province
examples: His provincial attitudes made him wary of anything unfamiliar or foreign.
She felt out of place among the sophisticated crowd, ashamed of her provincial accent.
cloze: The critic dismissed the novel as {{provincial}}, interested only in its small, local world.
mnemonic: PROVINCE far from the capital: out of touch with the big city.

definition: arranged or accepted for now, subject to change
examples: A provisional government ruled the country until elections could be organized.
The offer is provisional on the results of your final exams.
cloze: They signed a {{provisional}} agreement, which will be replaced by a permanent contract next month.
mnemonic: PROVISION for now: a stopgap supply.

definition: acting with care and good judgment about the future
examples: It would be prudent to save a portion of your income every month for emergencies.
The prudent investor spreads her money across many different assets rather than risking it all on one.
cloze: Given the storm warning, it was {{prudent}} to postpone the picnic until the weekend.
mnemonic: PRUDENT: the PRUDE is careful; so is the prudent person.

definition: childishly silly and immature
examples: His puerile jokes turned what should have been a serious meeting into an embarrassing scene.
The senator's puerile insults lowered the tone of an otherwise thoughtful and well-prepared debate.
cloze: Adults found the film's {{puerile}} humor, full of burping and name-calling, tiresome.
mnemonic: PUERILE: 'puer' is Latin for boy — boyish.

definition: quick to quarrel or fight; combative
examples: The pugnacious boxer challenged everyone in the room to a match.
Her pugnacious attitude made even small disagreements turn into shouting matches.
cloze: The {{pugnacious}} candidate seemed to relish every chance to attack his opponents.
mnemonic: PUG dogs scrap — a PUGnacious person likes a fight.

definition: powerful; having great strength or influence
examples: The puissant king commanded armies that no neighbor dared to challenge.
Her puissant speeches could move a hall of skeptics to tears.
cloze: The tribe's most {{puissant}} warrior was feared across the whole river valley.
mnemonic: Sounds like 'pissant', but the opposite: POWERFUL (puissance).

definition: very careful about correct behavior and details
examples: The punctilious butler never allowed a single fork to be misplaced.
Her punctilious attention to detail made her an excellent proofreader.
cloze: The {{punctilious}} diplomat followed every point of protocol, even the most trivial.
mnemonic: PUNCTILIOUS: attention to every PUNCTUATION point.

definition: an expert who gives opinions publicly
examples: The TV pundit predicted a landslide victory.
Political pundits dissected the debate for days.
cloze: The financial {{pundit}} was widely quoted, though his predictions were seldom right.
mnemonic: PUNDIT: from Sanskrit for learned scholar - sounds like 'pun-DIT'.

definition: having a sharp, strong taste or smell; biting
examples: The pungent smell of fresh garlic frying in oil filled the entire kitchen.
His pungent criticism of the plan left no one in the room in doubt about his view.
cloze: The {{pungent}} odor from the chemical plant made residents close their windows.
mnemonic: PUNGENT: it PUNCHES your nose.

definition: to follow or chase in order to achieve or catch something
examples: She decided to pursue a doctorate in marine biology.
Predators such as cheetahs pursue their prey across open grassland.
cloze: Many young scientists {{pursue}} careers in research because of their curiosity about nature.
mnemonic: PURSUE: PURSE-u the money you want.

definition: lacking courage; timid
examples: The pusillanimous leader refused to take a stand on the controversial issue, fearing the public's reaction.
Critics called the senator pusillanimous for dodging the vote that everyone expected him to support.
cloze: The {{pusillanimous}} guard fled at the first sign of danger.
mnemonic: PUSILLANIMOUS: a PUSSY-ILL ANIMAL-ous spirit — a small, timid creature.

definition: generally supposed or believed to be so, though not proven
examples: The putative author of the anonymous letter has never admitted to writing a single word of it.
Police questioned the putative leader of the smuggling ring for several hours but had no proof.
cloze: The {{putative}} cause of the fire was faulty wiring, but investigators had yet to confirm it.
mnemonic: PUTATIVE: it is 'put' as such, but not proved.

definition: won at such great cost that it amounts to defeat
examples: The team's pyrrhic victory left half its players injured for the rest of the season.
It was a pyrrhic triumph: the lawsuit was won but the company went bankrupt.
cloze: The general's {{pyrrhic}} victory cost so many soldiers that he could not hold the conquered city.
mnemonic: King PYRRHUS won battles but lost his army.

definition: to drink heartily
examples: The sailors quaffed their ale in great gulps after the long and exhausting voyage across the ocean.
He quaffed the cool, clear water gratefully, since he had not had a drink all day.
cloze: The thirsty travelers {{quaffed}} the cold lemonade in a single gulp.
mnemonic: QUAFF: sounds like 'cough-down' — gulping a drink down.

definition: to shrink back in fear; to cower
examples: The prisoners quailed before the cruel guard's raised whip.
Even brave soldiers quailed at the sight of the enormous army.
cloze: The young witness began to {{quail}} under the lawyer's fierce cross-examination.
mnemonic: A QUAIL bird freezes and trembles in fear when startled.

definition: to limit or modify a statement; to make less absolute
examples: She qualified her praise by noting the film's weak ending.
The scientist qualified her claim, noting that the data were still incomplete.
cloze: He tried to {{qualify}} his promise with several conditions that weakened it.
mnemonic: QUALITY control: you adjust the quality of a claim.

definition: an uneasy feeling of doubt about whether an action is right
examples: He felt no qualm about lying to protect his friend.
She had serious qualms about signing a contract she had not read.
cloze: The manager had no {{qualm}} about firing employees who broke the safety rules.
mnemonic: QUALM sounds like 'calm' — it disturbs your calm.

definition: a state of perplexity over what to do
examples: She was in a quandary over whether to accept the job or stay in school.
The captain faced a quandary: either risk the storm or abandon the cargo.
cloze: Torn between two excellent offers, he found himself in a {{quandary}} with no clear way forward.
mnemonic: QUANDARY: 'which way — QUAN-DARE-y?' — you cannot decide which way.

definition: to put an end to; to suppress
examples: Police used tear gas and barricades to quell the riot before it could spread to the next neighborhood.
The calm announcement from the central bank helped quell fears of a sudden banking collapse.
cloze: The captain's firm voice was enough to {{quell}} the growing panic among the crew.
mnemonic: QUELL sounds like 'quiet and well': make it quiet.

definition: complaining in a whining manner
examples: The querulous patient found fault with every meal the hospital served.
Her querulous tone made even a simple request sound like an accusation.
cloze: The {{querulous}} neighbor called the landlord weekly to complain about trivial noises.
mnemonic: QUERULOUS sounds like 'quarrel' — always quarreling.

definition: to argue over small, unimportant points
examples: They quibbled over the bill for nearly half an hour.
Let's not quibble about wording when the major issues remain unsolved.
cloze: The lawyers continued to {{quibble}} over minor details while the main question went unanswered.
mnemonic: QUIBBLE: a QUICK BIT of arguing over nothing.

definition: in a state of quiet, rest, or inactivity
examples: The volcano has been quiescent for centuries, but scientists still monitor it.
After the busy season, the quiescent town settled into a long silence.
cloze: The seeds remain {{quiescent}} in the soil until the first rains arrive.
mnemonic: QUIESCENT: from QUIET.

definition: a clever, witty remark
examples: His quip about the weather made the whole room laugh.
She answered the hostile question with a sharp quip.
cloze: The host's {{quip}} lightened the tense mood at the dinner table.
mnemonic: A QUIP is a quick wit-clip, like a quick lip.

definition: an odd habit or peculiarity of behavior
examples: One of her quirks is eating dessert before dinner, which always surprises her guests at the table.
The old car had a quirk: it would only start on the second or third try.
cloze: Everyone tolerated his {{quirk}} of talking to the plants.
mnemonic: QUIRK: sounds like 'quirky'.

definition: a traitor who collaborates with an occupying enemy
examples: After the invasion, he was branded a quisling for helping the occupiers rule his own people.
History remembers the quisling who handed his country over to foreign troops.
cloze: The villagers shunned him as a {{quisling}} who had betrayed them to the enemy.
mnemonic: Named for Vidkun Quisling, the Norwegian who collaborated with Nazi occupiers.

definition: extremely idealistic and impractical
examples: His quixotic plan to end poverty with a single speech never got off the ground.
She admired his quixotic crusade, though she knew it would likely fail.
cloze: The {{quixotic}} inventor spent decades pursuing a machine that could never work.
mnemonic: DON QUIXOTE tilting at windmills.

definition: occurring every day; ordinary
examples: The novel captures the quotidian routines of small-town life: the morning bakery line and the evening walk.
His quotidian tasks included feeding the animals, repairing fences, and carrying water to the barn each day.
cloze: She tried to find beauty in the {{quotidian}} details of her daily commute.
mnemonic: QUOTIDIAN: 'Quote of the day' every day.

definition: a person skilled at telling stories
examples: The raconteur kept the guests laughing with tales of his travels.
As a raconteur, he could turn any trip into an epic.
cloze: The famous {{raconteur}} captivated the dinner party with story after story.
mnemonic: RACONTEUR - French raconter: to recount.

definition: carelessly unconventional, slightly disreputable in a charming way
examples: The raffish painter wore a ragged coat and a wide, mischievous grin.
The bar had a raffish charm, with mismatched chairs and a noisy crowd.
cloze: He cut a {{raffish}} figure, with his untidy hair and roguish smile.
mnemonic: RIFF-RAFF who are fun: raffish.

definition: a large number or amount of something
examples: The committee received a raft of complaints after the new policy was announced.
A raft of new regulations arrived on the manager's desk this morning.
cloze: The senator proposed a {{raft}} of reforms designed to overhaul the whole tax system.
mnemonic: A raft is floating in numbers: a RAFT of things piled together.
